3.8 Docker Networking Basics

By default, each container gets its own network namespace — it has its own IP address and can be isolated from or connected to other containers. Docker provides several network drivers for different use cases.

🌉 Docker Bridge Network — The Default
🌍 Host (Your Laptop/Server)
localhost:8000
🌉 Docker Bridge Network (172.17.0.0/16)
📦 anihpj-web (172.17.0.2:8000) ←→ 📦 postgres (172.17.0.3:5432) Containers can reach each other by IP or container name (DNS)
🔗 Port Mapping: -p 8000:8000
Host port 8000 → Container port 8000
Network DriverDescriptionUse Case
bridgeDefault. Isolated network on single host. Containers communicate via IP/DNS.Most common. All anihpj containers on one host.
hostContainer uses host's network directly. No isolation.Maximum performance, no port mapping needed. ⚠️ Less secure.
noneNo networking. Container is completely isolated.Security-sensitive batch jobs that need zero network access.
overlayMulti-host networking for Docker Swarm.Containers across multiple servers (covered in Ch 4 + K8s).
🔑 Port Mapping Syntax

-p [host_port]:[container_port] — Maps a port on the host to a port in the container.
Example: docker run -p 8080:8000 anihpj:v1 → access at http://localhost:8080 (even though Django runs on 8000 inside).

3.9 Docker Volumes — Persisting Data That Outlives Containers

Containers are ephemeral by design — when you stop and remove a container, all its data disappears. Volumes solve this by providing persistent storage that exists independently of any container.

💾 How Volumes Work
📦 Container (Ephemeral)
anihpj-app writes to /var/data PostgreSQL writes to /var/lib/postgresql/data
🔗 Mount Point
Container path → Volume (persistent)
💾 Volume (Persistent — Survives Container Restart/Removal)
postgres_data → /var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres_data/_data redis_data → /var/lib/docker/volumes/redis_data/_data
🔑 Bind Mounts vs Named Volumes
  • Bind Mount: Maps a specific host path to container path. -v /home/user/data:/app/data. Good for development (live code sync).
  • Named Volume: Docker manages the storage location. -v postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data. Good for production (portable, managed by Docker).
⚠️ DON'T Store Data in Containers!

If your PostgreSQL data is inside the container (not in a volume), running docker rm postgres-container will permanently delete your entire database. Always use volumes for any data that must persist — databases, file uploads, logs.

💡 RUN Chaining — The Layer Minimization Trick

Every RUN instruction creates a new image layer. Too many layers = bloated images. The fix? Chain commands with &&:

❌ Naive (3 layers)
RUN apt-get update RUN apt-get install -y gcc RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
✅ Optimized (1 layer)
RUN apt-get update && \ apt-get install -y gcc && \ rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Why does this matter? Three reasons: (1) Smaller image — fewer layer metadata entries. (2) Cleaner — temporary files (like apt cache) are removed IN THE SAME LAYER, so they're truly gone. If you delete in a separate RUN, the previous layer still has the files — they're just "hidden." (3) Faster pulls — fewer layers to download.

📊 Chapter 3 — Docker: Key Takeaways

🐳 What Docker Is

Platform for building, shipping, running containers. CLI + Daemon + Image format + Registry. Made containers accessible to everyone.

🏗️ Architecture

Client (CLI) → Daemon (dockerd) via REST API. Daemon manages images, containers, networks, volumes.

📝 Dockerfile

8 key instructions: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, CMD, ENTRYPOINT. Order matters for caching!

⚡ Layer Caching

Copy requirements first → install deps → copy code. Changes to code don't invalidate dependency cache.

🌐 Networking

Bridge (default, isolated), Host (no isolation), None (no network), Overlay (multi-host). Port mapping: -p host:container.

💾 Volumes

Persistent storage independent of containers. Bind mounts (dev) vs named volumes (prod). Databases MUST use volumes.

💼 Chapter 3 — In Daily Work

🛠️ Every Developer's Workflow

Write code → docker build → docker run → test locally → docker push → deploy. This is the standard CI/CD pipeline. Docker is the bridge between "works on my machine" and "works in production."

🧠 KCNA Context

The KCNA exam won't ask you to write Dockerfiles, but you must understand Docker concepts. Kubernetes builds on Docker: Pods wrap containers, Deployments manage container replicas, Services expose container ports — all concepts that originate in Docker.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 3
📝 Dockerfile

Blueprint for building images. FROM → WORKDIR → COPY → RUN → EXPOSE → CMD. Each instruction = 1 layer.

▶️ CMD vs ENTRYPOINT

CMD = default args (override by docker run cmd). ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable. Together: ENTRYPOINT is the binary, CMD is default args.

📋 .dockerignore

Excludes files from build context (node_modules, .git, __pycache__). Smaller context = faster builds. Like .gitignore for Docker.

🏗️ Multi-Stage

Multiple FROM statements. Stage 1: build (with compilers). Stage 2: runtime (copy only binary). Tiny production image.

📝 Chapter 3 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What are the three main components of Docker architecture?
Show Answer
Answer

Docker Client (CLI), Docker Daemon (dockerd), and Docker Registry. The client sends commands via REST API to the daemon, which pulls/pushes images from registries.

Explanation

The client-server architecture is fundamental — the CLI doesn't do the work, the daemon does.

Q2
Which Dockerfile instruction MUST be the first line of every Dockerfile?
Show Answer
Answer

FROM — it specifies the base image. Every Dockerfile must start with FROM (or an ARG before FROM in very specific cases).

Explanation

FROM defines the starting point. Common bases: python:3.11-slim, node:18-alpine, ubuntu:22.04.

Q3
What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer
Answer

CMD provides default arguments/commands that CAN be overridden at runtime. ENTRYPOINT sets a fixed command that is harder to override — CMD becomes arguments to ENTRYPOINT.

Explanation

If both are present: ENTRYPOINT is the executable, CMD provides default arguments. Example: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"] = python app.py by default, but you can override the file.

Q4
Why does COPY requirements.txt . before COPY . . make builds faster?
Show Answer
Answer

Layer caching. Requirements rarely change, so the COPY + RUN pip install layers are cached. Only code changes (COPY . .) trigger a rebuild, and it only rebuilds from that layer onward — dependency installation is skipped.

Explanation

This is the single most important Dockerfile optimization. It can reduce build time from minutes to seconds.

Q5
What does the EXPOSE instruction actually do in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer
Answer

It's documentation only. EXPOSE tells readers (and tools) which port the app listens on, but it does NOT actually publish the port. You need -p or --publish at runtime for that.

Explanation

This is a common KCNA trap. EXPOSE = documentation. -p 8000:8000 = actual port mapping.

Q6
Which Docker command opens an interactive shell inside a running container?
Show Answer
Answer

docker exec -it container-name /bin/bash (or /bin/sh for Alpine-based images). The -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a pseudo-TTY.

Explanation

docker exec runs a NEW command in a running container. docker run creates a NEW container.

Q7
What is the purpose of a .dockerignore file?
Show Answer
Answer

It excludes files from the Docker build context — similar to .gitignore. This makes builds faster (smaller context), more secure (no secrets), and prevents unnecessary cache invalidation.

Explanation

Key exclusions: .git, env/, __pycache__, .env, db.sqlite3, *.pyc — all files that don't belong in a production image.

Q8
In Docker networking, what does the -p 8080:8000 flag do?
Show Answer
Answer

It maps host port 8080 to container port 8000. External traffic to localhost:8080 is forwarded to port 8000 inside the container.

Explanation

Format: -p [host]:[container]. The container port is what the app listens on (EXPOSE documents this). The host port is what external users access.

Q9
Why should you always use Docker volumes for database containers?
Show Answer
Answer

Containers are ephemeral — when a container is removed, all data inside it is lost. Volumes provide persistent storage that exists independently of any container lifecycle.

Explanation

Without volumes: docker rm postgres = entire database gone forever. With volumes: data survives container removal and can be attached to a new container.

Q10
Does Kubernetes still use Docker as its container runtime?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Kubernetes deprecated dockershim in v1.20 and removed it in v1.24. K8s now uses containerd or CRI-O directly via the CRI interface. Docker-built images still work fine on K8s.

Explanation

This is a VERY common KCNA question. Docker images (OCI-compliant) work everywhere. Docker as a runtime is no longer used by K8s.

Chapter 4: Docker Compose — Running Multi-Container Apps

Real applications rarely run in a single container. anihpj needs a web server (Django), a database (PostgreSQL), and maybe a cache (Redis). Docker Compose lets you define and run all these containers as one coordinated application — with a single command. This chapter bridges Docker and Kubernetes, showing how Compose concepts map directly to K8s resources.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🛠️ Hands-On 🐳 Compose

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why most real applications need multiple containers working together
  • ✅ What Docker Compose is and how it simplifies multi-container management
  • ✅ The docker-compose.yml structure — services, volumes, networks, environment
  • ✅ How to write a complete docker-compose.yml for anihpj (web + db + redis)
  • ✅ Docker Compose vs Kubernetes — the concept mapping and when to use which
🎓 KCNA Relevance Container Orchestration 22% Cloud Native App Delivery 8%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 4
  • Compose vs K8s — Know the difference: Compose is for single-server dev/prototyping. Kubernetes is for multi-server production at scale.
  • Concept Mapping — The KCNA exam loves mapping questions: "Which K8s resource is equivalent to a Compose service?" Answer: Deployment + Service.
  • depends_on — Know that Compose has depends_on for startup ordering, but Kubernetes doesn't have an exact equivalent (it uses Init Containers and probes instead).
  • Service Discovery — In Compose, services discover each other by service name (DNS). In Kubernetes, Services provide discovery.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 4

Docker Compose is tested as the multi-container tool. 3 key questions:

  1. "What is Docker Compose used for?" — Defining and running MULTI-CONTAINER apps on a SINGLE host. NOT for multi-host orchestration (that's K8s). docker-compose.yml defines services, networks, volumes.
  2. "Docker Compose vs Kubernetes — what's the difference?" — Compose = single host, simple YAML, no auto-scaling, no self-healing. K8s = multi-node cluster, declarative, auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates. Compose is for local dev; K8s is for production.
  3. "What happens with docker compose up?" — Reads docker-compose.yml → creates networks → creates volumes → starts containers in dependency order → attaches to logs. docker compose down tears everything down.

4.1 Why Multi-Container Apps?

Most real-world applications are composed of multiple services, each running in its own container. This is the microservices philosophy — each service does one thing well.

🏗️ anihpj — A Typical Multi-Service Architecture
🌐 Web Layer
Django App (anihpj) jobpost App REST API on Port 8000 Serves HTTP requests, HTML, JSON
🗄️ Data Layer
PostgreSQL 15 (Port 5432) Stores: Users, JobPosts, Skills, Locations Persistent volume for data safety
⚡ Cache Layer (Optional)
Redis 7 (Port 6379) Session storage, rate limiting, caching Makes repeated queries lightning fast
Each layer runs in its own container. They communicate over a shared Docker network. Compose manages them as one unit.
🤔 Why Not One Big Container?

You COULD put Django + PostgreSQL + Redis all in one container — but that violates container best practices (one process per container). It also means you can't scale services independently, update one without restarting all, or replace PostgreSQL with MySQL without rebuilding everything. Separate containers = separate lifecycles = flexibility.

4.2 What is Docker Compose?

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. You describe your entire application stack in a single YAML file, and Compose starts, stops, and manages everything together.

📋 Docker Compose Definition

Docker Compose is a tool that allows you to define and run multi-container Docker applications. Using a YAML file (docker-compose.yml), you configure all your application's services, networks, and volumes — then create and start them with a single command: docker compose up.

🎯 The Compose Promise — One Command Does Everything
📄
1 YAML File

docker-compose.yml defines web + db + redis

→
⚡
1 Command

docker compose up -d

→
📦
3 Containers

All services running, networked together

→
🌍
1 App

http://localhost:8000/jobs/ — fully functional!

🔑 Essential Compose Commands
  • docker compose up — Start all services (foreground, shows logs)
  • docker compose up -d — Start all services (detached/background)
  • docker compose down — Stop and remove all containers, networks
  • docker compose down -v — Also remove volumes (⚠️ deletes data!)
  • docker compose ps — List all services and their status
  • docker compose logs -f — Follow logs from all services
  • docker compose build — Rebuild all service images
  • docker compose restart web — Restart a specific service

4.3 docker-compose.yml — The Structure

A docker-compose.yml file has a clean, logical structure. Let's break down each section and what it does.

Top-Level KeyPurposeExample
versionCompose file format versionversion: '3.8' (optional in newer Compose)
servicesContainer definitions (THE main section)web:, db:, redis:
volumesNamed volumes for persistent datapostgres_data: (declared, then referenced in services)
networksCustom networks (optional, Compose creates default)anihpj_net: (explicit network config)
Service KeyPurposeKCNA Equivalent
image / buildPre-built image OR build from DockerfileDeployment's spec.containers.image
portsMap host:container portsService (K8s Service, different concept)
environmentSet environment variablesConfigMap / Secret
volumesMount volumes into containerPersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim
depends_onStartup ordering (start db before web)Init Containers / Startup Probes (no exact equivalent!)
restartRestart policyPod's restartPolicy
networksWhich networks to joinCNI plugins (Calico, Flannel, Cilium)
🔑 Service Discovery in Compose

Compose automatically creates a default network for your app. Each service can reach any other service by its service name as a DNS hostname. Example: The web service connects to PostgreSQL at db:5432 — just use the service name! No IP addresses needed.

4.4 Docker Compose for anihpj — Full Example

Here's the complete docker-compose.yml for anihpj with 3 services: web (Django), db (PostgreSQL), and redis (cache).

🏗️ anihpj Compose Architecture — 3 Containers, 1 Network
🌐 Compose Network (anihpj_default — auto-created)
🐍 web (Django) :8000 — DNS: web 🗄️ db (PostgreSQL 15) :5432 — DNS: db ⚡ redis (Redis 7) :6379 — DNS: redis
🔗 Service Communication (DNS-Based)
web → db:5432 (DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj:password@db:5432/anihpj) web → redis:6379 (REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0)
💾 Persistent Storage
postgres_data volume → /var/lib/postgresql/data (database files survive restart) redis_data volume → /data (cache survives restart)
📄 Complete docker-compose.yml for anihpj
version: '3.8'

services:
  # ---- Django Web Application ----
  web:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: anihpj-web
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj:securepassword@db:5432/anihpj
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
      - SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY:-dev-secret-key}
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/staticfiles

  # ---- PostgreSQL Database ----
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-db
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=anihpj
      - POSTGRES_USER=anihpj
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=securepassword
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj -d anihpj"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ---- Redis Cache ----
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-redis
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:
  static_volume:
🚀 Running the Stack
# Start everything
$ docker compose up -d
[+] Running 3/3
 ✔ Container anihpj-redis  Started
 ✔ Container anihpj-db     Healthy
 ✔ Container anihpj-web    Started

# Verify
$ docker compose ps
NAME            STATUS    PORTS
anihpj-web      running   0.0.0.0:8000->8000/tcp
anihpj-db       healthy   0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp
anihpj-redis    running   0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp

# Run migrations
$ docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate

# Access → http://localhost:8000/jobs/ ✅

# Stop everything
$ docker compose down

4.5 Docker Compose vs Kubernetes — The Concept Bridge

This section is where Docker Compose knowledge directly translates to Kubernetes understanding. Many Compose concepts have near-equivalents in K8s — understanding this mapping is key to the KCNA exam.

Docker ComposeKubernetesNotes
docker-compose.ymlMultiple YAML files (Deployment + Service + ConfigMap + PVC)Compose = 1 file. K8s = many files (or Helm chart).
services.webDeployment + ServiceK8s separates compute (Deployment) from networking (Service).
ports: "8000:8000"Service (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer)K8s has 4 service types with different exposure levels.
environment:ConfigMap + SecretK8s separates config from pod specs — better security.
volumes:PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaimK8s needs a PVC to "claim" storage from a PV.
depends_on:Init Containers / Startup ProbesK8s has NO direct depends_on equivalent! ⚠️
networks:CNI Plugin (Calico, Flannel, Cilium)K8s networking is plugin-based — more flexible but more complex.
restart: alwaysrestartPolicy: Always (default for Pods)K8s auto-restarts by default. Compose needs explicit config.
Service name DNSService DNS (service.namespace.svc.cluster.local)Both use DNS for discovery. K8s DNS is richer.
Single hostMultiple hosts (cluster)Compose = 1 server. K8s = many servers working together.
🧭 Decision Framework: Compose or Kubernetes?
🐳 Use Docker Compose When...
  • ✅ Single server deployment
  • ✅ Development and testing environments
  • ✅ Quick prototyping and demos
  • ✅ Learning containers and orchestration basics
  • ✅ Simple setups — one YAML file, one command
  • ✅ CI/CD pipelines (integration tests)
  • ✅ Small projects with predictable traffic
☸️ Use Kubernetes When...
  • ✅ Multiple servers needed (cluster)
  • ✅ Production at scale (100+ containers)
  • ✅ Auto-scaling required (traffic spikes)
  • ✅ Self-healing needed (auto-restart, auto-reschedule)
  • ✅ Rolling updates with zero downtime
  • ✅ Multi-cloud or hybrid deployments
  • ✅ Complex networking (service mesh, ingress)
🔄 The Typical Journey

Most projects start with Docker Compose for development and graduate to Kubernetes for production. This is a completely natural progression:

Phase 1
Docker

Containerize individual services

Phase 2
Docker Compose

Run multi-container apps locally + CI

Phase 3
Kubernetes

Deploy to production with scaling, self-healing, rolling updates

📊 Chapter 4 — Docker Compose: Key Takeaways

🎯 What Compose Is

Tool for defining and running multi-container apps. One YAML file, one command (docker compose up), all services running.

📝 YAML Structure

services (container defs), volumes (persistent storage), networks (comms). Service config: image/build, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on.

🔗 Service Discovery

Services reach each other by DNS name (service name = hostname). web connects to db at db:5432. No IPs needed.

☸️ Compose → K8s

Compose service → Deployment+Service. environment → ConfigMap/Secret. volumes → PVC. depends_on → Init Containers.

⚖️ When to Use

Compose: dev, testing, single-server, learning. Kubernetes: production, multi-server, auto-scaling, self-healing, zero-downtime.

🔄 Journey

Docker → Docker Compose → Kubernetes. Each step adds orchestration power for larger, more demanding deployments.

💼 Chapter 4 — In Daily Work

🛠️ Development Workflow with anihpj

docker compose up starts your entire stack in seconds. Make code changes → rebuild with docker compose build → docker compose up -d. New team members clone the repo and run docker compose up — no manual setup, no "works on my machine."

🧠 KCNA Context

Docker Compose is the conceptual bridge to Kubernetes. Understanding Compose services prepares you for K8s Deployments and Services. Understanding Compose volumes prepares you for PVCs. Understanding Compose networking prepares you for K8s Services and CNI.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 4
📄 docker-compose.yml

Declarative YAML defining services, networks, volumes for multi-container apps. Single host only — not for multi-node orchestration.

🔗 Service Discovery

Compose auto-creates a default network. Containers reach each other by SERVICE NAME (not IP). DNS resolution built-in.

📊 Compose vs K8s

Compose = single host, dev/test, simple. K8s = multi-node cluster, production, auto-scaling, self-healing. Different tools, different purposes.

🔄 docker compose up

Reads YAML → creates networks → creates volumes → starts containers in dependency order. docker compose down tears everything down.

📝 Chapter 4 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What is Docker Compose primarily used for?
Show Answer
Answer

Defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a single YAML file (docker-compose.yml) that configures all services, networks, and volumes.

Explanation

Compose is for multi-container apps on a single host. For multi-host orchestration, you use Kubernetes.

Q2
In a docker-compose.yml file, which top-level key defines the container configurations?
Show Answer
Answer

services — this is the main section where you define each container, its image, ports, environment variables, volumes, and other settings.

Explanation

The other top-level keys are version, volumes, and networks.

Q3
How do services in Docker Compose discover and communicate with each other?
Show Answer
Answer

By service name as a DNS hostname. Compose creates a default network where each service can reach any other service using its service name — e.g., the web service connects to PostgreSQL at db:5432.

Explanation

This is the same pattern Kubernetes uses — Service DNS. In K8s it's service.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

Q4
What does the depends_on key do in a Compose service definition?
Show Answer
Answer

It controls startup ordering — services listed in depends_on are started before the dependent service. However, it does NOT wait for the service to be "ready" (e.g., PostgreSQL accepting connections) unless combined with healthchecks.

Explanation

Kubernetes does NOT have a direct depends_on equivalent. It uses Init Containers and startup probes instead.

Q5
Which Kubernetes resource is the closest equivalent to a Docker Compose service definition?
Show Answer
Answer

A Deployment (for the container spec) combined with a Service (for networking/ports). K8s separates compute and networking into different resources.

Explanation

In Compose, one service block covers both the container and its port mapping. In K8s, these are separate: Deployment for the Pod template, Service for port exposure.

Q6
What is the Kubernetes equivalent of Compose's environment variables?
Show Answer
Answer

ConfigMap (for non-sensitive configuration) and Secret (for sensitive data like passwords). K8s separates configuration from the Pod specification.

Explanation

This separation is a key K8s design principle — you can update a ConfigMap without rebuilding your container image.

Q7
When should you use Docker Compose instead of Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Use Compose for single-server deployments, development/testing, quick prototyping, and learning. Use Kubernetes for multi-server, production-at-scale, auto-scaling, and self-healing deployments.

Explanation

Compose = simplicity and speed. Kubernetes = power and scale. Start with Compose, graduate to K8s when you need it.

Q8
What command stops and removes all containers, networks, and (optionally) volumes defined in a docker-compose.yml?
Show Answer
Answer

docker compose down. Add -v to also remove named volumes (⚠️ this deletes your data!).

Explanation

docker compose stop only stops containers (doesn't remove them). docker compose down cleans up everything.

Q9
How does Docker Compose handle persistent data storage for databases?
Show Answer
Answer

Through named volumes declared in the top-level volumes: section and mounted into service containers. Volumes persist data even when containers are removed.

Explanation

Without volumes, docker compose down would delete your database. With volumes, data survives across container restarts and removals.

Q10
A team has a Django app with PostgreSQL and Redis. They deploy to a single cloud VM for their staging environment. Which tool is most appropriate?
Show Answer
Answer

Docker Compose. For a single-server deployment (staging, dev, or small production), Compose provides the right balance of simplicity and capability. Kubernetes would be overkill for a single VM.

Explanation

KCNA expects you to match the tool to the scenario. Single server + multi-container = Compose. Multi-server + scale = Kubernetes.

Chapter 5: Kubernetes — What It Is and What It Does

You've learned containers and Docker. Now meet Kubernetes — the platform that takes containers from "running on my laptop" to "running at global scale." This chapter explains what Kubernetes IS, where it came from, what it can do, and — just as importantly — what it CANNOT do. By the end, you'll understand why K8s is the most important cloud native technology ever created.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Concepts ☸️ K8s Core

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The origin story: How Google Borg became Kubernetes (and what "K8s" means)
  • ✅ Kubernetes defined simply — the "orchestra conductor" analogy
  • ✅ The 8 superpowers that make Kubernetes indispensable
  • ✅ What Kubernetes is NOT — 5 common myths debunked
  • ✅ K8s vs Docker Compose vs Docker Swarm — the complexity spectrum
  • ✅ The K8s ecosystem — Prometheus, Helm, Istio, ArgoCD and beyond
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Cloud Native Architecture 16%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 5
  • K8s Origin — Know that K8s originated from Google Borg (not Docker!). It was donated to CNCF in 2015.
  • Declarative Model — The #1 concept: you declare desired state, K8s reconciles to make it happen. This appears in MANY exam questions.
  • What K8s is NOT — The exam LOVES to ask "Which of these does Kubernetes NOT do?" Know the 5 things K8s doesn't handle.
  • 8 Superpowers — Be able to list and explain them. Expect scenario questions: "A pod crashes. What K8s feature handles this?"
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 5

These 5 Kubernetes fundamentals questions are the backbone of the 46% domain:

  1. "Where did Kubernetes come from?" — Google Borg (internal system running Search/Gmail/YouTube for 15+ years). Donated to CNCF in 2015. Written in Go. NOT from Docker Inc.
  2. "What does 'Kubernetes' mean and what does 'K8s' stand for?" — Greek for "helmsman" or "pilot." K8s = "K" + 8 letters (ubernete) + "s" — a numeronym.
  3. "What is declarative configuration?" — You declare the DESIRED state ("I want 3 replicas of anihpj"), K8s RECONCILES to make it happen. Contrast with imperative ("do this, then this, then this").
  4. "What are the 8 K8s superpowers?" — Service Discovery, Load Balancing, Storage Orchestration, Automated Rollouts/Rollbacks, Self-Healing, Secret/Config Management, Horizontal Scaling, Batch Execution. Expect scenario matching questions.
  5. "What does Kubernetes NOT do?" — No source code building (CI), no logging/monitoring solution (plugs in Prometheus/Fluentd), no application-level services (message queues, databases), no machine configuration. K8s is a PLATFORM, not a PaaS.

5.1 The Origin Story: From Google Borg to Kubernetes

Kubernetes wasn't invented in a vacuum. It's the open-source descendant of Borg — Google's secret internal container orchestration system that has been running Google Search, Gmail, Maps, and YouTube for nearly two decades.

📜 The Kubernetes Origin Timeline
2003
Borg Created

Google builds Borg internally. Manages billions of containers across millions of machines. Kept secret for a decade.

2013
Docker Released

Docker makes containers mainstream. Suddenly, the world wants what Google has.

2014
Kubernetes v0.1

Google open-sources Kubernetes. Name: Greek for "helmsman" (κυβερνήτης). K8s = K + 8 letters + s.

2015
CNCF Founded

Google donates K8s to the new Cloud Native Computing Foundation. K8s v1.0 released.

2017
Market Dominance

K8s defeats Docker Swarm and Mesos. Becomes the de facto standard for container orchestration.

Today
Universal Platform

K8s runs on every major cloud, on-prem, and edge. 96% of organizations use or evaluate K8s.

📖 Why "Kubernetes"?

Kubernetes (κυβερνήτης) is Greek for "helmsman" or "pilot" — the person who steers a ship. The logo is a ship's wheel (☸). This is intentional: Kubernetes steers your container fleet, just as a helmsman steers a ship.

K8s is a numeronym: "K" + 8 letters (ubernete) + "s". Same pattern as i18n (internationalization), l10n (localization), a11y (accessibility).

🔬 Why Google Open-Sourced Kubernetes (When They Didn't Have To)

Google had Borg — a battle-tested, decade-old system that ran everything from Search to Gmail. They could have kept Kubernetes proprietary and sold it as a service. Instead, they open-sourced it and donated it to a new foundation (CNCF). Why?

  • AWS Threat: Amazon was dominating cloud with AWS. Google needed developers to build cloud-native apps that could run ANYWHERE — not just on AWS's proprietary services. An open-source standard for container orchestration meant apps built for K8s could run on Google Cloud, AWS, Azure, or on-prem.
  • Standard Wins: Google learned from Borg that a proprietary system limits innovation. By making K8s the universal standard, the entire industry builds tools (Helm, Prometheus, Istio) that work with Google's platform.
  • Talent & Innovation: Open-sourcing K8s attracted thousands of contributors — far more than Google could hire. Today, K8s has contributions from 3,000+ companies. Google benefits from all that free innovation.

KCNA Context: This is why CNCF exists — to ensure no single company controls cloud native technology. K8s became the "Linux of the cloud" — an open standard that leveled the playing field.

5.2 Kubernetes Defined (Simply)

📋 Official Definition

Kubernetes is an open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It groups containers into logical units for easy management and discovery.

🎻 The Orchestra Conductor Analogy
🎼 You (The Composer)
You write the score (YAML): "I want 3 violins (anihpj pods), 2 cellos (PostgreSQL), 1 timpani (Redis)"
🎻 Kubernetes (The Conductor)
Reads your score, directs musicians (containers), keeps tempo (health checks), replaces tired musicians (restarts), adds more if audience grows (scaling)
🎵 The Orchestra (Your Application)
All containers playing together in harmony, producing beautiful music (your app serving users)
🔄 The Declarative Model — Kubernetes' Secret Sauce
📝
You DECLARE

"I want 3 replicas of anihpj:v2 running on port 8000"

→
👁️
K8s OBSERVES

"Currently 2 anihpj pods are running"

→
⚖️
K8s COMPARES

"Desired=3, Actual=2 → DIFFERENCE!"

→
🔧
K8s ACTS

"Create 1 more pod to reach desired state"

→
🔄
REPEATS FOREVER

This loop runs continuously — this is WHY K8s self-heals!

This reconciliation loop is the SINGLE most important concept in Kubernetes. Every controller, every operator, every K8s component follows this pattern: Observe → Compare → Act → Repeat.
🔑 Imperative vs Declarative — The Mindset Shift

Imperative (the old way): "SSH into server 3, run docker start anihpj, then edit nginx.conf, then restart nginx." You specify HOW to achieve the state, step by step.

Declarative (the K8s way): "I want 3 healthy anihpj pods exposed on port 8000 with a load balancer." You specify WHAT you want. K8s figures out HOW.

This is the fundamental mental model shift when moving to Kubernetes. You stop being a server administrator and become a cluster composer — you describe the desired symphony, and K8s conducts it.

5.3 The 8 Superpowers of Kubernetes

Why do millions of developers and thousands of companies use Kubernetes? These 8 capabilities make it indispensable for running containers at scale.

💚 1. Self-Healing

Pod crashes? K8s restarts it. Node dies? K8s reschedules pods to healthy nodes. Container is unhealthy? K8s kills and replaces it. Users never notice.

📈 2. Auto-Scaling

Traffic spikes? HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) adds more pods. Traffic drops? HPA removes pods to save resources. Can also scale nodes (Cluster Autoscaler).

⚖️ 3. Load Balancing

Traffic is automatically distributed across all healthy pods. No need for external load balancers — K8s Services handle it natively.

🔄 4. Rollouts & Rollbacks

Deploy new versions gradually (rolling update). If something breaks, roll back instantly. Zero downtime. Users never see a broken app.

🌐 5. Service Discovery

Pods find each other by DNS name. No hardcoded IPs. anihpj-web reaches PostgreSQL at postgres-service:5432 — always.

🔐 6. Secret & Config Management

ConfigMaps for settings, Secrets for passwords/keys. Update config without rebuilding images. Secrets are encrypted at rest.

💾 7. Storage Orchestration

Auto-mount cloud disks (AWS EBS, GCP PD, Azure Disk) or network storage (NFS, Ceph). Pods travel between nodes and their storage follows.

⏰ 8. Batch Execution

Run one-off Jobs (database migration, report generation) and CronJobs (nightly backups, hourly cleanup). K8s manages the lifecycle.

5.4 What Kubernetes is NOT — 5 Common Myths

This is a favorite KCNA exam topic. Kubernetes is powerful, but it's NOT everything. Knowing what K8s DOESN'T do is just as important as knowing what it does.

❌ NOT a PaaS

Kubernetes doesn't hide infrastructure. You still manage nodes, networking, and upgrades. It's infrastructure-as-a-platform, not a fully-managed service (unless you use managed K8s like EKS/GKE/AKS).

❌ NOT a CI/CD System

K8s doesn't build your code, run tests, or push images. It integrates WITH CI/CD tools (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, ArgoCD) but isn't one itself.

❌ NOT a Docker Replacement

Kubernetes orchestrates containers — it doesn't build them. Docker (or Podman, Buildah) still builds your images. K8s just runs them at scale.

❌ Doesn't Build Code

K8s expects ready-to-run container images. It won't compile your Go code, install your npm packages, or run your pip install. That happens in CI.

❌ No Built-in Logging/Monitoring

K8s provides building blocks (metrics API, log aggregation API) but not the full solution. You need Prometheus+Grafana for monitoring, EFK/Loki for logging — these are add-ons.

5.5 Kubernetes vs Docker Compose vs Docker Swarm

You've learned Docker Compose. Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in orchestrator (simpler than K8s). Where does each fit?

📊 The Orchestration Complexity Spectrum

Learning Curve🟢 Low🟡 Medium🔴 Steep

5.6 The Kubernetes Ecosystem at a Glance

Kubernetes itself is a platform — but its real power comes from the ecosystem of tools that extend it. Think of K8s as the kernel of an operating system, and these tools as the applications.

📖 For KCNA: You need to KNOW these tools exist, not master them

The KCNA exam expects you to recognize the major CNCF projects and what category they belong to. You don't need to know how to configure Istio or write PromQL queries — just know that Prometheus = monitoring, Helm = package manager, Istio = service mesh, ArgoCD = GitOps.

📅 Kubernetes Release Cycle — What KCNA Expects You to Know

Kubernetes releases 3 minor versions per year (roughly every 4 months). Each version follows a predictable lifecycle:

  • Alpha (12 weeks): New features added. Disabled by default. Feature gates control access. Unstable — may change or be removed.
  • Beta (12 weeks): Features enabled by default. API is stable enough for testing. May still change but unlikely to be removed.
  • Stable/GA: Feature is production-ready. API is permanent. Available in the main API group.
  • Deprecated: Feature will be removed in a future release. Warning in logs. Migration path provided.

Support Window: Each minor version is supported for approximately 14 months (the current release + 2 previous releases). You should upgrade your cluster at least once per year to stay on a supported version.

KCNA Tip: The exam may ask about the K8s release cycle and support policy. Know that K8s has 3 releases/year and each is supported for ~14 months. Also know that dockershim was deprecated in v1.20 and removed in v1.24 — this is a common exam question.

5.6 kubeadm — How Kubernetes Clusters Are Created

While the KCNA exam doesn't test cluster installation, you should understand how clusters come into existence. kubeadm is the official tool for bootstrapping Kubernetes clusters — it's how most production and development clusters are created.

🔧 kubeadm — What It Does (Two Phases)
Phase 1: init (Control Plane)

kubeadm init on the first node: generates certificates (for TLS), starts kube-apiserver + etcd + controller-manager + scheduler as static pods, uploads config to etcd, generates bootstrap token for worker join, outputs kubeadm join command.

Phase 2: join (Worker Nodes)

kubeadm join on each worker: uses bootstrap token to authenticate to API Server, receives cluster CA certificate, starts kubelet + kube-proxy, node registers itself in the cluster. After join: install CNI plugin (Calico/Flannel) to enable networking.

🔑 Key kubeadm Facts for KCNA
  • kubeadm is NOT for production management — it only handles cluster creation (init/join) and upgrades (kubeadm upgrade). Day-to-day operations use kubectl.
  • Control plane components run as STATIC PODS — kubelet reads YAML from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and runs them directly. They are NOT Deployments — they're managed by kubelet, not the control plane itself.
  • kubeadm uses etcd by default — but can be configured to use an external etcd cluster for HA. This is the recommended production setup.
  • After kubeadm init, you MUST install a CNI plugin — without it, CoreDNS stays Pending and pods can't communicate across nodes. kubeadm does NOT install networking.
  • kubeadm token — The bootstrap token used for worker join expires after 24 hours by default. Use kubeadm token create --print-join-command to generate a new one.
💡 Managed Kubernetes vs kubeadm — What KCNA Expects

In real life, most teams use managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE) where the cloud provider runs the control plane. kubeadm is for self-managed clusters (on-premises or on VMs). KCNA tests awareness of both approaches:

  • Managed (EKS/AKS/GKE): Cloud provider handles control plane, upgrades, etcd backups. You manage worker nodes + workloads. Easier, but less control.
  • Self-managed (kubeadm): You control everything. Full flexibility, but you're responsible for etcd backup, control plane HA, upgrades, security patches.
🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam may ask "Which tool is used to bootstrap a Kubernetes cluster?" — Answer: kubeadm. Or "Where do control plane pods come from in a kubeadm cluster?" — Answer: They are static pods managed by kubelet, not Deployments. Know that kubeadm focuses on cluster lifecycle (init, join, upgrade, reset).

📊 Chapter 5 — Kubernetes: Key Takeaways

📜 Origin

Born from Google Borg (2003). Open-sourced 2014. Donated to CNCF 2015. Name = Greek "helmsman." K8s = numeronym.

🎯 Definition

Open-source container orchestration. You declare desired state, K8s continuously reconciles to make it reality.

💚 8 Superpowers

Self-healing, auto-scaling, load balancing, rolling updates, service discovery, secrets/config, storage orchestration, batch execution.

❌ NOT

Not a PaaS, not CI/CD, not Docker replacement, doesn't build code, no built-in logging/monitoring.

⚖️ vs Others

Compose = single server (dev). Swarm = small clusters (simpler). K8s = any scale (enterprise standard).

🌍 Ecosystem

Prometheus, Helm, Istio, ArgoCD, Falco, Rook — tools that make K8s a complete platform.

💼 Chapter 5 — In Daily Work

🛠️ Operational Mindset

You write YAML that declares what you want. You kubectl apply it. K8s makes it happen. When something breaks, you don't SSH into servers — you check kubectl describe and kubectl logs. The declarative mindset is the foundation of all K8s operations.

🧠 KCNA Context

This chapter covers 46% of the KCNA exam (Kubernetes Fundamentals domain). Every concept here — declarative model, reconciliation, self-healing, scaling — will appear in multiple questions. Master this chapter, and you've mastered nearly half the exam.

5.7 API Versioning — Alpha, Beta, Stable

Kubernetes uses a structured API versioning system to manage feature maturity. Understanding this system helps you know which API versions are safe for production and what happens when APIs change — a topic tested on KCNA.

📊 Kubernetes API Versioning — Three Stability Levels
LevelVersion PatternEnabled by Default?Production Safe?Can Be Removed?
Alphav1alpha1, v2alpha2❌ No — must enable feature gate❌ No — bugs expected✅ Yes, any release, no notice
Betav1beta1, v2beta3⚠️ Yes (since K8s 1.22)⚠️ Not recommended✅ Yes, after 9 months / 3 releases
Stable (GA)v1, v2✅ Yes — always available✅ Yes — fully supported❌ No — remains for the entire major version
🔑 API Groups — Core vs Named
  • Core (legacy) group: REST path /api/v1. apiVersion: just v1. Contains Pod, Service, Node, Namespace, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, etc.
  • Named groups: REST path /apis/$GROUP/$VERSION. apiVersion: $GROUP/$VERSION. Examples: apps/v1 (Deployment, StatefulSet), batch/v1 (Job, CronJob), networking.k8s.io/v1 (NetworkPolicy, Ingress)
⚠️ KCNA Exam Alert: dockershim Deprecation

The KCNA exam tests awareness of the dockershim deprecation timeline: deprecated in K8s v1.20, removed in K8s v1.24. This is the most famous API deprecation in K8s history. After v1.24, K8s uses containerd directly via CRI. If you see "Docker Engine" as a K8s runtime in an answer choice, it's wrong — unless the question specifically references pre-v1.24 clusters.

🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam may ask "Which API version should you use for production?" — Answer: Stable/GA (e.g., apps/v1). Or "What happens when a beta API is deprecated?" — It continues to work for 9 months/3 releases, then is removed. Know that alpha APIs are disabled by default and can disappear without notice.
🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 5
☸️ Kubernetes

Greek for "helmsman." Open-source container orchestration. Originated from Google Borg. Donated to CNCF in 2015. Written in Go.

📜 Declarative

You declare DESIRED state ("3 replicas of anihpj"). K8s RECONCILES to make it happen. NOT imperative ("do this, then this").

🔄 Self-Healing

Pod crashes → automatically replaced. Node fails → pods rescheduled. Health checks fail → restarted. All automatic.

🚫 NOT a PaaS

K8s doesn't build code, doesn't provide logging/monitoring, doesn't provide application-level services. It's an orchestration PLATFORM.

📝 Chapter 5 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
Kubernetes was originally developed by which company, based on which internal system?
Show Answer
Answer

Google, based on Borg. Google ran containers at massive scale with Borg for over a decade before open-sourcing Kubernetes in 2014.

Explanation

This is a classic KCNA origin question. Kubernetes = open-source version of Google Borg.

Q2
What does the name "Kubernetes" mean, and why is it abbreviated as "K8s"?
Show Answer
Answer

Greek for "helmsman" or "pilot" — the person who steers a ship. K8s is a numeronym: K + 8 letters + s.

Explanation

The ship's wheel logo (☸) and the name both reference the idea of steering/guiding — Kubernetes steers your container fleet.

Q3
What is the "reconciliation loop" in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A continuous cycle where K8s observes the current state, compares it to the desired state, and takes action to eliminate any difference. This loop runs forever — it's why K8s self-heals.

Explanation

Pattern: Observe → Compare → Act → Repeat. Every K8s controller follows this. This is the single most important K8s concept.

Q4
Which of the following is NOT a Kubernetes superpower?
Show Answer
Answer

Building container images. K8s orchestrates running containers but does not build them. Image building happens in CI/CD with tools like Docker, Podman, or Buildah.

Explanation

The 8 superpowers are: self-healing, auto-scaling, load balancing, rolling updates, service discovery, secrets/config, storage orchestration, batch execution.

Q5
A pod crashes. What Kubernetes feature automatically replaces it?
Show Answer
Answer

Self-healing. K8s detects the crashed pod and automatically creates a replacement to maintain the desired number of replicas.

Explanation

This is the reconciliation loop in action. The Deployment controller sees actual replicas < desired replicas and creates a new pod.

Q6
Is Kubernetes a Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Kubernetes is not a PaaS. You still manage nodes, networking, and cluster upgrades. It's infrastructure-level orchestration, not a fully-managed platform.

Explanation

Managed K8s services (EKS, GKE, AKS) are closer to PaaS, but raw K8s is not. This is a classic KCNA "what K8s is NOT" question.

Q7
Which tool is used for monitoring Kubernetes clusters and is a CNCF Graduated project?
Show Answer
Answer

Prometheus. It's the de facto standard for K8s monitoring and metrics collection. Grafana is commonly used for dashboards on top of Prometheus.

Explanation

KCNA expects you to know major CNCF projects by category: Prometheus=monitoring, Helm=package manager, Istio=service mesh, ArgoCD=GitOps.

Q8
What is the key difference between imperative and declarative approaches in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Imperative: you specify HOW (step-by-step commands). Declarative: you specify WHAT (desired state in YAML), and K8s figures out HOW to achieve it.

Explanation

The declarative approach enables self-healing — if reality drifts from the declaration, K8s automatically corrects it.

Q9
Which Kubernetes feature allows you to deploy a new application version with zero downtime?
Show Answer
Answer

Rolling Updates. K8s gradually replaces old pods with new ones, ensuring some pods are always available to serve traffic.

Explanation

Combined with rollbacks, this gives you safe deployments — deploy new version, monitor, roll back instantly if needed.

Q10
A team needs to orchestrate containers across 50 servers with auto-scaling and self-healing. Which tool is most appropriate?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes. Docker Compose only works on a single server. Docker Swarm can handle small clusters but lacks the ecosystem and enterprise features of K8s. For 50 servers with auto-scaling, K8s is the clear choice.

Explanation

KCNA expects you to match tools to scenarios: Compose=1 server, Swarm=small clusters, K8s=any scale.

Chapter 6: kubectl — Your Window into Kubernetes

kubectl (pronounced "cube-cuttle" or "cube-control") is your primary tool for interacting with Kubernetes. Every command, every query, every deployment goes through kubectl. If K8s is a ship, kubectl is the helm. This chapter teaches you the essential commands you'll use every single day — and the ones you'll need for the KCNA exam.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🛠️ Hands-On ⌨️ CLI

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What kubectl is and how it communicates with the K8s API server
  • ✅ 15+ essential kubectl commands organized by function
  • ✅ kubectl get — the most-used command, with all output formats
  • ✅ kubectl describe — when you need detailed debugging information
  • ✅ kubectl logs and exec — your debugging toolkit
  • ✅ kubectl explain — your built-in documentation (no internet needed!)
  • ✅ Contexts and namespaces — targeting the right cluster and namespace
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 6
  • kubectl explain — You can use this during the KCNA exam! There's no internet access, but kubectl explain works offline. Know how to use it to look up resource fields.
  • Command Categories — Know which command to use for which task: get (list), describe (details), logs (output), exec (shell), apply (deploy), delete (remove).
  • Output Formats — -o wide, -o yaml, -o json are frequently tested.
  • Namespaces — Know the default namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 6

kubectl is your primary interface. These 4 questions test your CLI knowledge:

  1. "What does kubectl talk to?" — kubectl talks ONLY to the API Server. It NEVER talks directly to nodes, pods, or etcd. The API Server handles authentication, authorization, and admission control before the request reaches the cluster.
  2. "What are the essential kubectl commands?" — get (list resources), describe (detailed info), logs (container output), exec (run commands in containers), apply (deploy from YAML), delete (remove resources), explain (documentation lookup).
  3. "How does kubectl know which cluster to talk to?" — kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config). Contains: cluster address, authentication (certificate/token), current context (cluster+user+namespace). Multiple contexts = multiple clusters.
  4. "What is kubectl explain?" — Built-in documentation. Shows available fields for any resource. Works OFFLINE during the exam. kubectl explain pods.spec.containers — shows all container spec fields.

6.1 What is kubectl?

kubectl is the command-line tool for Kubernetes. Every interaction with your cluster — deploying apps, checking status, debugging issues — goes through kubectl. It's your Swiss Army knife for K8s operations.

🔗 How kubectl Communicates with Kubernetes
⌨️
You type

kubectl get pods

→
🔐
kubectl authenticates

Reads ~/.kube/config (certificate, token, or password)

→
🌐
REST API call

HTTPS request to kube-apiserver:6443

→
🗄️
API Server queries etcd

Reads pod data from the cluster's database

→
📋
Response returned

Formatted output displayed in your terminal

📂 The kubeconfig File (~/.kube/config)

kubectl reads its configuration from ~/.kube/config (or the path in KUBECONFIG environment variable). This YAML file contains:

  • Clusters: API server URLs and certificate authorities
  • Users: Authentication credentials (certificates, tokens, passwords)
  • Contexts: Combinations of cluster + user + namespace (which cluster you're talking to as whom)

6.2 Basic kubectl Commands — The Essentials

Here are the commands you'll use every day, grouped by what they do. Master these and you can handle 90% of daily K8s operations.

CategoryCommandWhat It Does
📋 Viewingkubectl get podsList all pods in current namespace
kubectl get nodesList all cluster nodes
kubectl get servicesList all services
kubectl get deploymentsList all deployments
kubectl get allList everything in the namespace
🔍 Detailskubectl describe pod NAMEShow detailed info about a pod
kubectl logs POD-NAMEView container stdout/stderr
kubectl exec -it POD -- /bin/bashOpen shell inside a running container
🚀 Deployingkubectl apply -f file.yamlCreate/update resources from YAML file
kubectl create deployment NAME --image=IMGQuickly create a deployment
kubectl expose deployment NAME --port=80Create a Service for a deployment
🗑️ Removingkubectl delete pod NAMEDelete a specific pod
kubectl delete -f file.yamlDelete resources defined in YAML file
📝 Editingkubectl edit deployment NAMEEdit a resource in your default editor
kubectl scale deployment NAME --replicas=5Scale a deployment up/down

6.3 kubectl get — The Most Used Command

kubectl get is your go-to for checking the state of anything in your cluster. It's the first command you run when something seems wrong.

CommandOutputWhen to Use
kubectl get podsNAME, READY, STATUS, RESTARTS, AGEQuick health check
kubectl get pods -o wideAdds IP, NODE columnsNeed to know which node
kubectl get pods -o yamlFull YAML definitionSee complete configuration
kubectl get pods -o jsonFull JSON definitionScripting/automation
kubectl get pods -wWatch (live updates)Monitor changes in real-time
kubectl get pods --show-labelsShows labels columnDebugging label selectors
kubectl get pods -n NAMESPACEPods in specific namespaceMulti-tenant clusters
kubectl get pods --all-namespacesPods across ALL namespacesCluster-wide view

6.4 kubectl describe — When You Need Details

When kubectl get shows something wrong (CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, Error), kubectl describe tells you why.

📋 kubectl describe pod anihpj — What You Get
Basic Info
Name, Namespace, Node, IP, Labels, Annotations
Container Status
Image, Ports, State (Running/Waiting/Terminated), Restart Count
Conditions
PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready
⚠️ Events (MOST USEFUL!)
Scheduled, Pulling, Pulled, Created, Started, BackOff, Failed, Killing
The Events section is the GOLD STANDARD for debugging. It shows the chronological history of everything that happened to the pod — image pulls, scheduling decisions, crashes, restarts.

6.5 kubectl logs and exec — Debugging Tools

When kubectl describe tells you WHAT happened, kubectl logs tells you what the application says, and kubectl exec lets you look inside.

📜 kubectl logs
  • kubectl logs anihpj-abc123 — View logs from the pod's first container
  • kubectl logs anihpj-abc123 -c sidecar — View logs from a specific container (multi-container pods)
  • kubectl logs -f anihpj-abc123 — Follow logs in real-time (like tail -f)
  • kubectl logs --tail=50 anihpj-abc123 — Show only the last 50 lines
  • kubectl logs --since=1h anihpj-abc123 — Show logs from the last hour
🐚 kubectl exec
  • kubectl exec -it anihpj-abc123 -- /bin/bash — Open interactive shell
  • kubectl exec anihpj-abc123 -- ls /app — Run a single command
  • kubectl exec anihpj-abc123 -c sidecar -- /bin/sh — Shell into specific container
  • kubectl exec anihpj-abc123 -- python manage.py migrate — Run Django management commands inside the container
💡 When to Use Which Tool?
  • kubectl get: "Is it running?" Quick status check.
  • kubectl describe: "Why isn't it running?" Look at Events section.
  • kubectl logs: "What is the app saying?" Application output.
  • kubectl exec: "Let me look inside." Interactive debugging.

6.6 kubectl explain — Your Built-In Documentation

This is a KCNA exam superpower. During the exam, you have NO internet access — but kubectl explain works offline and gives you documentation for every K8s resource.

🔑 kubectl explain — Usage Examples
  • kubectl explain pod — What fields does a Pod resource have?
  • kubectl explain pod.spec — What's inside the Pod spec?
  • kubectl explain pod.spec.containers — Container configuration fields
  • kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec — Recursive exploration!
  • kubectl explain --recursive pod — Show ALL fields, deeply nested

KCNA Exam Tip: Forgot the exact field name for a liveness probe? kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe will show you. This is your built-in reference during the exam!

6.7 kubectl Context and Namespaces — Targeting the Right Place

When you work with multiple clusters (dev, staging, production) or multiple teams sharing one cluster, contexts and namespaces keep everything organized.

🗂️ Context → Cluster → Namespace Hierarchy
Context
"dev-cluster-as-admin" — which cluster, which user, which namespace
Cluster
API Server URL + Certificate Authority
Namespace (Virtual Cluster)
default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease, custom: anihpj-dev, anihpj-prod
CommandWhat It Does
kubectl config current-contextShow which context you're using
kubectl config get-contextsList all available contexts
kubectl config use-context CONTEXTSwitch to a different context
kubectl get namespacesList all namespaces in the cluster
kubectl get pods -n NAMESPACEList pods in a specific namespace
kubectl create namespace NAMECreate a new namespace
📦 Default Namespaces You Should Know
  • default: Where your resources go if you don't specify a namespace
  • kube-system: K8s system components (kube-dns, kube-proxy, metrics-server)
  • kube-public: Publicly readable (contains cluster-info ConfigMap)
  • kube-node-lease: Node heartbeat leases (for node failure detection)

6.8 Programmatic Access — Kubernetes Client Libraries

kubectl is great for humans, but what if you need to interact with Kubernetes from code? The Kubernetes project maintains officially supported client libraries for multiple languages — these are the same APIs kubectl uses internally.

💻 Officially Supported Kubernetes Client Libraries
🐹 Go

client-go — The canonical client. Used by kubectl, operators, controllers. Most feature-complete. github.com/kubernetes/client-go

🐍 Python

kubernetes-client/python — Official Python client. Useful for automation scripts, CI/CD, and Django apps like anihpj. pip install kubernetes

☕ Java

kubernetes-client/java — Official Java client. Used in Spring Boot apps, Jenkins plugins, enterprise integrations.

📜 JavaScript

kubernetes-client/javascript — Official JS/TS client. For Node.js backends, browser-based dashboards, serverless functions.

➕ Also: C# (kubernetes-client/csharp) and Haskell (kubernetes-client/haskell)

🔑 How Client Libraries Work

All client libraries follow the same pattern: Load kubeconfig → Create API client → Call API methods (which translate to REST calls to the API Server). Example in Python: from kubernetes import client, config; config.load_kube_config(); v1 = client.CoreV1Api(); pods = v1.list_namespaced_pod("default")

💡 kubectl vs Client Libraries — When to Use What
  • kubectl: Interactive debugging, one-off commands, CI/CD pipeline steps (kubectl apply in GitHub Actions), shell scripts
  • Client Libraries: Custom operators/controllers (Go), automation scripts (Python), integrating K8s into existing apps (Java/JS), building custom dashboards
  • For anihpj: A Python management command that auto-scales based on job post queue length — using the Python client library to call the K8s API directly from Django
🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam tests awareness of the Kubernetes ecosystem — client libraries are part of that. Know that K8s has officially supported clients for Go, Python, Java, JavaScript, C#, and Haskell. All talk to the same API Server via REST. All use kubeconfig for authentication — the same file kubectl uses.

📝 Chapter 6 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What file does kubectl use for its configuration (cluster, user, context info)?
Show Answer
Answer

~/.kube/config (or the path specified by the KUBECONFIG environment variable).

Explanation

This YAML file contains clusters, users, and contexts. A context binds a cluster + user + namespace together.

Q2
Which kubectl command would you use to see detailed information about why a pod is failing?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl describe pod POD-NAME — particularly the Events section, which shows the chronological history of everything that happened to the pod.

Explanation

kubectl get shows status. kubectl describe shows WHY. The Events section is the most valuable part.

Q3
How do you view the logs from a specific container in a multi-container pod?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl logs POD-NAME -c CONTAINER-NAME. The -c flag specifies which container's logs to view.

Explanation

Multi-container pods (like app + sidecar) have separate log streams. Without -c, kubectl logs shows the first container only.

Q4
Which kubectl command opens an interactive shell inside a running container?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl exec -it POD-NAME -- /bin/bash (or /bin/sh for minimal images). -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY.

Explanation

This is like SSH-ing into your container. Use it to inspect files, run diagnostic commands, or debug issues interactively.

Q5
What does kubectl get pods -o wide show that kubectl get pods doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer

It adds the IP address and NODE columns — showing which node each pod is running on and its cluster IP.

Explanation

Output formats: -o wide (extra columns), -o yaml (full YAML), -o json (JSON), -w (live watch).

Q6
Why is kubectl explain particularly valuable during the KCNA exam?
Show Answer
Answer

Because you have no internet access during the exam, but kubectl explain works offline. It shows field documentation for any K8s resource.

Explanation

Example: kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe shows all available probe configuration fields.

Q7
What is the difference between kubectl create and kubectl apply?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl create creates a NEW resource (fails if it already exists). kubectl apply creates OR updates a resource (idempotent — safe to run multiple times).

Explanation

In practice, always prefer kubectl apply. It's declarative: "make it look like this YAML." kubectl create is imperative: "create this now."

Q8
Which namespace contains Kubernetes system components like CoreDNS and kube-proxy?
Show Answer
Answer

kube-system. This namespace houses all K8s internal components. Never delete resources from kube-system unless you know exactly what you're doing.

Explanation

Default namespaces: default (user workloads), kube-system (system components), kube-public (public info), kube-node-lease (node heartbeats).

Q9
What does kubectl config use-context do?
Show Answer
Answer

It switches which cluster, user, and namespace kubectl targets. It modifies the current-context in ~/.kube/config.

Explanation

Use this to switch between dev/staging/prod clusters. Check current context with kubectl config current-context.

Q10
You deployed anihpj and see "CrashLoopBackOff" in kubectl get pods. What command should you run FIRST to diagnose the issue?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl describe pod (to see Events and understand WHY it's crashing), then kubectl logs (to see the application's error output).

Explanation

Debugging flow: get (spot problem) → describe (Events: why?) → logs (app output) → exec (interactive investigation).

Chapter 7: Pods — The Atomic Unit of Kubernetes

Everything in Kubernetes revolves around Pods. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — it wraps one or more containers with shared resources. Understanding Pods deeply is the foundation for understanding Deployments, Services, StatefulSets, and everything else in K8s. This chapter covers Pod anatomy, lifecycle, health probes, and what happens when anihpj runs as a Pod.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Concepts + Hands-On 🧬 Core

🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 7

Pods are the fundamental unit in K8s. These 5 questions are guaranteed:

  1. "What is a Pod?" — SMALLEST deployable unit. Wraps 1+ containers that share network namespace (same IP, talk via localhost) and storage volumes. Pod = atomic scheduling unit — the scheduler places entire pods, not individual containers.
  2. "Can multiple containers run in a Pod?" — YES. Sidecar pattern: main app + helper (log shipper, proxy, config reloader). They share localhost networking and volumes. Init containers run BEFORE the main container and must complete successfully.
  3. "What are the 4 Pod lifecycle phases?" — Pending (scheduled but not running), Running (at least one container running), Succeeded (all containers terminated with exit 0), Failed (at least one container terminated with non-zero exit).
  4. "What are the 3 probe types and when to use each?" — Liveness: "Is my app alive?" Restarts if probe fails. Readiness: "Is my app ready to serve traffic?" Removes from Service if fails. Startup: "Is my app still booting?" Disables liveness until success — for slow-starting apps.
  5. "What happens when a Pod dies?" — Pods are EPHEMERAL (mortal). When a pod dies, it's GONE — replaced by a new pod with a new IP. This is why you need Services (stable IP/DNS) and PersistentVolumes (stable storage) — never depend on pod IPs.

7.1 What is a Pod?

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It represents a single instance of a running process in your cluster. A Pod can contain one or more containers that are always scheduled together on the same node and share resources.

📋 Pod Definition

A Pod is a group of one or more containers with shared storage and network resources, and a specification for how to run them. Pods are the atomic unit of scheduling in Kubernetes.

🔬 Pod Anatomy — What's Inside
🌐 Shared Network Namespace
Single IP address (all containers share it) Shared port space (containers use localhost!) Same network namespace = same IP, same localhost
📦 Container 1 (Main App)
anihpj Django app Port 8000 Your application code
📦 Container 2 (Sidecar — Optional)
Log shipper (Fluentd) Proxy (Envoy) Helper that enhances the main app
💾 Shared Volumes (Optional)
Shared filesystem — all containers can read/write EmptyDir (temporary), ConfigMap, Secret, PersistentVolume
Key insight: Containers in the same Pod share the network namespace — they can communicate via localhost! The sidecar container can reach the main app at localhost:8000. This is NOT possible across different Pods.
💡 Pod = "Logical Host"

Think of a Pod as a miniature virtual machine — but instead of virtualizing hardware, it virtualizes the OS namespace. All containers in a Pod share: network (IP, port space), IPC (inter-process communication), and optionally storage volumes. They do NOT share: filesystem (each container has its own root), PID namespace (usually), or user namespace.

7.2 Single-Container vs Multi-Container Pods

Most Pods run a single container — this is the simplest and most common pattern. But multi-container Pods enable powerful patterns like the sidecar, where a helper container enhances the main application.

📦 Single-Container Pod (Most Common)
anihpj Django App
Pod Network (IP: 10.244.1.5)

One container = one concern. Simple, easy to reason about, easy to debug. Used for 90%+ of workloads.

📦📦 Multi-Container Pod (Sidecar Pattern)
anihpj (main app) :8000
Fluentd (log shipper) :24224
Pod Network (shared IP: 10.244.1.5)

Helper container augments the main app. Both share the same IP and can use localhost. Common for logging, proxying, monitoring.

🔑 Sidecar Pattern — Real Examples
  • Logging Sidecar: Main app writes to stdout → sidecar collects and forwards to log aggregator (Fluentd, Filebeat).
  • Proxy Sidecar: Sidecar (Envoy, Istio) handles network traffic — TLS termination, retries, circuit breaking — while main app stays simple.
  • Config Reloader: Sidecar watches ConfigMap changes and signals the main app to reload configuration.
  • Database Migrations: Init Container runs python manage.py migrate before the main Django container starts.
💡 Init Containers vs Sidecar Containers — Don't Confuse Them!

Both are multi-container patterns, but they serve DIFFERENT purposes. The KCNA exam expects you to know the difference:

🚀 Init Containers

• Run BEFORE main containers start
• Run to COMPLETION (exit 0) then stop
• Run SEQUENTIALLY (one after another)
• If init container fails, Pod restarts
• Use for: DB migrations, waiting for dependencies, setting up config, downloading files

🔄 Sidecar Containers

• Run ALONGSIDE main containers
• Run CONTINUOUSLY for Pod's entire life
• Run CONCURRENTLY (all at same time)
• If sidecar fails, it gets restarted
• Use for: log shipping, proxying, monitoring, config reloading

Example: anihpj Pod has an init container that runs python manage.py migrate (runs once, exits) and a sidecar container (Fluentd) that continuously ships logs to Elasticsearch.

7.3 The Pod Lifecycle — Every State Explained

A Pod goes through distinct phases from creation to termination. Understanding these states is essential for debugging — when you see "CrashLoopBackOff" or "Pending," you need to know what it means and what to do.

🔄 Pod Lifecycle State Machine
1️⃣ Pending
Pod created, waiting for node assignment + image pull. READY: 0/1. Fix: check node resources, image name, registry auth.
2️⃣ ContainerCreating
Image pulled, container being created. READY: 0/1. This is transitional — should complete quickly.
3️⃣ Running ✅
At least one container is running. READY: 1/1. The pod is healthy and serving. This is the desired steady state.
4️⃣ Succeeded
All containers exited with code 0. READY: 0/1. Normal for Jobs — the work is done. For services, this means the process exited.
❌ Failed
Container exited with non-zero code. READY: 0/1. Check kubectl logs for the error.
🔄 CrashLoopBackOff
Container crashes → K8s restarts → crashes again → K8s waits (exponential backoff: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s... max 5 min). Fix: check logs, fix the crash cause.
StateREADYMeaningYour Action
Pending0/1Waiting for node, pulling imageCheck node capacity, image name
ContainerCreating0/1Image pulled, creating containerWait — transitional state
Running1/1Healthy and serving✅ Desired state!
Succeeded0/1Completed successfully (exit 0)Normal for Jobs/init containers
Failed0/1Exited with errorkubectl logs → find the error
CrashLoopBackOff0/1Crashing repeatedly, K8s backing offkubectl describe (Events!) + logs
Unknown0/1Node unreachableCheck node status
⚠️ CrashLoopBackOff — Why It Happens

This is the most common pod problem you'll encounter. It means: container starts → crashes → K8s restarts it → crashes again → K8s waits (backoff) before trying again. Common causes:

  • Application bug: Your code throws an unhandled exception on startup
  • Missing config: Required environment variable or config file not present
  • Dependency unavailable: Database not reachable, causing startup failure
  • Wrong command: CMD/ENTRYPOINT points to a non-existent binary
  • OOMKilled: Container exceeds memory limit, Linux OOM killer terminates it

Fix flow: kubectl describe pod → check Events → kubectl logs → see application error → fix → redeploy.

7.4 How anihpj Runs as a Pod — A Complete Example

Let's see exactly what a Pod definition for anihpj looks like. This is the YAML you'd write to run our Django job board in Kubernetes.

📝 anihpj Pod YAML — Annotated
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod                          # This is a Pod resource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pod                  # Unique name for this Pod
  labels:
    app: anihpj                     # Labels for selection (used by Services)
    tier: frontend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj-container          # Container name
    image: registry.io/anihpj:v2    # Container image (from your registry)
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000           # Port the app listens on
      protocol: TCP
    env:                            # Environment variables
    - name: DATABASE_URL
      value: "postgres://anihpj:pass@postgres-service:5432/anihpj"
    - name: DEBUG
      value: "False"
    resources:                      # Resource requests & limits
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"             # Guaranteed minimum memory
        cpu: "250m"                 # 0.25 CPU core guaranteed
      limits:
        memory: "512Mi"             # Max memory (exceeding = OOMKill)
        cpu: "500m"                 # Max 0.5 CPU core
    livenessProbe:                  # Is the app alive?
      httpGet:
        path: /health/
        port: 8000
      initialDelaySeconds: 30       # Wait 30s before first check
      periodSeconds: 10             # Check every 10s
    readinessProbe:                 # Is the app ready for traffic?
      httpGet:
        path: /ready/
        port: 8000
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5
  restartPolicy: Always             # Always restart if it crashes
💻 What kubectl Shows for anihpj
$ kubectl get pods
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
anihpj-pod    1/1     Running   0          30s

$ kubectl get pods -o wide
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP           NODE
anihpj-pod    1/1     Running   0          45s   10.244.1.5   worker-01
🔬 Deep Dive: The Pod Lifecycle — What Happens Moment by Moment

When you run kubectl run anihpj --image=anihpj:v2, here's the complete timeline:

  1. T+0s: kubectl → API Server. kubectl reads your kubeconfig, constructs a REST POST to /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods with the Pod spec. API Server authenticates (who are you?), authorizes (are you allowed to create pods?), and validates (is the spec valid?).
  2. T+0.1s: API Server → etcd. The Pod object is serialized and written to etcd. At this point, the Pod exists in the cluster's desired state — but nothing is running yet. The pod's status is Pending with no node assigned.
  3. T+0.2s: Scheduler watches API. The scheduler has an open watch connection to the API Server. It sees a new Pod with spec.nodeName: "" (unassigned). It runs filtering (which nodes have enough CPU/memory?) and scoring (which node is least utilized?). The winner: worker-01. The scheduler updates the Pod object: spec.nodeName: "worker-01" via the API Server.
  4. T+0.5s: kubelet watches API. kubelet on worker-01 has a watch filtering for pods assigned to its node. It sees the new pod. kubelet calls the CRI (Container Runtime Interface): "Create a container with this image, these mounts, these env vars." containerd pulls the image (if not cached), creates the container via runc, and starts the process.
  5. T+2s: Container Running. The Django process inside the container starts. kubelet updates the Pod status: Running. But is it READY? Not yet — that depends on the readiness probe.
  6. T+5s: Readiness Check. If configured, the readiness probe runs (HTTP GET /healthz). Django responds 200 OK → kubelet sets Pod condition Ready=True. NOW the Pod is added to the Service's endpoints and starts receiving traffic.

🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam asks "Why is my pod stuck in Pending?" Common causes: no node has enough resources (check requests), nodeSelector doesn't match any node, taint blocking with no toleration, PVC not bound. Know this checklist.

7.5 Pod Health — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Kubernetes doesn't just start your containers and hope for the best — it continuously checks their health using probes. Three types serve different purposes, and choosing the right one is critical.

ProbeQuestion It AsksOn FailureUse When...
Startup"Has the app started?"Restart containerYour app is slow to start (Django migration, large dataset load). Disables liveness/readiness until startup succeeds.
Liveness"Is the app still alive?"Restart containerYour app can get stuck (deadlock, infinite loop) and needs a restart to recover.
Readiness"Is the app ready for traffic?"Stop sending traffic (no restart)Your app needs time to warm up or temporarily can't handle requests (overloaded, dependency down).
📊 Probe Timeline — Why Startup Probe Saves Slow Apps
❌ WITHOUT Startup Probe

Django app takes 30s to start (migrations). Liveness probe checks at 10s, 20s, 30s — all fail because the app isn't ready. After 3 failures, K8s KILLS the container! It restarts, and the cycle repeats forever. Your app never deploys.

✅ WITH Startup Probe

Startup probe checks every 5s. While it's failing, liveness and readiness are DISABLED. At 30s, the app is ready — startup probe succeeds. Liveness and readiness activate. Your app deploys successfully and stays running.

🔑 Probe Check Methods — 3 Ways to Check Health
  • httpGet: K8s makes an HTTP GET request. 2xx/3xx = healthy, 4xx/5xx = unhealthy. Best for web apps like anihpj.
  • tcpSocket: K8s tries to open a TCP connection. Success = healthy, refused = unhealthy. Best for databases (PostgreSQL :5432, Redis :6379).
  • exec: K8s runs a command inside the container. Exit 0 = healthy, non-zero = unhealthy. Best for custom health checks (e.g., python check_db.py).
💡 KCNA Probe Strategy — The Perfect Pair

Startup Probe + Liveness Probe = Perfect Combination

  • Set initialDelaySeconds on the startup probe to your app's maximum startup time (e.g., 60s).
  • Set a short periodSeconds on the liveness probe (e.g., 10s) — it only activates AFTER startup succeeds.
  • Set the liveness probe failureThreshold to 3-5 — don't restart on a single transient failure.
  • Set readiness probe with a shorter interval (5s) — you want to quickly detect when a pod can't serve traffic.

Golden Rule: Liveness probes should be LIGHTWEIGHT. If your liveness probe does something expensive (complex DB query), you risk crashing pods under load — exactly when you need them most.

⚠️ Common Probe Mistakes (That Will Fail Your Deployments)
  • Mistake 1: Liveness probe depends on external services. If your liveness probe checks a database connection and the DB is slow, ALL your pods restart simultaneously — cascading failure. Liveness should check LOCAL health only.
  • Mistake 2: No Startup probe for slow apps. Django with migrations takes 30-60s to start. Without a startup probe, the liveness probe kills it before it boots. Result: infinite crash loop, app never deploys.
  • Mistake 3: Readiness probe is too aggressive. If readiness checks every 1 second with a 1-failure threshold, a single hiccup removes the pod from service. Use failureThreshold: 3 and periodSeconds: 5 for production stability.
  • Mistake 4: Same endpoint for liveness AND readiness. They serve different purposes. Liveness = /healthz (basic aliveness). Readiness = /ready (can accept traffic, all dependencies up).
  • Mistake 5: No probes at all. Without probes, K8s doesn't know if your app is alive or dead. A deadlocked process runs forever, serving errors to users. Always configure at least a liveness probe.

KCNA Tip: The exam expects you to recognize probe misconfiguration scenarios. If a question describes "pod keeps restarting even though the app eventually works," the answer is usually "add a startup probe."
