💼 Chapter 7 — In Daily Work

🛠️ Pod Operations

Every anihpj instance runs as a Pod. When you deploy with kubectl apply, K8s creates Pods from your Deployment template. You check them with kubectl get pods, debug with kubectl describe and kubectl logs. When a Pod misbehaves, the probe configuration you set determines whether it restarts, gets traffic removed, or stays healthy.

🧠 KCNA Context

Pod concepts appear across ALL KCNA domains. Probes are in the "Container Orchestration" domain. Lifecycle states are in "Kubernetes Fundamentals." Sidecar patterns are in "Cloud Native Architecture." Master Pods, and you've mastered the fundamental building block of everything in K8s.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 7
📦 Pod

Smallest deployable unit. Wraps 1+ containers sharing network namespace (same IP, localhost) and volumes. Atomic scheduling unit.

🔄 Lifecycle

Pending→Running→Succeeded/Failed. CrashLoopBackOff = container keeps crashing. ImagePullBackOff = can't pull image.

🔍 3 Probes

Liveness: "Am I alive?" (restart). Readiness: "Can I serve?" (remove from Service). Startup: "Am I still booting?" (disable liveness until success).

💀 Ephemeral

Pods are MORTAL. When a pod dies, it's GONE — replaced by new pod with new IP. Use Services for stable networking, PVCs for stable storage.

📝 Chapter 7 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A Pod. Pods are the atomic unit of scheduling in Kubernetes. You never deploy individual containers — you deploy Pods that contain containers.

Explanation

This is THE most fundamental K8s concept. Pods wrap containers with shared networking and storage.

Q2
What do containers within the same Pod share?
Show Answer
Answer

Network namespace (same IP address, same port space, can communicate via localhost) and storage volumes (if configured). They can also share IPC (inter-process communication).

Explanation

This is why sidecar patterns work — the sidecar can reach the main container at localhost:port. Containers do NOT share filesystems by default.

Q3
What is the sidecar pattern in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A helper container that runs alongside the main application container in the same Pod, enhancing or extending its functionality (e.g., log shipping, proxying, config reloading).

Explanation

Common sidecars: Fluentd (log collection), Envoy/Istio (service mesh proxy), config reloaders, backup agents.

Q4
A Pod shows status "CrashLoopBackOff." What does this mean?
Show Answer
Answer

The container crashes repeatedly after starting. K8s restarts it, but after each crash it waits progressively longer (backoff: 10s → 20s → 40s → 80s → max 5 min) before the next restart attempt.

Explanation

Common causes: application bug, missing config, unreachable dependency, wrong CMD/ENTRYPOINT, OOMKilled (memory limit exceeded).

Q5
What is the difference between a Liveness probe and a Readiness probe?
Show Answer
Answer

Liveness: "Is the app alive?" — on failure, K8s RESTARTS the container. Readiness: "Is the app ready for traffic?" — on failure, K8s stops sending traffic but does NOT restart the container.

Explanation

Liveness = restart. Readiness = stop traffic. Both are critical but serve different purposes.

Q6
Your Django app takes 45 seconds to start (database migrations). Without a Startup probe, what happens?
Show Answer
Answer

The Liveness probe may kill the container before it finishes starting. K8s restarts it, migrations run again, liveness kills it again — an infinite restart loop. The app never deploys successfully.

Explanation

A Startup probe disables liveness/readiness checks until the app is ready, giving slow-starting apps time to boot.

Q7
Which probe check method is best for a PostgreSQL database container?
Show Answer
Answer

tcpSocket — K8s attempts a TCP connection to port 5432. If PostgreSQL is accepting connections, the probe passes. Simpler and more reliable than exec or httpGet for databases.

Explanation

httpGet is best for web apps (HTTP endpoints). tcpSocket is best for databases and message queues. exec is for custom checks.

Q8
What happens when a Pod's container exceeds its memory limit?
Show Answer
Answer

The container is OOMKilled (Out Of Memory Killed) by the Linux kernel. K8s restarts the container according to the Pod's restartPolicy. The Pod status shows "OOMKilled" in the termination reason.

Explanation

Resource limits are enforced by cgroups. CPU limit: throttled (slowed down). Memory limit: OOMKilled (process terminated).

Q9
What is the "ContainerCreating" status, and how long should it last?
Show Answer
Answer

A transitional state after the image is pulled but before the container has started. It should last only seconds. If it persists, the image pull may be slow or the container runtime may be having issues.

Explanation

If ContainerCreating persists for minutes, check: large image size, slow registry, image pull secrets missing, or node disk pressure.

Q10
Why should Liveness probes be lightweight?
Show Answer
Answer

Heavy liveness probes can cause cascading failures under load. If the probe does a complex database query and the DB is slow, ALL pods fail their liveness checks simultaneously — K8s restarts them all at once, making the situation worse. Liveness probes should check basic aliveness, not end-to-end functionality.

Explanation

Golden rule: Liveness = "am I alive?" (lightweight). Readiness = "can I serve?" (can be more thorough). Startup = "have I booted?" (run once).

Chapter 8: The Kubernetes Cluster — Nodes, Control Plane, and Workers

Now that you understand Pods — the atomic unit — let's zoom out and see the cluster that runs them. A Kubernetes cluster is like a well-organized port: a control tower directs operations, docks (worker nodes) handle cargo (containers), and everything communicates through a central authority. This chapter explains the architecture that makes it all possible.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🏗️ Architecture ☸️ Core

  • ✅ What a Kubernetes cluster IS — nodes, control plane, workers
  • ✅ The maritime port metaphor — the BEST way to understand K8s architecture
  • ✅ All 5 control plane components and what each one does
  • ✅ Worker node components — kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime
  • ✅ How components communicate (hub-and-spoke model via API server)
  • ✅ Cluster addons — CoreDNS, Dashboard, CNI plugins, monitoring

💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 8
  • Control Plane Components — Know all 5: kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, cloud-controller-manager. The exam WILL ask about them.
  • API Server is Central — ALL communication goes through it. Only API server talks to etcd. This is the most common KCNA architecture question.
  • Worker Components — kubelet (node agent), kube-proxy (network rules), container runtime (runs containers). Know what each does.
  • Hub-and-Spoke — The API server is the hub; all other components are spokes. They watch the API server for changes — not each other.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 8

Architecture is heavily tested. 5 must-know questions:

  1. "What are the Control Plane components?" — kube-apiserver (front door, all communication goes through it), etcd (cluster memory, stores ALL state), kube-scheduler (assigns pods to nodes), kube-controller-manager (runs reconciliation loops), cloud-controller-manager (cloud integrations).
  2. "What are the Worker Node components?" — kubelet (node agent, ensures containers are running), kube-proxy (network rules for Services), Container Runtime (containerd/CRI-O, actually runs containers).
  3. "Which component talks to etcd?" — ONLY the API Server. kubelet watches API Server for pod assignments; scheduler writes assignments to API Server. Nothing else touches etcd directly — this is the #1 security and architecture pattern.
  4. "What is the reconciliation loop?" — Controller watches current state (via API Server) → compares with desired state → takes action to close the gap → repeats. This is K8s' core operating principle. Self-healing comes from this infinite loop.
  5. "How does data flow in a K8s cluster?" — kubectl → API Server (auth/authz/admission) → etcd (store) → Scheduler (assign node) → kubelet (run container) → CRI (start container). Trace this path forwards AND backwards.

8.1 What is a Kubernetes Cluster?

A Kubernetes cluster is a set of machines (nodes) that run containerized applications. It has two distinct parts: the Control Plane (the brain) that manages everything, and Worker Nodes (the muscles) that actually run your application Pods.

🏗️ Kubernetes Cluster — High-Level Architecture
🧠 Control Plane (The Brain)
API Server — Front door to the cluster etcd — Cluster database (all state) Scheduler — Decides where Pods run Controller Manager — Maintains desired state
💪 Worker Nodes (The Muscles — Run Your Apps)
Node 1: kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime → Pods (anihpj, redis) Node 2: kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime → Pods (anihpj, postgres) Node 3: kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime → Pods (anihpj, nginx)
🌐 Networking (CNI Plugin — Calico/Flannel/Cilium)
All Pods can communicate across all nodes. Pod network is flat — every Pod gets its own IP.
📏 Cluster Sizing Guidelines
  • Development: 1 node (minikube/kind) — all-in-one, control plane + worker on same machine
  • Staging: 3 nodes — 1 control plane + 2 workers. Some redundancy, limited HA.
  • Production: 5+ nodes — 3 control planes (HA) + 3+ workers. Full high availability.
  • Maximum: 5,000 nodes, 150,000 pods, 300,000 containers (theoretical K8s limits)

8.2 The Maritime Metaphor — Kubernetes as a Port

This is the most intuitive way to understand Kubernetes architecture. Imagine a busy shipping port:

🚢 Maritime Port = Kubernetes Cluster
🏗️ Port Element☸️ Kubernetes ComponentWhat It Does
Harbor Master's TowerControl Plane (API Server)Directs ALL operations. Every ship, dock worker, and crane reports to the tower.
DocksWorker NodesWhere ships (containers) are loaded, unloaded, and processed.
Shipping ContainersPodsStandardized, stackable units. Any container fits any dock.
Dock WorkerkubeletThe agent on every dock. Ensures containers are where they should be.
Berth Plannerkube-schedulerDecides which dock each incoming ship (Pod) goes to.
Traffic Controllerkube-proxyRoutes traffic to the correct dock and container.
Port Registry/LogbooketcdRecords EVERYTHING — which ship is at which dock, what cargo, when it arrived.
CranesContainer RuntimeActually loads/unloads containers (starts/stops containers).

8.3 Control Plane Components — The Brain

The control plane makes all global decisions about the cluster. It's typically run on dedicated nodes (not running user applications) and is replicated for high availability.

🧠 Control Plane — All 5 Components
🌐 kube-apiserver (Port 6443)
The FRONT DOOR. ALL requests go through it. Authentication, authorization, admission control. ONLY component that talks to etcd. REST API.
🗄️ etcd
Distributed key-value store. ALL cluster state lives here. Raft consensus for consistency. 3-5 nodes for HA. THE source of truth.
🎯 kube-scheduler
Watches for new Pods with no node. FILTERS nodes (which CAN run it?), SCORES nodes (which is BEST?), ASSIGNS the winner.
📋 kube-controller-manager
Runs MANY controllers in one binary: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Service, Endpoint, Job controllers. Each controller reconciles its resource type.
☁️ cloud-controller-manager (Cloud only)
Cloud-specific logic: Node management (cloud VMs), Route management (cloud networking), Load balancer provisioning. Only present on cloud providers.
🔑 The API Server is THE Most Important Component

Every operation in Kubernetes flows through the API server:

  • kubectl → API Server (user commands)
  • kubelet → API Server (reports node/pod status)
  • Scheduler → API Server (reads pod specs, writes node assignments)
  • Controller Manager → API Server (reads desired state, writes changes)
  • etcd ← API Server (ONLY the API server talks to etcd directly)

If the API server is down, you can't deploy, scale, or query anything — but existing Pods keep running (they're managed locally by kubelet).

8.4 Worker Node Components — The Muscles

🤖 kubelet

The node agent that runs on EVERY worker node. It watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node and ensures they're running. Reports node and Pod status back to the API server. If a container crashes, kubelet restarts it.

🌉 kube-proxy

The network proxy that runs on EVERY node. Maintains network rules (iptables/IPVS) so Pods and Services can communicate. Handles Service-to-Pod traffic routing. Every Service update triggers kube-proxy to update routing rules.

📦 Container Runtime

The software that actually runs containers. Usually containerd or CRI-O. Implements the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). Pulls images, creates containers, manages their lifecycle. NOT part of Kubernetes itself — it's a plugin.

🔬 Deep Dive: Why the Control Plane Components Are Designed This Way

Every design choice in the Kubernetes control plane is driven by specific requirements. Understanding the WHY helps you remember the WHAT:

  • API Server is stateless (can have multiple replicas): The API Server stores NOTHING locally — all state is in etcd. This means you can run 3 API Servers behind a load balancer for HA. If one crashes, the others continue serving. All three write to the same etcd cluster. This design pattern (stateless front-end + stateful backend) is why K8s is so resilient.
  • Only API Server talks to etcd: This is NOT just a convention — it's a critical SECURITY boundary. etcd has no built-in RBAC for individual resources. If every component could talk directly to etcd, anyone with controller credentials could read ALL secrets. By funneling everything through the API Server, K8s applies authentication, authorization, and admission control to EVERY request before it reaches etcd.
  • Scheduler doesn't run pods — it only ASSIGNS: The scheduler updates spec.nodeName on the Pod object. That's it. The kubelet on the target node detects the assignment and does the actual work. This separation of concerns (decide vs execute) is a recurring K8s pattern — it's why components are loosely coupled and independently scalable.
  • Controller Manager is actually MANY controllers in one binary: Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller, Node controller, Service controller, Job controller, etc. Each runs an independent reconciliation loop. They share the same binary for efficiency but operate independently. If the ReplicaSet controller crashes, Deployments still work — the controllers are independent.

🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam LOVES architecture questions. "Which component writes to etcd?" (API Server). "What happens if the scheduler crashes?" (Existing pods run fine; new pods stay Pending — no node assignment). "What happens if a controller manager crashes?" (The specific controller stops reconciling — e.g., no new ReplicaSets from Deployments. It restarts automatically.)

8.5 How Components Communicate — Hub-and-Spoke

⭐ Hub-and-Spoke: API Server at the Center
🌐 kube-apiserver (The Hub)
ALL communication passes through me. I am the only component that talks to etcd.
Spokes → Hub (WATCH for changes)
kubelet WATCHES for Pods assigned to its node kube-proxy WATCHES for Service/Endpoint changes Scheduler WATCHES for unassigned Pods Controllers WATCH for resource changes
🔒 All Communication is TLS-Encrypted
Certificates authenticate every component. No plaintext communication anywhere.
⚠️ What Happens When Components Fail?
  • API Server down: Can't deploy/query, but existing Pods keep running (kubelet manages them locally).
  • etcd down (loses quorum): Cluster is READ-ONLY. No new deployments, no scaling. Existing Pods keep running but cluster can't change state.
  • Scheduler down: New Pods stay Pending (no node assigned). Existing Pods unaffected.
  • Controller Manager down: No reconciliation. If a Pod crashes, it won't be replaced automatically.
  • kubelet down: Node shows NotReady. Pods on that node are unmanaged. Control plane assumes they're dead after timeout.
🏗️ Stacked vs External etcd — Production Architecture Decision

When setting up a production cluster, you must decide where etcd runs:

  • Stacked etcd: etcd runs on the SAME nodes as the other control plane components. Simpler setup, fewer nodes. Most common for small-to-medium clusters. Risk: if a CP node fails, you lose both etcd and other CP components on that node.
  • External etcd: etcd runs on DEDICATED separate nodes. More secure (etcd isolated), better performance (no resource contention), but requires more nodes and separate management. Recommended for large production clusters.

KCNA Tip: Know the trade-off. Stacked = simpler, fewer nodes but shared fate. External = more secure, better performance but more nodes. The exam may ask which architecture suits different scenarios.

8.6 Addons — Extending the Cluster

🌐 CoreDNS

DNS-based service discovery. Every Service gets a DNS name: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Pods resolve this to the Service's ClusterIP. Runs as a Deployment in kube-system.

🖥️ Dashboard

Web UI for cluster management. View resources, deploy apps, troubleshoot. NOT installed by default — you must deploy it separately. Requires authentication.

📊 Metrics Server

Collects CPU/memory metrics from kubelets. Powers kubectl top and HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler). Lightweight — one Deployment per cluster.

🌉 CNI Plugin (Required!)

Container Network Interface. Enables Pod-to-Pod networking across nodes. Calico, Flannel, Cilium are popular choices. Without CNI, Pods can't communicate — cluster is useless.

📊 Chapter 8 — Kubernetes Cluster: Key Takeaways

🏗️ Cluster

Set of nodes: Control Plane (brain) + Workers (muscles). Min: 1 CP + 1 worker. Production: 3 CP (HA) + 3+ workers.

🧠 Control Plane

API Server (front door), etcd (database), Scheduler (placement), Controller Manager (reconciliation), Cloud Controller Manager (cloud integration).

💪 Worker Node

kubelet (node agent, runs Pods), kube-proxy (network rules), container runtime (runs containers via CRI).

⭐ Hub-and-Spoke

API Server is the hub — ALL communication passes through it. Only API Server talks to etcd. All TLS-encrypted.

🚢 Maritime Metaphor

Control Plane = Harbor Master, Nodes = Docks, Pods = Containers, Scheduler = Berth Planner, etcd = Logbook.

🔌 Addons

CoreDNS (service discovery), Dashboard (UI), Metrics Server (monitoring), CNI plugin (networking — REQUIRED!).

💼 Chapter 8 — In Daily Work

When you run kubectl get nodes, you're seeing the worker nodes. kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows the control plane and addon components. Understanding this architecture helps you diagnose issues: "Is the API server reachable? Is etcd healthy? Is the CNI plugin working?" These are the questions you ask when the cluster behaves unexpectedly.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 8
🧠 Control Plane

API Server + etcd + Scheduler + Controller Manager. The brain. Makes global decisions. Detects and responds to cluster events.

💪 Worker Nodes

kubelet + kube-proxy + Container Runtime. The muscles. Actually run your application pods. Report status to control plane.

🔒 API Server

THE front door. ALL communication flows through it. ONLY component that talks to etcd. Hub in hub-and-spoke architecture.

🔄 Reconciliation

Watch current state → compare with desired → take action → repeat. This infinite loop IS Kubernetes. Self-healing emerges from it.

The Control Plane (specifically the API Server). All operations are directed from the tower — every ship, dock worker, and crane reports to it.

It runs many controllers in one binary — Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller, Node controller, Service controller, Job controller, etc. Each controller watches for changes and reconciles actual state toward desired state.

Chapter 9: etcd — The Cluster's Brain Database

If Kubernetes is a living organism, etcd is its memory. Every Pod, every Service, every Secret — everything you create in Kubernetes is stored in etcd. If etcd loses its data, the cluster has amnesia. Understanding etcd is critical because it's THE most important component to back up and protect.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What etcd IS — a distributed, reliable key-value store
  • ✅ How etcd achieves consistency with the Raft consensus algorithm
  • ✅ Why etcd is THE most critical component — and what happens when it fails
  • ✅ What exactly etcd stores — the entire cluster state in one database
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 9
  • etcd = Source of Truth — All cluster state is in etcd. Know this.
  • Raft Consensus — etcd uses Raft. Quorum = majority (N/2 + 1). 3-node: quorum=2, can lose 1. 5-node: quorum=3, can lose 2.
  • etcd Failure — If etcd loses quorum, the cluster becomes READ-ONLY. This is a critical KCNA concept.
  • Backup — etcd backup is THE single most important cluster maintenance task. The exam may ask about disaster recovery.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 9

etcd is the cluster's brain. 4 critical questions:

  1. "What is etcd and why is it critical?" — Distributed key-value store. Stores ALL cluster state (nodes, pods, configs, secrets, RBAC). Uses Raft consensus. If etcd loses quorum → cluster becomes READ-ONLY. Lose etcd without backups = lose the cluster.
  2. "What is the Raft quorum formula?" — Quorum = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1. 3 nodes: quorum=2, tolerates 1 failure. 5 nodes: quorum=3, tolerates 2 failures. Always use ODD number of etcd members to avoid split-brain.
  3. "Which component can write to etcd?" — ONLY the API Server. Controller Manager, Scheduler, kubelet — ALL read/write through the API Server. Direct etcd access is a security anti-pattern.
  4. "What is the etcd backup strategy?" — etcdctl snapshot save → stores to secure location. Backups are THE most critical cluster maintenance task. Without backups, etcd failure = permanent cluster loss. Test your restores!

9.1 What is etcd?

etcd is a distributed, reliable key-value store. Think of it as a super-reliable Python dictionary that's replicated across multiple servers. It stores ALL Kubernetes cluster data — configuration, state, and metadata.

📋 etcd Definition

etcd (pronounced "et-cee-dee") is a strongly consistent, distributed key-value store that provides a reliable way to store data that needs to be accessed by a distributed system or cluster of machines. It's the primary datastore for Kubernetes.

📖 Fun Fact: What Does "etcd" Stand For?

The name has two origins: (1) /etc + "d" — on Linux, /etc stores configuration files; etcd stores distributed configuration. (2) The "d" stands for "distributed." It was developed by CoreOS (now part of Red Hat) and is a CNCF Graduated project.

9.2 How etcd Works — Raft Consensus

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to keep data consistent across all its members. This is what makes it reliable — even if some members fail, the cluster continues working as long as a majority (quorum) is healthy.

🗳️ Raft Consensus — How etcd Keeps Data Consistent
1
Client Sends Write

Write goes to Leader (or forwarded to Leader)

→
2
Leader Logs Entry

Leader appends to its log

→
3
Sends to Followers

AppendEntries RPC to all followers

→
4
Majority Acknowledges

2/3 (quorum) say "Got it!"

→
5
Leader Commits

Entry is committed → followers commit → client gets OK

Cluster SizeQuorum NeededCan LoseUse Case
3 nodes2 (N/2+1 = 2)1 nodeMost common. Good balance of HA and cost.
5 nodes3 (N/2+1 = 3)2 nodesHigher fault tolerance. More overhead (5 copies).
1 node10 nodesDevelopment only. NO fault tolerance.

9.3 Why etcd Matters — It's THE Most Critical Component

⚠️ If etcd Fails, the Cluster Has Amnesia

etcd stores everything you've ever created in the cluster. If etcd loses its data (no backup!) or loses quorum:

  • The cluster becomes READ-ONLY — existing Pods keep running, but you can't deploy, scale, or modify anything.
  • If etcd data is corrupted or lost, the cluster forgets what's running. Pods might still exist on nodes, but K8s doesn't know about them.
  • Recovery without backup: You must recreate EVERYTHING — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets — from scratch.
  • Recovery WITH backup: Restore etcd from snapshot → cluster remembers everything → normal operations resume.
🔑 etcd Backup — THE Most Important Cluster Maintenance Task

etcd backup is non-negotiable for production clusters. You should:

  • Take regular snapshots (daily minimum, hourly for critical clusters)
  • Store backups OFF the cluster (different storage, different region)
  • Test restoration regularly — a backup you haven't tested is not a backup
  • Use etcdctl snapshot save to create snapshots
⚠️ How etcd Handles Network Partitions — The Split-Brain Scenario

What happens if the network between etcd members breaks? This is the classic "split-brain" problem:

  • Scenario: 5-node etcd cluster. Network partition splits it into Group A (3 nodes, including Leader) and Group B (2 nodes, isolated).
  • Group A (3 nodes = quorum): Can still elect a leader and process writes. The cluster CONTINUES to work. This is why odd numbers matter!
  • Group B (2 nodes = no quorum): Cannot elect a leader. Cannot process writes. Becomes READ-ONLY. It knows it lost quorum and refuses writes to prevent data inconsistency.
  • When partition heals: Group B members rejoin, catch up on missed log entries from the leader, and the cluster returns to full health automatically.

This is why Raft requires ODD numbers of members. With an even number (e.g., 4), a 2-2 split means NEITHER side has quorum — the entire cluster stops. Always use 3 or 5 etcd members in production.

9.4 What etcd Stores — The Entire Cluster State

🗂️ What Lives in etcd?
Pods
Every Pod definition, status, assigned node
Services & Endpoints
Service definitions, ClusterIPs, endpoint lists
Deployments & ReplicaSets
Desired replicas, update strategy, revision history
ConfigMaps & Secrets
Configuration data, passwords, TLS certificates
Nodes
Node objects, status, capacity, conditions
Namespaces, RBAC, ServiceAccounts
Access control, roles, permissions, identities
Everything Else
PersistentVolumes, Ingresses, CRDs, Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets, StatefulSets...
Every kubectl apply, kubectl create, or kubectl edit ultimately writes to etcd (through the API server). When you run kubectl get, you're reading from etcd.

📊 Chapter 9 — etcd: Key Takeaways

🗄️ What etcd Is

Distributed key-value store. ALL K8s state lives here. CNCF Graduated. Developed by CoreOS/Red Hat.

🗳️ Raft Consensus

Leader + Followers. Writes go through Leader. Quorum = majority (N/2+1). 3 nodes → quorum 2, lose 1 max.

⚠️ Failure Impact

Lose quorum = READ-ONLY cluster. Lose data = cluster amnesia. Backup is THE #1 maintenance priority.

💾 What's Stored

Pods, Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Nodes, RBAC, Namespaces — literally everything you create.

🔐 Access

ONLY API Server talks to etcd directly. All other components read/write through the API server. TLS-encrypted.

📦 HA Config

Production: 3 or 5 etcd nodes on control plane. Stacked (same nodes as CP) or external (dedicated etcd cluster).

💼 Chapter 9 — In Daily Work

🛡️ Operations Reality

etcd backup is the first thing you set up in any production cluster. You schedule regular snapshots (via CronJob or external script), store them in cloud object storage (S3/GCS/Blob), and test restoration quarterly. Without tested etcd backups, your cluster is one disaster away from being rebuilt from scratch.

The KCNA exam expects you to understand etcd as the cluster's single source of truth. Expect questions about: what etcd stores, Raft consensus basics, quorum requirements (N/2+1), what happens on quorum loss, and why backup is critical. The exam won't ask you to actually perform etcdctl commands — just understand the concepts.

📝 Chapter 9 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What type of database is etcd?
Show Answer
Answer

A distributed key-value store. It's not a relational database — it's a simple key→value mapping, but distributed across multiple nodes with strong consistency.

Think of it like a Python dictionary that's replicated across 3-5 servers with guaranteed consistency.

Q2
What consensus algorithm does etcd use?
Show Answer
Answer

Raft. Raft ensures all etcd members agree on the data. One member is the Leader (handles writes), others are Followers (replicate data).

Explanation

Raft provides leader election, log replication, and safety guarantees. It's simpler than Paxos but provides the same guarantees.

Q3
In a 3-node etcd cluster, what is the quorum and how many nodes can fail?
Show Answer
Answer

Quorum = 2 (N/2+1 = 2). Can lose 1 node. With 3 nodes, you need 2 healthy members to maintain quorum and continue operating.

Explanation

5-node cluster: quorum=3, can lose 2. This is why production etcd clusters use odd numbers.

Q4
What happens to a Kubernetes cluster if etcd loses quorum?
Show Answer
Answer

The cluster becomes READ-ONLY. Existing Pods keep running, but no new deployments, scaling, or modifications are possible. The API server can't write new state.

Explanation

This is a critical KCNA concept. etcd = cluster memory. Lose memory = can't learn new things.

Q5

Only kube-apiserver. All other components (scheduler, controllers, kubelet, kubectl) access etcd indirectly through the API server.

Q6

Show Answer
Answer

Because etcd stores ALL cluster state. If etcd data is lost without backup, you must recreate every Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, and all other resources from scratch.

Node failures can be replaced. Pod failures auto-heal. But etcd data loss = complete cluster amnesia. Backup is your only safety net.

Q7

/etc + "d" (distributed). On Linux, /etc stores configuration; etcd stores distributed configuration. Developed by CoreOS, now a CNCF Graduated project.

Q8
Where does etcd typically run in a Kubernetes cluster?
Show Answer

On control plane nodes. In production, etcd runs on 3 or 5 dedicated control plane nodes. It can be stacked (on same nodes as other CP components) or external (separate cluster).

Q9
Which of these is NOT stored in etcd?
Show Answer
Answer

Chapter 10: How Kubernetes Runs anihpj — The Full Request Flow

This is the chapter where everything clicks. You'll trace the complete journey of kubectl apply -f anihjp-deployment.yaml — from your terminal, through the API server, into etcd, through the scheduler, onto a worker node, and finally into a running container. By the end, you'll understand exactly how all the components you've learned about work together to run your application.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Declarative vs Imperative — the mindset shift that makes K8s powerful
  • ✅ The complete 8-step journey: kubectl → API Server → etcd → Controllers → Scheduler → kubelet → Container Runtime → Running Pod
  • ✅ Self-healing in action — what happens when an anihpj pod crashes
  • ✅ Rolling updates — deploying anihpj v2 with zero downtime
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Container Orchestration 22%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 10
  • Declarative Model — The #1 K8s concept. You declare WHAT you want, K8s figures out HOW. This enables self-healing.
  • 8-Step Deployment Flow — Be able to trace the path: kubectl→API→etcd→Deployment Controller→ReplicaSet Controller→Scheduler→kubelet→Container Runtime.

🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 10

The full deployment flow is the most important sequence in KCNA. 3 key questions:

  1. "Trace the full path of kubectl apply to a running pod." — kubectl → API Server (auth/authz/admission) → etcd (store) → Deployment Controller (creates ReplicaSet) → ReplicaSet Controller (creates Pod object) → Scheduler (assigns node) → kubelet (detects assignment) → CRI (starts container). MUST know this chain cold.
  2. "How does self-healing work?" — ReplicaSet controller constantly compares desired (3 replicas) with actual (2 running, 1 crashed). Detects gap → creates new Pod. Scheduler assigns it. kubelet runs it. Full cycle: ~30 seconds. Fully automatic — no human needed.
  3. "What happens during a rolling update?" — New ReplicaSet created → scales up 1 new pod → waits for Ready → scales down 1 old → repeats until all new. maxSurge (default 25%) limits extra pods. maxUnavailable (default 25%) limits unavailable pods. Zero downtime — traffic always hits healthy pods.

10.1 Declarative Model — You Say WHAT, Not HOW

This is the most important mental model shift in Kubernetes. In the old world, you told servers what to DO. In Kubernetes, you tell the cluster what you WANT.

❌ Imperative (The Old Way)
# SSH into each server and run commands: ssh server1 "docker pull anihpj:v1" ssh server1 "docker stop anihpj-old" ssh server1 "docker run -d -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v1" ssh server2 "docker pull anihpj:v1" ssh server2 "docker run -d -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v1" # What if server1 fails? Manual intervention!
✅ Declarative (The K8s Way)
# Write what you WANT in a YAML file: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment spec: replicas: 3 template: spec: containers: - image: anihpj:v1 ports: [{containerPort: 8000}] # kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml # K8s figures out HOW to make it happen!
🔄 The Reconciliation Loop — K8s' Secret Sauce

Kubernetes continuously runs a loop: Observe current state → Compare to desired state → Act to eliminate differences → Repeat forever. This is why K8s self-heals — if a Pod crashes, the loop detects "actual=2, desired=3" and creates a new one. No human intervention needed.

10.2 From kubectl to Running Pod — The 8-Step Journey

You type kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml. What happens next is a beautifully orchestrated sequence involving every major K8s component.

🚀 Complete Deployment Sequence — 8 Steps
Step 1 👨‍💻
You run: kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml (declaring: 3 replicas of anihpj:v1 on port 8000)
Step 2 🌐
kubectl converts YAML→JSON, authenticates, sends HTTPS POST to kube-apiserver:6443
Step 3 🔍
API Server validates (YAML syntax, namespace exists, RBAC OK), then writes Deployment object to etcd
Step 4 📋
Deployment Controller sees new Deployment → creates a ReplicaSet object (anihpj-7d8f9c6b5)
Step 5 📦
ReplicaSet Controller sees desired=3 pods, actual=0 → creates 3 Pod objects in etcd (Status: Pending, Node: none)
Step 6 🎯
Scheduler watches for unassigned Pods → FILTERS nodes (enough CPU/RAM?), SCORES nodes (least loaded?), ASSIGNS best node: Pod1→worker-1, Pod2→worker-2, Pod3→worker-3
Step 7 🏗️
kubelet on worker-2 sees assigned Pod → tells containerd to pull anihpj:v1 → containerd creates container with CPU/RAM limits, network namespace → starts gunicorn on :8000
Step 8 ✅
kubelet reports Pod=Running to API Server → etcd updated. kubectl get pods shows 3/3 Running! 🎉
🔑 Key Insight: Controllers Create Objects, Scheduler Assigns Nodes, Kubelet Runs Containers

Each component has ONE job. The Deployment Controller only creates ReplicaSets. The ReplicaSet Controller only creates Pods. The Scheduler only assigns nodes. The kubelet only runs containers on its node. This separation of concerns is what makes K8s modular, debuggable, and extensible.

🔬 Deep Dive: The Reconciliation Loop — K8s' Secret Sauce

Every controller in Kubernetes runs the same infinite loop. Understanding this ONE pattern explains ALL K8s behavior:

  1. WATCH: The controller opens a long-lived HTTP connection to the API Server (watch API). It says "Tell me whenever a Deployment changes." The API Server streams events — created, updated, deleted — in real time. No polling needed.
  2. COMPARE: An event arrives: "Deployment anihpj updated — replicas changed from 3 to 5." The controller reads the CURRENT state (how many ReplicaSets and Pods exist for this Deployment?) and compares it with the DESIRED state (5 replicas of template X).
  3. ACT: There's a gap — only 3 pods exist, we need 5. The controller calls the API Server: "Create 2 more Pods with these specs." It doesn't run pods — it just creates Pod objects in etcd. The scheduler and kubelet do the rest.
  4. REPEAT: The controller goes back to watching. If nothing changes, nothing happens. This is why K8s is "eventually consistent" — there might be a brief moment where desired ≠ actual (3 pods exist, 5 desired), but the controller WILL close the gap.

Critical insight: Controllers NEVER directly manipulate running containers. They ONLY create/update/delete API objects in etcd. Physical changes (starting containers) happen through the scheduler→kubelet→CRI chain. This levels of indirection is what makes K8s so robust — controllers are just manipulating data, not infrastructure.

🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam asks "How does K8s achieve self-healing?" The answer: the reconciliation loop. Controllers constantly compare desired state (in etcd) with actual state (reported by kubelets) and take action to close any gap. This is not a scheduled job — it's a continuous, event-driven process.

10.3 Self-Healing in Action — The anihpj Crash Recovery

This is Kubernetes' most impressive feature — and it happens automatically, without any human intervention.

💚 Self-Healing Timeline — Pod Crash to Recovery
T+0s 💥
anihpj Pod on worker-2 crashes (out of memory — OOMKilled). Container process terminated.
T+5s 👁️
kubelet on worker-2 detects container stopped, reports Pod status change to API Server.
T+10s 📋
ReplicaSet Controller observes: desired=3, actual=2 → creates NEW Pod object in etcd.
T+15s 🎯
Scheduler sees unassigned Pod → picks healthy worker-3 → assigns Pod to worker-3.
T+25s 🏗️
kubelet on worker-3 pulls image, creates container, starts gunicorn.
T+30s ✅
New Pod is Running! 3/3 replicas restored. Users never noticed the crash. No human needed!

10.4 Rolling Update — Deploying anihpj v2 Without Downtime

🔄 Rolling Update — v1 → v2 with Zero Downtime
Phase 1: Before Update
3 Pods running anihpj:v1. All traffic served by v1.
Phase 2: Update Triggered
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj anihpj-container=anihpj:v2 → Deployment creates NEW ReplicaSet for v2.
Phase 3: Rolling (Pod by Pod)
OLD ReplicaSet scales down (3→2→1→0). NEW ReplicaSet scales up (0→1→2→3). Traffic flows to both during transition.
Phase 4: Complete
OLD ReplicaSet: 0 pods (kept for rollback). NEW ReplicaSet: 3 pods running anihpj:v2. Users never saw downtime!
💡 If v2 Has Bugs — Rollback in Seconds!

kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj — This instantly reverts to v1. The old ReplicaSet is still there (scaled to 0), so K8s just scales it back up and scales v2 down. No image rebuild, no redeployment — just a ReplicaSet scale operation. This is why K8s keeps revision history by default (10 revisions).

🔑 maxSurge and maxUnavailable — Controlling the Rolling Update Speed

Two parameters control how aggressive your rolling update is:

  • maxSurge: How many EXTRA pods (above desired count) can exist during the update. Default: 25%. Example: with 4 replicas and maxSurge=25%, at most 5 pods (4+1) can run during the update — Kubernetes creates 1 new pod before terminating 1 old pod.
  • maxUnavailable: How many pods can be UNAVAILABLE during the update. Default: 25%. Example: with 4 replicas and maxUnavailable=25%, at most 1 pod can be down during the update — Kubernetes never has fewer than 3 pods serving traffic.

Strategy trade-offs: High maxSurge + low maxUnavailable = FASTER update but uses MORE resources temporarily. Low maxSurge + high maxUnavailable = SLOWER update but uses FEWER resources. The defaults (25%/25%) are balanced for most workloads.

📊 Chapter 10 — Full Request Flow: Key Takeaways

📝 Declarative Model

You declare WHAT you want (YAML). K8s figures out HOW. Reconciliation loop: Observe→Compare→Act→Repeat forever.

🚀 8-Step Journey

kubectl→API Server→etcd→Deployment Controller→ReplicaSet Controller→Scheduler→kubelet→Container Runtime→Running Pod.

💚 Self-Healing

Pod crashes → kubelet detects → ReplicaSet creates new Pod → Scheduler assigns → kubelet starts → 30s total recovery. Zero human touch.

🔄 Rolling Update

New ReplicaSet scales UP while old scales DOWN. Traffic flows to both during transition. Zero downtime. Rollback in seconds.

🔑 Component Roles

Controllers CREATE objects. Scheduler ASSIGNS nodes. Kubelet RUNS containers. Each has one job — separation of concerns.

📦 Revision History

K8s keeps 10 revisions by default. Old ReplicaSets stay (scaled to 0). Rollback = just scaling the right ReplicaSet.

🛠️ Deployment Reality

Every time you kubectl apply, this 8-step sequence fires. Understanding it helps you debug: "Pod stuck Pending?" → scheduler issue. "Container keeps crashing?" → check application logs, not K8s. "Rolling update taking forever?" → adjust maxSurge/maxUnavailable. Knowing the flow makes you a faster troubleshooter.

You need to mentally walk through the 8 steps and identify where the chain is broken. The reconciliation loop concept appears across multiple domains.

You declare WHAT ("3 replicas"), K8s figures out HOW. Enables self-healing. Contrast: imperative = step-by-step commands.

📝 Chapter 10 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What is the key difference between imperative and declarative approaches in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Imperative: you specify HOW (step-by-step commands). Declarative: you specify WHAT (desired state in YAML), and K8s figures out HOW.

Explanation

Declarative enables self-healing — if reality drifts from declaration, K8s automatically corrects it without human intervention.

Q2
After kubectl apply, which component stores the Deployment in the cluster database?
Show Answer
Answer

kube-apiserver writes to etcd. The API server validates the request, then stores the Deployment object in etcd.

Explanation

Only the API server talks to etcd. kubectl talks to the API server; the API server persists to etcd.

Q3
Which controller creates ReplicaSets from Deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

The Deployment Controller (part of kube-controller-manager). It watches for new Deployments and creates corresponding ReplicaSets.

Explanation

Hierarchy: Deployment → Deployment Controller creates → ReplicaSet → ReplicaSet Controller creates → Pods.

Q4
How does the Scheduler decide which node to place a Pod on?
Show Answer
Answer

Two phases: Filtering (which nodes HAVE enough CPU/RAM, no taints, match selectors?) then Scoring (which node is BEST — least loaded, best spread?). The highest-scoring node wins.

Explanation

The scheduler doesn't run Pods — it only decides WHERE. The kubelet on the target node actually starts the container.

Q5
What happens when a Pod crashes in a Deployment with replicas: 3?
Show Answer
Answer

The ReplicaSet Controller detects desired=3 but actual=2, and creates a new Pod. The Scheduler assigns it to a healthy node, and kubelet starts it. Total recovery: ~30 seconds, fully automatic.

Explanation

This is self-healing — the reconciliation loop in action. No human intervention needed.

Q6
During a rolling update, how does Kubernetes ensure zero downtime?
Show Answer
Answer

K8s creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version and gradually scales it up while scaling the old ReplicaSet down. Both versions run simultaneously during the transition, so traffic is always served.

Explanation

maxSurge and maxUnavailable control how many extra/new pods can exist during the update.

Q7
How do you instantly roll back a Deployment to the previous version?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl rollout undo deployment/NAME. K8s keeps old ReplicaSets (scaled to 0) — rollback simply scales the old one up and the new one down.

Explanation

No image rebuild needed. Old ReplicaSet already has the correct Pod template. Rollback = scale operation, takes seconds.

Q8
What is the role of kubelet in the Pod creation process?
Show Answer
Answer

kubelet watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node, then tells the container runtime to pull the image and start the container. It also reports Pod status back to the API server.

Explanation

kubelet is the "dock worker" — it's the agent that actually does the work of running containers on each node.

Q9
How many ReplicaSets exist after a successful rolling update from v1 to v2?
Show Answer
Answer

Two: the old ReplicaSet (v1, scaled to 0 pods) and the new ReplicaSet (v2, scaled to 3 pods). The old one is kept for rollback purposes.

Explanation

K8s keeps revision history (default: 10). Each revision has its own ReplicaSet. Old ones stay at 0 replicas until cleanup.

Q10
What would happen if the kube-scheduler failed while you deployed a new application?
Show Answer
Answer

New Pods would stay in Pending state (no node assigned). The ReplicaSet Controller still creates Pod objects, but without the scheduler, they never get a node. Existing Pods continue running normally.

Explanation

Each component failure has different impacts. Scheduler failure = new Pods can't start, but existing workloads are unaffected.

Pods are great, but you never deploy individual Pods in production. You use Deployments — the most common Kubernetes resource — which manage Pods through ReplicaSets. Deployments give you scaling, rolling updates, rollbacks, and self-healing. This chapter covers everything you need to run anihpj reliably in production.

🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 11

Deployments are the most-used workload resource. 4 key questions:

  1. "What is the Deployment hierarchy?" — Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. Deployment manages ReplicaSets (for rollouts). ReplicaSet ensures correct number of Pod replicas. You create a Deployment; it creates ReplicaSets; they create Pods.
  2. "Horizontal vs Vertical scaling — which is cloud native?" — Horizontal (HPA): more pods (scale out). Vertical (VPA): bigger pods (scale up). Cloud native favors HORIZONTAL — more resilient (no single pod is critical), elastic (scale down when idle), K8s-native (built into HPA).
  3. "How does rollout undo work?" — Old ReplicaSets are kept at 0 replicas (not deleted). kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj → scales up previous ReplicaSet → scales down current. Rollback is as fast as scaling — seconds.
  4. "Recreate vs RollingUpdate — when to use each?" — Recreate: stops ALL old pods first, then starts new. DOWNTIME. Use when app can't handle two versions running simultaneously. RollingUpdate (DEFAULT): gradual replacement, zero downtime. Use for stateless web apps (like anihpj).

11.1 What is a Deployment?

A Deployment is the most common way to run applications on Kubernetes. You declare "I want 3 copies of anihpj running at all times," and the Deployment ensures it stays that way — through crashes, node failures, and updates.

📊 Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod Hierarchy
Deployment (Fleet Manager)
"I want 3 replicas of anihpj:v2, with rolling updates" — manages the big picture: version, replicas, update strategy
ReplicaSet (Ship Class)
"Ensure exactly 3 Pods matching this template exist" — watches Pod count, creates/deletes to match desired number
Pods (Individual Ships)
Pod-abcde, Pod-fghij, Pod-klmno — actual running instances of anihpj. Ephemeral, replaceable.
🔑 You Almost NEVER Create ReplicaSets Directly

Deployments manage ReplicaSets automatically. When you update a Deployment (new image version), it creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales the old one down. You never manually create or edit ReplicaSets — the Deployment controller handles everything.

11.2 Deployments for anihpj — A Complete Example

📝 Complete Deployment YAML for anihpj
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-deployment
  labels:
    app: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3                     # "I want 3 copies of anihpj"
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj                 # Which Pods does this Deployment manage?
  template:                       # Pod template (same as Pod YAML minus apiVersion/kind)
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-container
        image: registry.io/anihpj:v2
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: "postgres://anihpj:pass@db-service:5432/anihpj"
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"

11.3 Scaling Applications — Horizontal vs Vertical

📈 Horizontal Scaling (Scale OUT/IN)

kubectl scale deployment anihpj --replicas=5

More Pods → distributed across nodes. Better fault tolerance (lose one pod, others still serve). No node resource limit (pods spread across many nodes). The Kubernetes-native way to scale.

More capacityBetter HAK8s-native
📊 Vertical Scaling (Scale UP/DOWN)

Edit Deployment → increase CPU/RAM limits per pod.

Bigger Pods → same number of pods, more resources each. Limited by node capacity (pod can't exceed node). Requires pod restart. Useful when app can't be horizontally scaled.

More resourcesLimited by nodeNeeds restart
🎯 KCNA Tip: Horizontal = More Cows, Vertical = Bigger Cow

Horizontal scaling is the cloud native way — cattle, not pets. More cheap, replaceable pods > one big, precious pod. Kubernetes makes horizontal scaling trivial (kubectl scale), while vertical scaling requires pod restarts and has node limits.

11.4 Rolling Updates and Rollbacks

StrategyBehaviorDowntimeUse Case
RollingUpdate (default)Replace pods one-by-one. Old + new run simultaneously during transition.✅ ZeroWeb apps, APIs — anything that must stay available
RecreateKill ALL old pods first, then create ALL new pods.❌ YesDatabases, stateful apps that can't have two versions running
🔑 Essential Rollout Commands
  • kubectl set image deployment/anihpj anihpj-container=anihpj:v2 — Trigger a rolling update
  • kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj — Watch the update progress
  • kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj — Instant rollback to previous version
  • kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj --to-revision=2 — Rollback to specific revision
  • kubectl rollout pause/resume deployment/anihpj — Pause/resume a rollout

11.5 Deployment Status and History

📜 Revision History — Every Change is Saved
Revision 1
Initial deployment: anihpj:v1, replicas=3. ReplicaSet: anihpj-7d8f9c (scaled to 3)
Revision 2
Updated image: anihpj:v2. NEW ReplicaSet: anihpj-8e9g0d (scaled to 3). OLD ReplicaSet: anihpj-7d8f9c (scaled to 0 — kept for rollback)
Rollback!
kubectl rollout undo → K8s scales OLD ReplicaSet back to 3, NEW to 0. Revision 2 → Revision 3 (rollback creates a new revision!)
📋 Key Commands for History
  • kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj — See all revisions with change-cause
  • kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj --revision=2 — See details of a specific revision
  • Default: K8s keeps 10 revisions (configurable via revisionHistoryLimit)
  • Add --record flag or annotation to capture the command that triggered each revision

📊 Hierarchy

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. Deployment manages version+replicas. ReplicaSet ensures exact Pod count. Pods are the actual instances.

📈 Scaling

Horizontal = more pods (kubectl scale). Vertical = bigger pods (edit resources). Horizontal is cloud native — cattle, not pets.

🔄 Rolling Update

Default strategy. Zero downtime. Old+new pods run simultaneously. maxSurge and maxUnavailable control speed.

⏪ Rollback

kubectl rollout undo → instant rollback. Old ReplicaSets kept at 0 replicas. Rollback = scale operation, takes seconds.

📜 History

10 revisions stored by default. Each revision = a ReplicaSet. Rollback creates a new revision (doesn't delete history).

📝 YAML

replicas, selector, template (Pod spec). Deployment YAML = Pod YAML wrapped in deployment management layer.

Deployments are your daily driver in Kubernetes. Every anihpj update: kubectl set image → kubectl rollout status → verify with kubectl get pods. If something breaks: kubectl rollout undo. Scaling for traffic: kubectl scale --replicas=10. This is the 90% workflow of running apps on K8s.
