Chapter 12: Scheduling — How Kubernetes Decides Where Pods Run

You've declared "I want 3 anihpj pods." But where do they actually run? The scheduler makes that decision — filtering and scoring every node to find the best fit. You can influence this with resource requests, node selectors, affinity rules, and taints/tolerations. This chapter teaches you how to guide the scheduler to place your pods exactly where you want them.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🎯 Scheduling 🔧 Configuration

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How the scheduler works — Filtering + Scoring = Best Node
  • ✅ Resource requests and limits — how they affect scheduling and runtime
  • ✅ Node selectors and affinity — controlling WHERE pods go
  • ✅ Taints and tolerations — the VIP access system for nodes
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Container Orchestration 22%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 12
  • Scheduler Phases — Filtering (which nodes CAN?) then Scoring (which is BEST?). Know this two-phase process.
  • Requests vs Limits — Requests = guaranteed minimum (scheduler uses for placement). Limits = maximum allowed (CPU throttled, Memory OOMKilled).
  • Affinity Types — nodeSelector (simple), nodeAffinity (advanced expressions), podAffinity (co-locate), podAntiAffinity (spread — key for HA).
  • Taints & Tolerations — Taint on node = "No entry." Toleration on pod = "VIP pass." Control plane has default taint — that's why your pods don't run there.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 12

Scheduling determines WHERE pods run. 4 key questions:

  1. "What is the scheduler's two-phase process?" — Filtering: which nodes CAN run this pod? (enough CPU/memory, no taint conflicts, node selector match). Scoring: of the qualifying nodes, which is BEST? (least requested ratio, pod spreading, custom priorities). Assign to highest-scoring node.
  2. "Requests vs Limits — what's the difference?" — Requests = GUARANTEED minimum (scheduler uses this for bin-packing). Limits = MAXIMUM allowed (CPU throttled above limit, memory OOMKilled above limit). Pod with no requests can be scheduled anywhere but may be evicted first.
  3. "What are Taints and Tolerations?" — Taint on node = restriction ("only special pods here"). Toleration on pod = permission ("I'm allowed on tainted nodes"). Control plane has NoSchedule taint. Tolerations DON'T guarantee scheduling to a node — they just allow it. Use nodeAffinity to attract.
  4. "nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity vs podAffinity?" — nodeSelector: simple key=value match ("disktype=ssd"). nodeAffinity: advanced expressions (In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt). podAffinity: co-locate pods together. podAntiAffinity: spread pods across nodes/zones for HA.

12.1 The Scheduler's Job — Filter, Score, Assign

The scheduler watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node. For each Pod, it runs a two-phase process:

🎯 Scheduler Decision Flow
🔍
FILTER

Which nodes CAN run it? Enough CPU/RAM? No taints? Matching nodeSelector? Node is Ready?

→
⭐
SCORE

Which node is BEST? Least loaded? Best spread of pods? Affinity preferences match?

→
📌
ASSIGN

Set pod.spec.nodeName = "worker-2". kubelet on worker-2 sees the assignment and starts the container.

12.2 Resource Requests and Limits

📥 Requests (Minimum)

What the container is guaranteed. The scheduler uses this to decide where to place the pod. If no node has enough request capacity, the pod stays Pending.

resources: requests: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "250m"
📤 Limits (Maximum)

What the container is allowed to use. Enforced by kubelet/cgroups. CPU: throttled if exceeded. Memory: OOMKilled if exceeded.

resources: limits: memory: "512Mi" cpu: "500m"
🔑 CPU and Memory Units
  • CPU: Measured in millicores. 100m = 0.1 CPU core = 10% of a core. 1000m = 1 full core.
  • Memory: Measured in bytes. Mi (Mebibytes), Gi (Gibibytes). 256Mi = ~268 MB.
  • Best Practice: Always set requests and limits. Without them, pods can starve each other or consume all node resources.
🔑 QoS Classes — How K8s Prioritizes Pods Under Pressure

Kubernetes assigns every Pod a Quality of Service (QoS) class based on its requests and limits:

  • Guaranteed (Highest Priority): Every container has BOTH requests AND limits set, AND they are EQUAL for CPU and memory. These pods are last to be killed when the node runs out of resources. Use for production-critical workloads.
  • Burstable (Medium Priority): Requests are set but limits are different (or some containers have no limits). Can burst above requests when resources are available. Killed after BestEffort pods but before Guaranteed.
  • BestEffort (Lowest Priority): No requests or limits set at all. First to be killed when the node is under memory pressure. Use ONLY for development or truly disposable workloads.

KCNA Tip: Know the 3 QoS classes and their priority order. The exam may ask "Which pod gets killed first under memory pressure?" — answer: BestEffort pods die first, Guaranteed pods survive longest.

12.3 Node Selectors and Affinity

MechanismHow It WorksFlexibilityExample
nodeSelectorSimple key-value match. Pod only runs on nodes with matching label.Basic (equals only)disk: ssd → only SSD nodes
nodeAffinityRich expressions: In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt. "Required" (hard) or "Preferred" (soft).Advanced"Require zone=us-east-1a, prefer SSD"
podAffinitySchedule pods NEAR other pods. "Run near the cache pod."Co-locationRun anihpj-web near anihpj-redis
podAntiAffinitySchedule pods AWAY from other pods. "Don't run on the same node."Spread-outSpread anihpj replicas across nodes for HA
🎯 Production Pattern: podAntiAffinity for High Availability

Use podAntiAffinity to ensure your anihpj replicas spread across different nodes. If one node fails, only ONE replica goes down — the others continue serving. Without anti-affinity, all 3 replicas might land on the same node (single point of failure).

12.4 Taints and Tolerations — VIP Access for Nodes

🚫 Taint (on Node)

"No pods allowed here!" — applied to a node to REPEL pods that don't have the matching toleration.

kubectl taint nodes gpu-node gpu=true:NoSchedule # Effect: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute
🎫 Toleration (on Pod)

"I can handle that taint" — added to a Pod to ALLOW it on tainted nodes.

tolerations: - key: "gpu" operator: "Equal" value: "true" effect: "NoSchedule"
🔑 Why Your Pods Don't Run on Control Plane Nodes

The control plane has a default taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule. Only system pods (with the matching toleration) can run there. Your anihpj pods don't have this toleration — so they're automatically kept off the control plane. This is a security and stability feature.

📊 Chapter 12 — Scheduling: Key Takeaways

🎯 Scheduler

Filter → Score → Assign. Filters out impossible nodes, scores remaining ones, picks the best.

📥 Requests

Minimum guaranteed resources. Scheduler uses requests for placement. Pod stays Pending if no node has enough.

📤 Limits

Maximum allowed resources. CPU: throttled. Memory: OOMKilled. Always set both requests and limits.

🏷️ Selectors/Affinity

nodeSelector (simple), nodeAffinity (advanced), podAffinity (co-locate), podAntiAffinity (spread — essential for HA).

🚫 Taints

Applied to nodes — "No entry!" Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute.

🎫 Tolerations

Applied to pods — "VIP pass." Only pods with matching tolerations can run on tainted nodes.

💼 Chapter 12 — In Daily Work

You set resource requests/limits in every Deployment. You use podAntiAffinity to spread replicas for HA. You taint GPU nodes and add tolerations to ML training pods. When pods get stuck Pending, you check: did I request too much? Is there a taint blocking? Does my nodeSelector match any nodes?

12.5 Well-Known Labels, Annotations & Taints — K8s Conventions

Kubernetes has well-known labels, annotations, and taints that tools and controllers recognize automatically. These trigger specific behavior in the cluster — not just arbitrary key-value pairs.

🏷️ Essential Well-Known Labels
LabelExamplePurpose
app.kubernetes.io/nameanihpjApplication name. Used by Helm, Kustomize, dashboards.
app.kubernetes.io/instanceanihpj-prodUnique instance. Distinguishes multiple deploys of same app.
app.kubernetes.io/versionv2.1.0Current version. Used for canary and rollbacks.
app.kubernetes.io/componentweb, api, dbComponent within architecture. Organizes microservices.
app.kubernetes.io/managed-byhelmTool managing this resource. Helm auto-sets on releases.
kubernetes.io/hostnameworker-01Node hostname. Auto-set by kubelet.
kubernetes.io/archamd64, arm64CPU architecture. Target ARM vs x86 nodes.
topology.kubernetes.io/zoneus-east-1aAvailability zone. Use with podAntiAffinity for HA across zones.
🚫 Well-Known Taints (Auto-Applied by Node Controller)
Taint KeyEffectTrigger
node-role.kubernetes.io/control-planeNoSchedulePrevents regular pods on control plane nodes
node.kubernetes.io/not-readyNoExecuteNode not ready — pods evicted after 300s
node.kubernetes.io/unreachableNoExecuteNode unreachable — pods evicted after 300s
node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressureNoScheduleLow disk — no new pods scheduled
node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressureNoScheduleLow memory — prevents OOM situations
🔑 KCNA Scenario Matching
  • "Pod won't schedule on control plane" → Control plane has NoSchedule taint; pod needs toleration
  • "Spread pods across availability zones" → podAntiAffinity with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
  • "ARM pod fails on amd64 nodes" → nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/arch: arm64
  • "Node goes down, how long until pods move?" → node.kubernetes.io/unreachable taint with 300s tolerationSeconds
🎯 KCNA Insight: Recognize app.kubernetes.io/* as the standard labeling convention. Know that kubernetes.io/* labels are auto-set. Understand that taints like node.kubernetes.io/not-ready are automatically applied by the node controller — you don't create them manually.
🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 12
🎯 Filter+Score

Filter: which nodes CAN run this pod? (resources, taints, affinity). Score: which node is BEST? Assign to highest scorer.

📏 Requests/Limits

Requests = guaranteed minimum (scheduler uses). Limits = maximum cap (CPU throttled, mem OOMKilled). Always set both.

🚫 Taints

Taint on node = restriction. Toleration on pod = permission. Control plane has NoSchedule taint. Tolerations don't guarantee — use affinity to attract.

🧲 Affinity

nodeSelector: simple key=value. nodeAffinity: advanced expressions. podAffinity: co-locate pods. podAntiAffinity: spread for HA.

📝 Chapter 12 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What are the two phases of the Kubernetes scheduler's decision process?
Show Answer
Answer

Filtering (which nodes CAN run the pod?) and Scoring (which node is BEST?). The highest-scoring node wins.

Explanation

The scheduler doesn't run pods — it only assigns them to nodes. The kubelet on the target node does the actual work.

Q2
What is the difference between resource requests and limits?
Show Answer
Answer

Requests: minimum guaranteed (scheduler uses for placement). Limits: maximum allowed (CPU throttled, memory OOMKilled if exceeded).

Explanation

Requests = what you're promised. Limits = what you're allowed to burst to. Always set both.

Q3
What does 500m CPU mean?
Show Answer
Answer

500 millicores = 0.5 CPU cores = 50% of one core. 1000m = 1 full core. "m" stands for millicores.

Explanation

This is the standard unit for CPU in Kubernetes. Memory uses Mi/Gi.

Q4
What is the simplest way to ensure a Pod only runs on nodes with SSD disks?
Show Answer
Answer

Use nodeSelector with disk: ssd. The pod will only be scheduled on nodes that have the label disk=ssd.

Explanation

nodeSelector is simple key-value matching. nodeAffinity gives more flexibility with operators like In, NotIn, Exists.

Q5
How do you ensure anihpj replicas are spread across different nodes?
Show Answer
Answer

Use podAntiAffinity — "don't schedule this pod on a node that already has a pod with label app=anihpj."

Explanation

This is a production best practice. Without anti-affinity, all 3 replicas might accidentally land on the same node.

Q6
What is a taint in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A node property that repels pods unless they have a matching toleration. Effects: NoSchedule (don't schedule new pods), PreferNoSchedule (try to avoid), NoExecute (evict existing pods).

Explanation

Taint = "No Entry" sign on a node. Toleration = "VIP Pass" on a pod.

Q7
Why don't your application pods run on control plane nodes by default?
Show Answer
Answer

The control plane has a default taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule. Your pods don't have the matching toleration, so they're excluded.

Explanation

This protects the control plane from being overwhelmed by application workloads. Only system pods have the toleration.

Q8
What happens if a container exceeds its memory limit?
Show Answer
Answer

The container is OOMKilled (terminated by the Linux OOM killer). K8s restarts it according to the pod's restartPolicy.

Explanation

CPU limit: throttled (slowed down, not killed). Memory limit: OOMKilled (process terminated). This is a critical distinction.

Q9
What's the difference between required and preferred node affinity?
Show Answer
Answer

Required: HARD rule — pod WON'T be scheduled if no node matches. Preferred: SOFT rule — scheduler tries but will schedule elsewhere if no match.

Explanation

Required = must match (like nodeSelector). Preferred = nice to have but not mandatory.

Q10
A Pod stays in Pending state with "0/3 nodes are available." What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

No node meets the pod's requirements — possible causes: resource requests too high, nodeSelector doesn't match any node, taints on all nodes without tolerations, or nodes are simply full.

Explanation

kubectl describe pod will show the exact reason in the Events section. Check resource requests, node selectors, and taints.

Chapter 13: Other Workload Resources — Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets, StatefulSets

Deployments handle the most common case — long-running web apps like anihpj. But Kubernetes has specialized workload resources for other patterns: Jobs for one-time tasks, CronJobs for scheduled tasks, DaemonSets for node-level agents, and StatefulSets for stateful applications like databases.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour ⚙️ Workloads

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Jobs — run-once tasks that must complete successfully
  • ✅ CronJobs — jobs that run on a schedule (cron syntax)
  • ✅ DaemonSets — one pod per node for cluster-wide agents
  • ✅ StatefulSets — for stateful apps needing stable identity and storage
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 13
  • Job vs CronJob — Job = run once. CronJob = run on a schedule (cron syntax). Know the difference and use cases.
  • DaemonSet — Guarantees exactly one Pod per node. Used for agents: log collectors, monitoring, CNI plugins. Know that kube-proxy and CNI run as DaemonSets.
  • StatefulSet — For stateful apps needing stable identity (pod-0, pod-1) and persistent storage per pod. Know the differences from Deployments: ordered names, ordered startup, dedicated PVCs.
  • Job Parameters — completions (total successful runs), parallelism (concurrent pods), backoffLimit (max retries). Exam may ask scenario-based questions.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 13

Beyond Deployments, K8s has specialized workload types. 4 key questions:

  1. "Job vs CronJob — what's the difference?" — Job = run ONCE to completion (DB migration, batch processing). CronJob = run on a SCHEDULE using cron syntax (daily backup at 2 AM, hourly report generation). CronJob creates Job objects at scheduled times.
  2. "What is a DaemonSet and when do you use it?" — One pod per node, guaranteed. Use cases: log collectors (Fluentd), monitoring agents (Prometheus node-exporter), CNI plugins, kube-proxy. New node joins → DaemonSet pod automatically starts on it.
  3. "StatefulSet vs Deployment — which for databases?" — StatefulSet: stable pod name (postgres-0, postgres-1), ordered startup (0→1→2), each pod has OWN PVC (not shared), stable network identity. Deployment: random pod names, shared PVC model. Databases = StatefulSet.
  4. "What are init containers?" — Containers that run BEFORE the main app container, in sequence, to completion. Use cases: wait for database, run migrations, set up config. If init container fails, Pod restarts. They run in order, not in parallel.

13.1 Jobs — Run Once, Then Done

A Job creates Pods that run until they complete successfully. Unlike Deployments (which keep pods running forever), Jobs are for finite tasks.

🎯 Job Characteristics
  • Runs to completion: Pod exits with code 0 → Job is done
  • completions: How many successful runs needed (default: 1)
  • parallelism: How many pods can run simultaneously
  • backoffLimit: How many retries before Job is marked Failed (default: 6)
  • Completed pods are NOT deleted — kept for logs
🛠️ anihpj Use Cases
  • Database migrations: python manage.py migrate
  • Data import: Load job listings from CSV into PostgreSQL
  • Report generation: Generate monthly analytics PDF
  • One-time cleanup: Delete expired job postings

13.2 CronJobs — Run on a Schedule

A CronJob is a Job that runs on a repeating schedule — like Linux cron, but Kubernetes-native.

⏰ Cron Syntax: minute hour day month weekday
# Every day at 2:00 AM
schedule: "0 2 * * *"

# Every hour
schedule: "0 * * * *"

# Every 30 minutes
schedule: "*/30 * * * *"

# Monday at 9 AM
schedule: "0 9 * * 1"

anihpj examples: Nightly database backup at 2 AM. Hourly cleanup of expired sessions. Daily job listing report at 8 AM. Weekly analytics email on Monday.

13.3 DaemonSets — One Pod Per Node

A DaemonSet ensures that all (or some) nodes run a copy of a specific Pod. As nodes are added, pods are automatically added. As nodes are removed, pods are garbage collected.

🎯 Common DaemonSet Use Cases
  • Log collectors: Fluentd, Filebeat — collect logs from every node
  • Monitoring agents: Prometheus Node Exporter, Datadog agent
  • Storage daemons: Ceph, GlusterFS — storage on every node
  • Network plugins: Calico, Flannel, Cilium — CNI runs as DaemonSet
🆚 vs Deployment

Deployment: "I want N replicas, anywhere." Pods can be on any node, density varies.

DaemonSet: "I want EXACTLY ONE pod on every node." Guaranteed coverage — every node gets one.

13.4 StatefulSets — For Stateful Applications

StatefulSets are for applications that need stable identity and persistent storage — unlike Deployments where pods are interchangeable and disposable.

FeatureDeploymentStatefulSet
Pod NamesRandom: anihpj-7d8f-abcdeOrdered: postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2
Pod IdentityInterchangeable — any pod can replace any otherStable — pod-0 is always pod-0, even after restart
StorageShared or none. Pod restart = new empty storageDedicated PVC per pod. pod-0's storage survives pod-0's restart
Startup OrderAll pods start simultaneouslyOrdered: 0→1→2 (scale up), 2→1→0 (scale down)
Network IdentityService load-balances across all podsHeadless Service gives each pod a DNS name: pod-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local
Use CaseStateless web apps (anihpj Django)Databases (PostgreSQL), message queues (Kafka), distributed systems
⚠️ StatefulSets are Complex — Don't Default to Them

StatefulSets are powerful but complex. Use Deployments for stateless apps (web servers, APIs, workers). Only use StatefulSets when you genuinely need stable identity or dedicated persistent storage per pod. Many databases now have operators (e.g., CloudNativePG, Zalando) that manage StatefulSets for you — you may never write one directly.

🎯 When to Use Which Workload — Decision Framework for anihpj

Every anihpj component maps to a specific K8s workload:

  • Deployment: Stateless web apps, APIs — "I want N copies running forever." → anihpj Django server, jobpost API.
  • Job: Finite tasks — "Run once and stop when done." → Database migrations, data imports.
  • CronJob: Scheduled tasks — "Run at 2 AM every day." → Nightly backups, daily cleanup, weekly reports.
  • DaemonSet: Node-level agents — "One copy on every node." → Log collectors, monitoring agents, CNI plugins.
  • StatefulSet: Stateful apps — "Stable identity, dedicated storage." → PostgreSQL, Kafka, Elasticsearch.

📊 Chapter 13 — Other Workloads: Key Takeaways

🏃 Jobs

Run to completion. Finite tasks: migrations, imports, cleanup. Completed pods kept for logs.

⏰ CronJobs

Jobs on a schedule. Cron syntax. Backups, reports, periodic cleanup.

🖥️ DaemonSets

One pod per node. Log collectors, monitoring agents, CNI plugins, storage daemons.

🗄️ StatefulSets

Stable identity + persistent storage. Ordered deployment. For databases and stateful apps.

💼 Chapter 13 — In Daily Work

You use Jobs for anihpj migrations. CronJobs for nightly backups. DaemonSets for cluster-wide monitoring agents (they're usually deployed by platform teams). StatefulSets only when you need state — most of your workloads will be Deployments. Know what each resource is for, and you'll choose the right tool for every job.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 13
🏃 Job

Run to COMPLETION (migrations, batch processing). completions=N runs N successful pods. parallelism=N runs N concurrently.

⏰ CronJob

Job on a SCHEDULE (cron syntax). "0 2 * * *" = daily at 2 AM. Creates Job objects at scheduled times. Use for backups, reports.

👮 DaemonSet

ONE pod per NODE. Auto-adds on new nodes. Use: log collectors, monitoring agents, CNI plugins, kube-proxy.

🗄️ StatefulSet

Stable pod names (pod-0, pod-1), ordered startup, each pod has OWN PVC. For databases, queues, distributed systems.

📝 Chapter 13 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What type of workload is best for a one-time database migration?
Show Answer
Answer

A Job. Jobs run to completion and stop. Perfect for finite tasks like migrations, imports, or cleanup scripts.

Explanation

Deployments keep pods running forever. Jobs are for tasks that should complete and stop.

Q2
What CronJob schedule runs a job every day at midnight?
Show Answer
Answer

"0 0 * * *" — minute=0, hour=0, every day, every month, every weekday.

Explanation

Cron format: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), day of week (0-6, 0=Sunday).

Q3
What ensures exactly one Pod runs on every node in the cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

A DaemonSet. It guarantees every node (or a subset) runs exactly one copy of a Pod. Common for log collectors and monitoring agents.

Explanation

Unlike Deployments (N replicas anywhere), DaemonSets ensure per-node coverage.

Q4
What is the main difference between Deployment and StatefulSet pod names?
Show Answer
Answer

Deployment pods: random names (anihpj-7d8f-abcde). StatefulSet pods: ordered names (postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2). StatefulSet pod names are stable and predictable.

Explanation

Stable identity is critical for stateful apps — pod-0 is always the same logical entity, even after restart.

Q5
What happens to completed Job Pods by default?
Show Answer
Answer

They are NOT deleted — they stay in Succeeded state so you can view their logs. You can configure automatic cleanup with ttlSecondsAfterFinished.

Explanation

This is different from Deployments where old ReplicaSet pods are terminated during updates.

Q6
Which workload type is used to run a CNI plugin like Calico on every node?
Show Answer
Answer

DaemonSet. CNI plugins need to run on EVERY node to set up networking. DaemonSet guarantees exactly one pod per node.

Explanation

Calico, Flannel, Cilium, and kube-proxy all run as DaemonSets.

Q7
In what order do StatefulSet pods start during scale-up?
Show Answer
Answer

Sequentially: pod-0 starts first, must be Ready before pod-1 starts, pod-1 must be Ready before pod-2 starts, etc. Scale-down is reverse: highest index first.

Explanation

This ordered startup is critical for clustered databases where pod-0 is the primary and others are replicas.

Q8
What is a CronJob in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

A Kubernetes resource that creates Jobs on a repeating schedule — like Linux cron. Defined with cron syntax: minute hour day month weekday.

Explanation

CronJobs are perfect for periodic tasks: nightly backups, report generation, cleanup, health checks.

Q9
Why would you use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment for PostgreSQL?
Show Answer
Answer

PostgreSQL needs stable identity (pod-0 is primary, pod-1 is replica) and persistent storage (each pod's data must survive restarts and remain attached to the same pod).

Explanation

Deployments treat pods as interchangeable — they can't guarantee pod-0's data goes to the new pod-0 after a restart.

Q10
How many Pods can run simultaneously in a Job with parallelism: 3 and completions: 10?
Show Answer
Answer

3 Pods at a time. The Job runs up to 3 Pods in parallel. When one completes, a new one starts. Total: 10 successful completions needed.

Explanation

parallelism = max concurrent pods. completions = total successful runs needed. backoffLimit = max retry attempts.

Chapter 14: Kubernetes Networking Fundamentals

Networking in Kubernetes is fundamentally different from traditional networking. Every Pod gets its own IP address — and Pods on any node can communicate with Pods on any other node without NAT. This chapter explains the K8s networking model, CNI plugins that make it work, DNS-based service discovery, and Network Policies that act as a firewall.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🌐 Networking 🔗 Core

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The Kubernetes networking model — flat, pod-to-pod, no NAT
  • ✅ CNI plugins — Calico, Flannel, Cilium and how they enable networking
  • ✅ CoreDNS — how Pods find each other by DNS name
  • ✅ Network Policies — firewalling Pod-to-Pod communication
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Cloud Native Architecture 16%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 14
  • Flat Network Model — Every Pod gets its own IP. Pods communicate directly without NAT. This is THE defining characteristic of K8s networking.
  • CNI is REQUIRED — K8s doesn't ship with networking. You MUST install a CNI plugin. Know the names: Calico, Flannel, Cilium.
  • CoreDNS — Service DNS format: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. This appears in exam questions.
  • NetworkPolicy — Default: all traffic allowed. Policies are ADDITIVE (allow rules only). Need a CNI that supports them (Calico, Cilium — NOT Flannel).
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 14

Networking is a core K8s concept. 4 key questions:

  1. "What are the 3 K8s networking requirements?" — Every pod gets its own IP (no NAT between pods on same node), pods on any node can communicate with pods on any other node (no NAT cross-node), agents (kubelet) can communicate with pods on their own node. This flat model is unique to K8s.
  2. "What is CNI and why is it required?" — Container Network Interface. K8s does NOT ship with networking — you MUST install a CNI plugin. Calico (policy-rich, BGP), Flannel (simple overlay), Cilium (eBPF-based, high performance). Without CNI, pods stay in Pending state.
  3. "What is the DNS format for a Service?" — service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Example: anihpj-web.default.svc.cluster.local. CoreDNS provides this. Pods use DNS for service discovery.
  4. "What is a NetworkPolicy?" — Pod-level firewall. Controls ingress (who can talk TO this pod) and egress (where this pod can talk OUT). Default: all pods can communicate. Policies are allow-only (no deny rules). Requires CNI support (Calico/Cilium).

14.1 The Kubernetes Networking Model — Flat, Pod-to-Pod, No NAT

Kubernetes imposes fundamental requirements on networking: every Pod gets its own routable IP address, and Pods on any node can communicate directly with Pods on any other node — no Network Address Translation (NAT) required.

🌐 The Flat K8s Network Model
Pod Network (10.244.0.0/16 — flat, cluster-wide)
anihpj-web (10.244.1.5) on worker-1 → postgres (10.244.2.9) on worker-2 — DIRECT communication, no NAT!
Node 1 (worker-1: 192.168.1.10)
Pod IPs: 10.244.1.1 → 10.244.1.254. CNI creates routes: traffic to 10.244.1.x goes to worker-1
Node 2 (worker-2: 192.168.1.11)
Pod IPs: 10.244.2.1 → 10.244.2.254. CNI creates routes: traffic to 10.244.2.x goes to worker-2
Physical Network
Underlay network routes traffic between nodes. CNI encapsulates or routes pod traffic through it.
🔑 The 3 K8s Networking Requirements
  1. Pods can communicate with ALL other Pods on any node without NAT.
  2. Agents on a node (kubelet, system daemons) can communicate with ALL Pods on that node.
  3. Pods see their own IP as the same IP that other Pods see (no source NAT to node IP).

14.2 CNI — Container Network Interface

Kubernetes doesn't provide networking out of the box. The CNI (Container Network Interface) is a plugin system — you install a CNI plugin, and it makes the networking model work.

CNI PluginApproachNetworkPolicyBest For
CalicoBGP routing (no overlay). High performance.✅ YesProduction, performance-critical, policy-heavy
FlannelSimple overlay (VXLAN/host-gw). Easy setup.❌ NoLearning, simple deployments
CiliumeBPF-based. Advanced observability + security.✅ YesCloud-native, security-focused, large scale
WeaveMesh overlay. Encrypted by default.✅ YesSimple setup with encryption needs
🔑 CNI is MANDATORY — Without It, Pods Can't Communicate

When you set up a cluster with kubeadm, you must install a CNI plugin AFTER cluster initialization. Until the CNI is running, all Pods are stuck in Pending state (CoreDNS won't work either). This is the #1 thing to check when a new cluster has networking issues.

🔑 kube-proxy Modes — iptables vs IPVS

kube-proxy has two main modes for routing Service traffic to Pods:

  • iptables (default): Uses Linux iptables rules. Each Service creates rules on every node. Simple and reliable. BUT: for thousands of Services, the rule table grows huge, and updates are O(n) — slow. Good for small-to-medium clusters.
  • IPVS (IP Virtual Server): Uses the Linux IPVS kernel module — a Layer 4 load balancer built into the kernel. Supports multiple scheduling algorithms (round-robin, least connections, etc.). Scales to 10,000+ Services. O(1) lookups. Recommended for large clusters.

KCNA Tip: Know that iptables is default, IPVS is better at scale. The exam may ask which mode to use for large clusters.

14.3 DNS in Kubernetes — CoreDNS

Pods come and go, and their IPs change. You never hardcode pod IPs. Instead, you use DNS names — and CoreDNS (running in kube-system) provides name resolution.

🔍 DNS Resolution — From Name to IP
📛
Pod queries DNS

"What is postgres-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local?"

→
🔍
CoreDNS resolves

Checks Service registry → finds ClusterIP: 10.96.100.50

→
📡
Returns IP

Pod connects to 10.96.100.50:5432 → kube-proxy routes to healthy PostgreSQL Pod

📝 DNS Name Structure

service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local

  • service-name: The Service's name (e.g., postgres-service)
  • namespace: The namespace (e.g., anihpj)
  • svc.cluster.local: Fixed suffix for cluster-internal services

Within the same namespace, you can use just the service name: postgres-service.

14.4 Network Policies — The Kubernetes Firewall

By default, ALL Pods can communicate with ALL other Pods. Network Policies let you restrict this — like a firewall for Pod-to-Pod traffic.

❌ Without NetworkPolicy

Any Pod can talk to any Pod. Database is accessible from everywhere in the cluster. A compromised frontend Pod can directly access the database.

✅ With NetworkPolicy

Only anihpj-web Pods can talk to PostgreSQL Pods on port 5432. Redis only accessible from web Pods on port 6379. Everything else is BLOCKED.

🔑 NetworkPolicy Rules
  • Ingress: Who can send traffic TO my Pods?
  • Egress: Where can my Pods send traffic TO?
  • Pod Selector: Which Pods does this policy apply to?
  • Default: All traffic is ALLOWED. Policies only RESTRICT. You need a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium — NOT Flannel).

📊 Chapter 14 — Networking: Key Takeaways

🌐 Flat Network

Every Pod gets its own IP. Pod-to-pod communication without NAT. Pods see their real IPs.

🔌 CNI

Plugin system for networking. Calico (BGP, high perf), Flannel (simple overlay), Cilium (eBPF, advanced). Must install one!

🔍 CoreDNS

DNS-based service discovery. Format: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local. Runs as Deployment in kube-system.

🛡️ NetworkPolicy

Pod-level firewall. Ingress/egress rules. Default: allow all. Requires CNI that supports it (Calico/Cilium).

📝 DNS Shortcuts

Same namespace: just service-name. Different namespace: svc.ns. Full: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local.

⚠️ CNI Required

Without CNI, pods can't communicate. CoreDNS stays Pending. #1 cause of new cluster networking issues.

💼 Chapter 14 — In Daily Work

You configure your anihpj Deployment to reach PostgreSQL at postgres-service:5432 — not an IP. CoreDNS resolves the name. If services can't communicate, you check: is CoreDNS running? Is the CNI plugin healthy? Are NetworkPolicies blocking traffic? Understanding the networking model is essential for debugging connectivity issues.

14.X Ports and Protocols — Essential K8s Networking Reference

For Kubernetes to function, specific ports must be open on control plane and worker nodes. The KCNA exam may ask about firewall requirements — knowing the key ports helps you reason about cluster communication.

🔌 Essential Kubernetes Ports
ComponentPortProtocolDirectionUsed By
kube-apiserver6443TCP (TLS)Inboundkubectl, kubelet, controllers, all components
etcd (client)2379TCPInboundkube-apiserver → etcd
etcd (peer)2380TCPBidirectionaletcd ↔ etcd (Raft consensus)
kubelet API10250TCPInboundkube-apiserver → kubelet (logs, exec, metrics)
kubelet read-only10255TCPInboundMetrics (deprecated, use 10250)
kube-scheduler10259TCPInboundHealth checks, metrics
kube-controller-manager10257TCPInboundHealth checks, metrics
NodePort Services30000-32767TCP/UDPInboundExternal traffic to NodePort Services
CoreDNS53UDPInboundDNS queries from all pods
Calico (BGP)179TCPBidirectionalInter-node routing (if using BGP mode)
🔑 KCNA Memory Hook — The "Big 4" Ports

You don't need to memorize every port. Focus on these four:

  • 6443 — API Server (the front door — EVERYTHING talks to this)
  • 2379/2380 — etcd (client/peer — the database ports)
  • 10250 — kubelet API (how API Server gets logs, execs into containers)
  • 30000-32767 — NodePort range (external access range)
🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam may present a scenario: "You can't access the cluster via kubectl." Likely cause: port 6443 (API Server) is blocked by a firewall. Or "etcd cluster is healthy but API Server can't connect" → port 2379 blocked. Think in terms of which component talks to which on what port.
🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 14
🌐 Flat Network

Every pod gets its own routable IP. Pods communicate directly WITHOUT NAT across nodes. The defining K8s networking principle.

🔌 CNI Required

K8s ships WITHOUT networking. MUST install CNI plugin: Calico (policy-rich), Flannel (simple), Cilium (eBPF). No CNI = pods stay Pending.

🔒 NetworkPolicy

Pod-level firewall. Ingress + egress rules. Default: ALL traffic allowed. Policies are ADDITIVE (allow only). Requires Calico/Cilium.

📡 CoreDNS

Cluster DNS. svc.ns.svc.cluster.local → Service ClusterIP. Watches API for new Services. CNCF Graduated. Runs in kube-system.

📝 Chapter 14 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What is the fundamental requirement of the Kubernetes networking model?
Show Answer
Answer

Every Pod gets its own IP address, and Pods on any node can communicate with Pods on any other node without NAT (Network Address Translation).

Explanation

This flat network model is THE defining characteristic of K8s networking. It enables simple service discovery and direct pod-to-pod communication.

Q2
What does CNI stand for and why is it required?
Show Answer
Answer

Container Network Interface — a plugin system. K8s doesn't ship with networking built in; you MUST install a CNI plugin to enable Pod-to-Pod communication.

Explanation

Without CNI, pods can't communicate across nodes and CoreDNS stays Pending. CNI is mandatory.

Q3
Which CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer

Calico, Cilium, Weave support NetworkPolicy. Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy.

Explanation

If you need NetworkPolicy, you can't use Flannel alone. You must choose Calico, Cilium, or combine Flannel with a policy engine.

Q4
What is the full DNS name format for a Kubernetes Service?
Show Answer
Answer

service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local

Explanation

Within the same namespace, you can just use service-name. Cross-namespace: svc.ns. Full format: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local.

Q5
What provides DNS resolution in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

CoreDNS — it runs as a Deployment in kube-system and provides service discovery by resolving Service names to ClusterIPs.

Explanation

CoreDNS watches the API server for new Services and automatically creates DNS records for them.

Q6
By default, can all Pods communicate with each other in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes — by default, all Pods can communicate with all other Pods across all namespaces. NetworkPolicies are needed to RESTRICT this.

Explanation

NetworkPolicies are additive (allow rules only). If no policies exist, all traffic is allowed. Once you create a policy, only explicitly allowed traffic passes.

Q7
What are the two types of NetworkPolicy rules?
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress (traffic TO the pod) and Egress (traffic FROM the pod). Combined with pod selectors and namespace selectors for fine-grained control.

Explanation

Ingress = who can call me. Egress = who can I call. Both are optional; you can define either or both.

Q8
Why can't you use Flannel if you need NetworkPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer

Flannel is a simple overlay network and does NOT implement NetworkPolicy enforcement. You need Calico, Cilium, or Weave for NetworkPolicy support.

Explanation

This is a common KCNA question. Flannel = simple but limited. Calico/Cilium = full-featured with security policies.

Q9
How do Pods on different nodes communicate without NAT?
Show Answer
Answer

The CNI plugin creates routes or overlays. Example: Calico uses BGP to advertise pod CIDRs between nodes; Flannel uses VXLAN to encapsulate traffic. Pods see each other's real IPs.

Explanation

The CNI plugin is responsible for ensuring every node knows how to reach every pod IP. This is what enables the flat network model.

Q10
A pod in the "dev" namespace wants to reach a Service named "api" in the "prod" namespace. What DNS name should it use?
Show Answer
Answer

api.prod.svc.cluster.local — service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

Explanation

Cross-namespace communication requires the full DNS name. Same-namespace: just "api" is enough.

Chapter 15: Services — How Users and Pods Find Each Other

Pods are ephemeral — they get new IPs when restarted. You can't rely on pod IPs. Services solve this by providing a stable IP address and DNS name that never changes, automatically routing traffic to healthy Pods. This chapter covers all 4 Service types plus Ingress — the smart HTTP router.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🌐 Networking 🔗 Services

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why Services exist — the ephemeral Pod problem
  • ✅ All 4 Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName
  • ✅ How ClusterIP works — stable IP, kube-proxy, load balancing
  • ✅ NodePort for simple external access (port 30000-32767)
  • ✅ LoadBalancer for production external access (cloud integration)
  • ✅ Ingress — Layer 7 HTTP routing with host/path rules
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Cloud Native App Delivery 8%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 15
  • 4 Service Types — Know them: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort (node IP:30000+), LoadBalancer (cloud external LB), ExternalName (DNS CNAME).
  • Port Types — port (Service port), targetPort (container port), nodePort (NodePort range 30000-32767). Know the chain.
  • Service Discovery — Services get DNS names. kube-proxy manages routing rules. This is THE way Pods find each other.
  • Ingress vs Service — Service = Layer 4 (TCP). Ingress = Layer 7 (HTTP routing by hostname/path). One Ingress can expose multiple Services.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 15

Services provide stable networking. 4 key questions:

  1. "What problem do Services solve?" — Pod IPs are EPHEMERAL (change on restart). A Service provides a STABLE virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name that load-balances to healthy pods. Service uses labels to select pods — any pod with matching labels gets traffic.
  2. "What are the 4 Service types and when to use each?" — ClusterIP (DEFAULT): internal only, for pod-to-pod communication. NodePort: exposes on every node's IP at port 30000-32767, for external access without cloud LB. LoadBalancer: provisions cloud load balancer, for production external access. ExternalName: DNS CNAME alias to external service.
  3. "What are the 3 port types in a Service?" — port: the Service's own port (clients connect here). targetPort: the container port the Service forwards to (must match containerPort in pod spec). nodePort: the port on each node (30000-32767, only for NodePort/LoadBalancer). Flow: client → port → targetPort.
  4. "Ingress vs Service — when to use which?" — Service: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), one port per Service, basic load balancing. Ingress: Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), path-based routing (/api → api-service, / → web-service), host-based routing (api.anihpj.com vs anihpj.com), TLS termination. Ingress routes to Services.

15.1 The Problem Services Solve

❌ WITHOUT Services

anihpj Pod has IP 10.244.1.5. Pod crashes → ReplicaSet creates new Pod → new IP: 10.244.2.99. All connections break. You can't hardcode pod IPs — they're ephemeral!

✅ WITH Services

anihpj Service has stable IP 10.96.100.50 and DNS name anihpj-service. Service always routes to healthy Pods behind it. Pod IPs change — the Service IP NEVER changes.

15.2 Service Types — 4 Ways to Expose Your App

TypeAccess FromPort RangeUse Case
ClusterIP (default)Inside cluster ONLYAnyInternal microservices: web→api→db
NodePortNode IP from anywhere30000-32767Dev, debug, simple external access
LoadBalancerInternet (via cloud LB)AnyProduction external access
ExternalNameInside cluster (DNS only)N/AProxy to external service (api.stripe.com)
🔬 Deep Dive: How kube-proxy Actually Routes Traffic

When you create a Service, kube-proxy creates REAL network rules on every node. Here's exactly what happens:

  1. Service Created: You create a Service: "anihpj-service, ClusterIP 10.96.100.50, port 80, target pods with label app=anihpj." This is stored in etcd.
  2. kube-proxy Watches: kube-proxy (running as a DaemonSet on every node) watches the API Server for Service and Endpoint changes. It sees the new Service.
  3. iptables Rules Created (default mode): kube-proxy writes iptables rules on the node. A simplified version: "If a packet arrives with destination 10.96.100.50:80, randomly pick one of these pod IPs [10.244.1.5:8080, 10.244.2.9:8080, 10.244.3.12:8080] and rewrite the destination." This is DNAT (Destination NAT) — the packet's destination IP:port is rewritten from the Service ClusterIP to a specific Pod IP.
  4. IPVS Mode (better performance): In IPVS mode (Linux kernel load balancer), kube-proxy creates a virtual server at 10.96.100.50:80 with real servers being the pod IPs. IPVS supports multiple scheduling algorithms (round-robin, least connections). iptables mode has O(n) rules (one per service-port combination); IPVS has O(1) lookup — important at scale (1000+ services).
  5. Endpoint Updates: When a pod dies and is replaced, the Endpoints object changes. kube-proxy detects this and updates the iptables/IPVS rules within seconds. The old pod IP is removed; the new one is added. This is how Services always route to healthy pods.

🎯 KCNA Insight: The exam asks "How does a Service route traffic to pods?" The answer: kube-proxy maintains network rules (iptables/IPVS) that map the Service ClusterIP to healthy Pod IPs. The key point: kube-proxy is NOT a proxy in the traditional sense — it doesn't sit in the data path. It configures the KERNEL to do the routing. Traffic goes directly from source pod to destination pod; kube-proxy just writes the rules.

15.3 ClusterIP Deep Dive — The Default Service

🔄 ClusterIP — How Traffic Reaches Pods
ClusterIP: 10.96.100.50 (stable, virtual IP)
DNS: anihpj-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → 10.96.100.50
kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS rules on every node)
Round-robin load balances to healthy Pod IPs: 10.244.1.5:8000, 10.244.2.9:8000, 10.244.3.4:8000
Healthy Pods (selected by labels)
Pod-abcde (10.244.1.5), Pod-fghij (10.244.2.9), Pod-klmno (10.244.3.4)
💡 Services Without Selectors — Manual Endpoints

Most Services use label selectors to automatically discover Pods. But you can create a Service without a selector and manually define Endpoints — useful for:

  • External databases: Point a Service to an external PostgreSQL (not in K8s). Pods use the Service name like any internal service.
  • Services in another cluster: Bridge to services in a different K8s cluster.
  • Migration: Gradually migrate from external to in-cluster by updating Endpoints.

Example: Create a Service named "external-db" → manually create an Endpoint pointing to 192.168.1.100:5432 → anihpj connects to external-db:5432 as if it were in-cluster.

15.4 NodePort — Opening a Door on Every Node

NodePort exposes the Service on each Node's IP at a static port (30000-32767). You can reach the Service from outside the cluster via <Any-Node-IP>:<NodePort>.

🔑 The Three Ports in a NodePort Service
  • nodePort: 30080 (on every node's IP — external access)
  • port: 80 (the Service's listening port — internal)
  • targetPort: 8000 (the container's port — where the app listens)

Traffic flow: Internet → NodeIP:30080 → Service:80 → Pod:8000

15.5 LoadBalancer — Production External Access

LoadBalancer creates an external load balancer from your cloud provider (AWS ELB/NLB, GCP LB, Azure LB). It gets a public IP and routes traffic to your Service.

15.6 Ingress — Smart HTTP Routing

Ingress is Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) — it can route based on hostname and URL path. One Ingress can expose multiple Services behind a single IP.
