📊 Chapter 15 — Services: Key Takeaways

🎯 Why Services

Pods are ephemeral — IPs change. Services provide a STABLE IP and DNS name that never changes.

🔒 ClusterIP

Default. Internal only. Stable virtual IP. kube-proxy load-balances to healthy Pods via iptables/IPVS.

🚪 NodePort

Exposes on every node's IP at port 30000-32767. chain: Internet→NodeIP:30080→Service:80→Pod:8000.

☁️ LoadBalancer

Creates cloud provider LB. Gets public IP. Production external access. Used with Ingress for HTTPS.

🧭 Ingress

Layer 7 HTTP routing. Host/path rules. One IP → multiple Services. Needs Ingress Controller (nginx).

🔍 Discovery

DNS: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local. kube-proxy manages routing. Labels connect Services to Pods.

💼 Chapter 15 — In Daily Work

Every anihpj component gets a Service: ClusterIP for internal APIs, LoadBalancer for external access, Ingress for HTTP routing. Your Django settings use postgres-service:5432 — a DNS name, not an IP. When a Pod restarts and gets a new IP, the Service automatically updates. This is why you never hardcode IPs in K8s.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 15
🔗 ClusterIP

DEFAULT. Internal-only virtual IP. Pods reach Service at this IP. Stable across pod restarts. Used for pod-to-pod communication.

🚪 NodePort

Exposes on every node's IP at port 30000-32767. NodeIP:30001 → Service. For external access without cloud LB.

☁️ LoadBalancer

Provisions cloud load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP LB). Public IP → Service. Production external access. Builds on NodePort.

🛤️ Ingress

Layer 7 HTTP routing. Path-based: /api→api-svc, /→web-svc. Host-based: api.x.com vs x.com. TLS termination. Requires Ingress Controller.

📝 Chapter 15 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
Why are Services needed in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods are ephemeral — they get new IPs when restarted. Services provide a stable IP and DNS name that automatically routes to healthy Pods behind them.

Explanation

Services are the abstraction that makes service discovery possible in a world of constantly changing Pod IPs.

Q2
What is the default Service type if you don't specify one?
Show Answer
Answer

ClusterIP — internal-only access. The Service gets a stable virtual IP only reachable from within the cluster.

Explanation

ClusterIP is the most common type. It's used for internal microservice communication.

Q3
What port range does NodePort use?
Show Answer
Answer

30000-32767 — assigned to each node. External traffic to NodeIP:NodePort is forwarded to the Service.

Explanation

You can specify a port or let K8s auto-assign one from this range.

Q4
How does kube-proxy route traffic to healthy Pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Using iptables or IPVS rules. kube-proxy watches the API server for Service/Endpoint changes and updates routing rules on every node to load-balance to healthy Pod IPs.

Explanation

kube-proxy is the traffic cop. It ensures Service IP → Pod IP mapping is always up to date.

Q5
Which Service type creates a cloud provider load balancer?
Show Answer
Answer

LoadBalancer. It provisions an external load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP LB, Azure LB) that gets a public IP and routes traffic to the Service.

Explanation

LoadBalancer builds on NodePort — it creates a NodePort Service first, then configures the cloud LB to forward traffic.

Q6
What is the difference between Service (L4) and Ingress (L7)?
Show Answer
Answer

Service: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — routes by IP and port. Ingress: Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) — routes by hostname and URL path. One Ingress can expose multiple Services.

Explanation

Use Ingress when you need to route based on URL paths or hostnames. Use Service for simple TCP/UDP exposure.

Q7
How does an Ingress route traffic to different Services?
Show Answer
Answer

Using host-based routing (api.anihpj.com → api-service) or path-based routing (anihpj.com/jobs/ → jobpost-service). An Ingress Controller (nginx, Traefik) enforces these rules.

Explanation

Ingress requires an Ingress Controller — it's NOT built into K8s. You install one (nginx-ingress, Traefik, HAProxy).

Q8
What does ExternalName Service type do?
Show Answer
Answer

Maps a Service to an external DNS name (CNAME). No proxying — just DNS resolution. Example: stripe-api → api.stripe.com.

Explanation

Use when you want pods to access an external service using a K8s Service name, without proxying traffic through kube-proxy.

Q9
In the port chain NodeIP:30080 → Service:80 → Pod:8000, what are the 3 port types called?
Show Answer
Answer

nodePort (30080), port (80), targetPort (8000). nodePort is on every node. port is the Service port. targetPort is the container port.

Explanation

This 3-port concept is a common KCNA question. Memorize: nodePort → port → targetPort.

Q10
You need to expose anihpj to the internet with HTTPS and path-based routing. What should you use?
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress with TLS configured. LoadBalancer gives you external access, but Ingress adds Layer 7 routing (hostname/path) and TLS termination. The production pattern is: Internet → LoadBalancer → Ingress → ClusterIP Services → Pods.

Explanation

The full production chain: DNS → Cloud LB → Ingress Controller → Ingress Rules → Services → Pods. Each layer adds capability.

Chapter 16: Volumes and Persistent Storage

Containers are ephemeral — when they stop, all their data disappears. But your PostgreSQL database, user uploads, and application state need to survive container restarts. Kubernetes provides Volumes, PersistentVolumes (PV), PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC), and StorageClasses to manage storage independently of Pod lifecycles.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 💾 Storage 📂 Data

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why storage is a problem in ephemeral container environments
  • ✅ Volume types: emptyDir, hostPath, PV, PVC, ConfigMap, Secret
  • ✅ How PV and PVC work — the "parking spot" analogy
  • ✅ StorageClasses and dynamic provisioning — storage on demand
  • ✅ What storage anihpj needs: PostgreSQL data, media uploads, static files
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 16
  • PV vs PVC — PV = cluster resource (admin creates). PVC = user request. Think: parking spot (PV) vs. "I need a parking spot" (PVC).
  • Access Modes — RWO (ReadWriteOnce — single node), ROX (ReadOnlyMany), RWX (ReadWriteMany). Know these abbreviations.
  • StorageClass — Enables dynamic provisioning. PVC + StorageClass = automatic PV creation. Reclaim policy: Delete (default) or Retain.
  • Volume Types — emptyDir (temporary, pod lifetime), hostPath (node filesystem, use sparingly), persistentVolumeClaim (durable).
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 16

Storage is critical for stateful apps. 4 key questions:

  1. "PV vs PVC — who does what?" — PV (PersistentVolume): the actual storage resource — admin provisions or StorageClass dynamically creates. PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim): the USER'S REQUEST — "I need 5Gi of fast SSD storage." K8s matches PVC to a PV with sufficient capacity and matching access mode. Think: parking lot (PV) vs parking ticket (PVC).
  2. "What are the 3 access modes?" — RWO (ReadWriteOnce): one node can read/write. Most common. ROX (ReadOnlyMany): many nodes can read. RWX (ReadWriteMany): many nodes can read/write. Know these abbreviations — they appear on the exam.
  3. "What is a StorageClass?" — Enables DYNAMIC provisioning. Instead of admin manually creating PVs, user creates PVC with a StorageClass → K8s automatically provisions the PV. Reclaim policy: Delete (default, removes when PVC deleted) or Retain (PV persists after PVC deletion — manual cleanup needed).
  4. "emptyDir vs hostPath vs PVC — when to use each?" — emptyDir: temporary scratch space, tied to pod lifecycle, deleted when pod is removed. hostPath: mounts a file/directory from the NODE filesystem — use sparingly (pod becomes node-dependent). PVC: persistent, durable storage that survives pod restarts and rescheduling.

16.1 The Storage Problem — Ephemeral Containers

❌ Without Volumes

PostgreSQL container writes data to /var/lib/postgresql/data. Container restarts (crash, node reboot, pod reschedule) → ALL data is GONE. Your production database just vanished.

✅ With Volumes

PostgreSQL writes to a PersistentVolume mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data. Container restarts → new container mounts the SAME volume. Data is exactly as it was. Zero data loss.

16.2 Volume Types Overview

Volume TypeLifetimePersistenceUse Case
emptyDirPod lifetimeDeleted with PodTemporary cache, scratch space, sharing between containers in a Pod
hostPathNode lifetimeSurvives Pod, tied to nodeNode-level logs, Docker socket (use sparingly!)
PersistentVolume (PV)IndependentSurvives everythingDatabases, user uploads, any stateful data
ConfigMapIndependentSurvives PodsConfiguration files, non-sensitive settings
SecretIndependentSurvives PodsPasswords, API keys, TLS certs (use sparingly as volume)

16.3 PersistentVolumes (PV) and PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC)

Think of PVs as parking spots in a garage and PVCs as "I need a parking spot" requests. The admin provisions parking spots (PVs). Users request them (PVCs). Kubernetes matches requests to available spots.

🅿️ PV-PVC Binding — The Parking Spot Analogy
1
Admin Creates PV

"Parking spot #1: 10Gi, SSD, RWO" (Available)

→
2
User Creates PVC

"I need 5Gi, RWO" (Pending — looking for match)

→
3
K8s Matches

PVC 5Gi ≤ PV 10Gi ✅ RWO matches ✅ → BOUND!

→
4
Pod Uses PVC

Pod references PVC → volume mounted → PostgreSQL data persists!

🔑 Access Modes — 3 Options
  • RWO (ReadWriteOnce): Single node can read/write. Most common. Use for PostgreSQL, single-instance databases.
  • ROX (ReadOnlyMany): Many nodes can read. Use for shared config files, read-only datasets.
  • RWX (ReadWriteMany): Many nodes can read/write. Requires shared filesystem (NFS, Ceph). Use for shared uploads, CMS.

16.4 StorageClasses — Storage on Demand

Manually creating PVs for every PVC is tedious. StorageClasses enable dynamic provisioning — when a PVC is created, a PV is automatically provisioned by the cloud provider or storage system.

⚡ Dynamic Provisioning Flow

User creates PVC with StorageClass: "fast-ssd" → StorageClass tells provisioner (AWS EBS, GCE PD) → Provisioner creates actual storage → PV created automatically → PVC bound!

Reclaim Policy: What happens when PVC is deleted? Delete (default — storage is deleted, good for dev). Retain (storage kept, must be manually cleaned — good for production).

16.5 Storage for anihpj — What Needs Persistence

🗄️ Needs Persistent Storage
  • PostgreSQL data: PVC with RWO, fast SSD StorageClass
  • User uploads (resumes): PVC with RWX (shared across web pods)
  • Redis data (optional): PVC for AOF/RDB persistence
📦 Does NOT Need Persistence
  • Application code: In Docker image
  • Static files (CSS/JS): In image or CDN
  • Temporary files: emptyDir or in-memory
  • Session data: Redis (itself may need PVC)
🔄 StatefulSet + PVC = The Perfect Pair for Databases

When you use a StatefulSet, each Pod gets its own dedicated PVC that follows it for life. This is the pattern for running databases on K8s:

  • postgres-0 always mounts postgres-data-postgres-0 PVC — even if the Pod is rescheduled to a different node
  • postgres-1 always mounts postgres-data-postgres-1 PVC — its own dedicated storage
  • You define a volumeClaimTemplates in the StatefulSet spec (not a separate PVC). K8s creates PVCs automatically for each Pod.

KCNA Tip: Deployment + PVC = shared storage (all Pods mount same PVC). StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates = dedicated storage per Pod. Know which pattern to use for which workload.

📊 Chapter 16 — Storage: Key Takeaways

💾 The Problem

Containers are ephemeral. Volumes provide storage with an independent lifecycle that survives container restarts.

🅿️ PV + PVC

PV = cluster storage resource. PVC = user request. K8s matches and binds them. Dynamic provisioning via StorageClass.

🔑 Access Modes

RWO (single node r/w), ROX (many read), RWX (many r/w). RWO is most common. RWX needs shared filesystem.

⚡ StorageClass

Enables dynamic provisioning. PVC + StorageClass = automatic PV. Reclaim: Delete (default) or Retain (production).

📂 Volume Types

emptyDir (pod lifetime), hostPath (node, risky), PV/PVC (durable), ConfigMap/Secret (inject config).

🗄️ anihpj Storage

Persistent: PostgreSQL data, user uploads. Ephemeral: app code, static files, temp files, sessions.

💼 Chapter 16 — In Daily Work

Every database Deployment includes a PVC. You create StorageClasses once per cluster. When a database Pod restarts, the new Pod mounts the same PVC and picks up where the old one left off. This is the foundation of running stateful workloads on Kubernetes.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 16
💾 PV

PersistentVolume = actual storage resource. Admin provisions or StorageClass creates dynamically. Cluster-scoped. Independent of pods.

📋 PVC

PersistentVolumeClaim = USER's request. "I need 5Gi RWO." K8s matches to a PV. Namespace-scoped. Like a ticket for storage.

🏷️ Access Modes

RWO (ReadWriteOnce — single node). ROX (ReadOnlyMany — many read). RWX (ReadWriteMany — many read/write). KCNA expects you to know these abbreviations.

⚡ StorageClass

Enables DYNAMIC provisioning. PVC + StorageClass = auto-created PV. Reclaim: Delete (default) or Retain. Define per provisioner (EBS, NFS).

📝 Chapter 16 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
Why are volumes needed in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Containers are ephemeral — data inside a container is lost when it stops. Volumes provide storage with an independent lifecycle.

Explanation

Without volumes, database data would be lost on every restart. Volumes decouple storage from container lifecycle.

Q2
What is the difference between a PV and a PVC?
Show Answer
Answer

PV (PersistentVolume): A piece of storage in the cluster (admin creates). PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim): A request for storage by a user (like "I need 5Gi of RWO storage").

Explanation

Analogy: PV = parking spot (resource). PVC = "I need a spot" (request). K8s matches PVCs to suitable PVs.

Q3
What does RWO stand for in storage access modes?
Show Answer
Answer

ReadWriteOnce — the volume can be mounted as read-write by a single node. Most common for databases.

Explanation

ROX = ReadOnlyMany (many nodes read). RWX = ReadWriteMany (many nodes read/write, needs shared filesystem).

Q4
What does a StorageClass enable?
Show Answer
Answer

Dynamic provisioning — PVCs automatically create PVs. No need for admins to manually create PVs for every request.

Explanation

StorageClass defines a "class" of storage (fast-ssd, slow-hdd) and a provisioner (AWS EBS, GCE PD) that creates the actual storage.

Q5
What happens to an emptyDir volume when its Pod is deleted?
Show Answer
Answer

The data is permanently deleted. emptyDir's lifetime is tied to the Pod. Use only for temporary data (cache, scratch space).

Explanation

emptyDir = temporary. PV/PVC = persistent. Know which to use for what kind of data.

Q6
What reclaim policy should you use for production database storage?
Show Answer
Answer

Retain — the PV is NOT deleted when the PVC is deleted. This prevents accidental data loss. You must manually clean up later.

Explanation

Delete (default) automatically removes storage when PVC is deleted — dangerous for production. Retain is safer.

Q7
Which volume type mounts a directory from the node's filesystem?
Show Answer
Answer

hostPath — mounts a file or directory from the host node into the Pod. Use sparingly — it ties the Pod to a specific node.

Explanation

hostPath is rarely used except for system daemons (node log collectors, Docker socket access). Not for application data.

Q8
Can two Pods on different nodes use the same RWO volume simultaneously?
Show Answer
Answer

No. RWO (ReadWriteOnce) means only ONE node can mount the volume at a time. For multi-node access, you need RWX (ReadWriteMany).

Explanation

This is a common trap. RWO = single node. If two pods on different nodes need the same volume, use RWX with shared filesystem.

Q9
How does a Pod use a PVC?
Show Answer
Answer

By referencing the PVC in the Pod spec under volumes: persistentVolumeClaim.claimName: my-pvc. The volume is then mounted at the container's mountPath.

Explanation

Pod → references PVC → PVC is bound to PV → PV is the actual storage. The Pod never references the PV directly.

Q10
What storage does anihpj's PostgreSQL pod need?
Show Answer
Answer

A PVC with RWO access mode backed by a fast SSD StorageClass. The database writes to the mounted volume, and data survives pod restarts, node reboots, and rescheduling.

Explanation

PostgreSQL = single instance = RWO is sufficient. Use Retain reclaim policy for production safety.

Chapter 17: ConfigMaps and Secrets — Configuration Management

Hardcoding configuration in your application is a bad practice. It's even worse in Kubernetes where you want the same container image to run in dev, staging, and production — just with different settings. ConfigMaps and Secrets let you separate configuration from code, so you can change settings without rebuilding images.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour ⚙️ Configuration 🔐 Secrets

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why separating config from code is essential for cloud native apps
  • ✅ ConfigMaps — for non-sensitive configuration (DB URLs, feature flags)
  • ✅ Secrets — for sensitive data (passwords, API keys, TLS certs)
  • ✅ How Pods consume configuration — env vars, envFrom, volume mounts
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 17
  • ConfigMap vs Secret — ConfigMap = non-sensitive (DB URLs, feature flags). Secret = sensitive (passwords, API keys, TLS certs). Know what goes where.
  • Secrets are base64 encoded, NOT encrypted! — This is a critical KCNA concept. For production, enable encryption at rest.
  • Consumption Methods — env (individual vars), envFrom (all keys from a ConfigMap/Secret), volume mounts (files). Know all three.
  • Update Behavior — ConfigMaps/Secrets mounted as volumes update automatically (after kubelet sync). env vars do NOT update — pod restart needed.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 17

Configuration management is frequently tested. 4 key questions:

  1. "ConfigMap vs Secret — what data goes where?" — ConfigMap: non-sensitive (database URLs, feature flags, app settings). Secret: sensitive (passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, tokens). NEVER put passwords in ConfigMaps — they're plain text. Secrets are base64-ENCODED (not encrypted) by default.
  2. "Are Secrets actually encrypted?" — NO! Secrets are base64-encoded at rest — which is encoding, NOT encryption. Anyone with etcd access can decode them. For actual encryption, you MUST enable EncryptionConfiguration or use external KMS. This is the #1 KCNA security misconception.
  3. "How do pods consume ConfigMaps/Secrets?" — Three methods: (1) env: individual keys as environment variables, (2) envFrom: ALL keys as env vars from a ConfigMap/Secret, (3) Volume mounts: each key becomes a file in a mounted directory. Volume mounts UPDATE automatically; env vars do NOT.
  4. "What happens when a ConfigMap is updated?" — Volume-mounted ConfigMaps/Secrets update automatically after kubelet sync period (~90 seconds). Environment variables NEVER auto-update — pod restart required. This is a critical exam distinction.

17.1 Why Separate Configuration from Code?

❌ Configuration in Code

settings.py has DEBUG=True hardcoded. To deploy to production, you must change code → rebuild image → redeploy. Every config change = new image build. Dev/staging/prod need different images.

✅ Configuration in ConfigMap

settings.py reads DEBUG from environment variable. SAME anihpj:v2 image used everywhere. ConfigMap sets DEBUG=True in dev, False in prod. Change config → restart pod → done. No rebuild!

17.2 ConfigMaps — Non-Sensitive Configuration

📝 What Goes in ConfigMaps
  • Database URLs (host, port, db name)
  • Feature flags (ENABLE_NEW_UI=true)
  • Environment names (ENV=staging)
  • API endpoint URLs
  • Logging levels (LOG_LEVEL=INFO)
  • Django settings: ALLOWED_HOSTS, DEBUG
🔧 How to Create
  • kubectl create configmap NAME --from-literal=key=value
  • kubectl create configmap NAME --from-file=config.properties
  • From YAML: data section with key-value pairs

17.3 Secrets — Sensitive Configuration

⚠️ Secrets are Base64 Encoded — NOT Encrypted!

This is one of the most important KCNA facts. By default, Secrets are stored as base64-encoded strings in etcd — anyone with etcd access can decode them. For production, you MUST enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration) so Secrets are actually encrypted in etcd.

🔑 Secret Types
  • Opaque (default): Generic key-value pairs. Most common. DB passwords, API keys.
  • kubernetes.io/tls: TLS certificate + private key. Used by Ingress for HTTPS.
  • kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson: Docker registry credentials. Used for pulling private images.

17.4 Environment Variables in Kubernetes — 3 Ways Pods Get Config

MethodSyntaxUpdates Live?Best For
env (individual)env: [{name: X, valueFrom: {configMapKeyRef: ...}}]❌ No (needs restart)Stable config that rarely changes
envFrom (all keys)envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: X}}]❌ No (needs restart)Importing all settings at once
Volume Mount (as files)volumes: [{configMap: {name: X}}]✅ Yes (auto-updated)Config that changes frequently, config files
📝 anihpj ConfigMap Example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
data:
  DEBUG: "False"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "anihpj.com,www.anihpj.com"
  DATABASE_HOST: "postgres-service"
  DATABASE_PORT: "5432"
  REDIS_URL: "redis://redis-service:6379/0"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"

📊 Chapter 17 — ConfigMaps & Secrets: Key Takeaways

🎯 Why Separate

Same image, different config per environment. Change settings without rebuilding. Cloud native best practice.

📝 ConfigMaps

Non-sensitive data. DB URLs, feature flags, env names. Created from literals, files, or YAML.

🔐 Secrets

Sensitive data. Passwords, API keys, TLS certs. Base64 encoded (NOT encrypted!). Enable encryption at rest.

📥 Consumption

env (individual vars), envFrom (all keys), volume mounts (files, auto-update). env vars need pod restart.

⚠️ Secret Security

Default: base64 in etcd = NOT secure. Enable EncryptionConfiguration. Use external secret managers (Vault) for production.

🔄 Updates

Volume mounts: auto-update (~1 min). env vars: need pod restart. Plan accordingly for dynamic config.

💼 Chapter 17 — In Daily Work

Every anihpj Deployment references ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration. DATABASE_URL comes from a Secret. DEBUG and ALLOWED_HOSTS come from a ConfigMap. When you need to change a setting, you update the ConfigMap and restart the pods — no image rebuild, no redeployment, no downtime with rolling updates.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 17
📋 ConfigMap

Non-sensitive config: DB URLs, feature flags, app settings. Plain text. Mount as env vars or volume files. Volume mounts auto-update.

🔐 Secret

Sensitive data: passwords, API keys, TLS certs. Base64 ENCODED (not encrypted!). Enable EncryptionConfiguration for real encryption.

📥 3 Methods

env: individual key→env var. envFrom: ALL keys→env vars. Volume mount: each key→file. Volume mounts auto-update; env vars do NOT.

🔄 Update Behavior

Volume-mounted ConfigMaps update ~90s after change. env vars NEVER auto-update — pod restart required. Critical KCNA distinction.

📝 Chapter 17 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
Why should configuration be separated from container images?
Show Answer
Answer

So the same image can run in dev, staging, and production with different settings. Changing config shouldn't require rebuilding images.

Explanation

This is a core cloud native principle. Code changes rarely; config changes often. They have different lifecycles.

Q2
What types of data go in ConfigMaps vs Secrets?
Show Answer
Answer

ConfigMaps: non-sensitive (URLs, feature flags, env names). Secrets: sensitive (passwords, API keys, TLS certs, tokens).

Explanation

ConfigMap = public config. Secret = private config. Know what goes where for KCNA.

Q3
Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Secrets are only base64-encoded — NOT encrypted. Anyone with etcd access can decode them. Enable encryption at rest for production.

Explanation

This is THE most important Secret security concept for KCNA. Base64 = encoding, not encryption.

Q4
How can a Pod consume a ConfigMap?
Show Answer
Answer

3 ways: env vars (individual keys), envFrom (all keys), volume mounts (as files). Volume mounts auto-update; env vars require pod restart.

Explanation

KCNA expects you to know all three methods and the update behavior differences.

Q5
Do environment variables from ConfigMaps update automatically when the ConfigMap changes?
Show Answer
Answer

No. env vars are set at pod startup and never change. You must restart the pod to pick up new values. Volume mounts auto-update.

Explanation

This is a common trap. Use volume mounts for config that changes frequently. Use env vars for stable config.

Q6
What Secret type is used for Docker registry credentials?
Show Answer
Answer

kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson — used to authenticate to private container registries. Referenced in Pod spec as imagePullSecrets.

Explanation

Secret types: Opaque (generic), kubernetes.io/tls (TLS certs), kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (registry auth).

Q7
How do you create a Secret from literal values?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl create secret generic NAME --from-literal=key=value. Example: kubectl create secret generic db-password --from-literal=password=s3cr3t

Explanation

Similar to ConfigMap creation. Secrets can also be created from files or YAML manifests.

Q8
What does envFrom do in a Pod spec?
Show Answer
Answer

Imports ALL keys from a ConfigMap or Secret as environment variables. No need to list each key individually.

Explanation

envFrom is convenient but can expose unintended keys. Use specific env references for tighter control.

Q9
Where should anihpj's DATABASE_URL be stored?
Show Answer
Answer

In a Secret — it contains the database password. The host and port can go in a ConfigMap, but anything with credentials belongs in a Secret.

Explanation

Pattern: split sensitive parts (password) into Secret, non-sensitive parts (host, port, db name) into ConfigMap.

Q10
How can you improve Secret security beyond base64 encoding?
Show Answer
Answer

Enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration in kube-apiserver), use RBAC to restrict Secret access, and consider external secret managers like HashiCorp Vault or cloud provider secret stores.

Explanation

KCNA expects you to know that base64 is NOT encryption and that additional security measures are needed for production.

Chapter 18: Kubernetes Security Fundamentals

Security in Kubernetes is layered — from the cloud infrastructure down to your application code. This chapter covers the 4 Cs of cloud native security, how K8s authenticates users and service accounts, RBAC for authorization, pod-level security contexts, and Pod Security Standards that enforce hardening policies.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔐 Security 🛡️ Protection

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The 4 Cs of Cloud Native Security: Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code
  • ✅ Authentication — users vs service accounts, and how K8s identifies you
  • ✅ RBAC — Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and the principle of least privilege
  • ✅ Security Context — running containers as non-root, dropping capabilities
  • ✅ Pod Security Standards — Privileged, Baseline, Restricted levels
🎓 KCNA Relevance Kubernetes Fundamentals 46% Cloud Native Architecture 16%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 18
  • 4 Cs — Know the 4 layers: Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code. Each layer assumes the one below is secure.
  • RBAC — Role = namespace-scoped permissions. ClusterRole = cluster-wide. RoleBinding connects subjects to roles.
  • Service Accounts — Every pod gets one. Used for pod-to-API-server authentication. Different from user accounts.
  • Pod Security Standards — Privileged (unrestricted), Baseline (minimal restrictions), Restricted (heavily restricted). Know the three levels.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 18

Security is tested conceptually. 4 key questions:

  1. "What are the 4 Cs of cloud native security?" — Cloud (infrastructure: IAM, firewalls) → Cluster (K8s: RBAC, NetworkPolicies, etcd encryption) → Container (image scanning, no root, read-only FS) → Code (input validation, TLS, secrets). Each layer assumes the one below it is secure. Defense in depth.
  2. "What is RBAC and how does it work?" — Role (namespace-scoped permissions) + RoleBinding (connects user/SA to Role). ClusterRole (cluster-wide) + ClusterRoleBinding. Permissions are ADDITIVE only — no deny rules. Verbs: get, list, create, update, delete, watch.
  3. "ServiceAccount vs User Account — what's the difference?" — ServiceAccount: for PODS (pod-to-API authentication). Automatically mounted at /var/run/secrets. User Account: for HUMANS (kubectl users). Every pod always has a ServiceAccount — default if not specified.
  4. "What are the 3 Pod Security Standard levels?" — Privileged: unrestricted (legacy). Baseline: minimal restrictions (blocks known privilege escalations — default for new clusters). Restricted: heavily restricted (no hostPath, no hostNetwork, must run as non-root, read-only root FS).

18.1 The 4 Cs of Cloud Native Security

🛡️ The 4 Cs Security Pyramid
☁️ Cloud (Infrastructure)
Data center security, network firewalls, IAM roles, encrypted storage. The foundation — if this is compromised, everything above is too.
🏗️ Cluster (Kubernetes)
API Server TLS, etcd encryption, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, Pod Security Standards. Securing the K8s components themselves.
📦 Container
Image scanning, no root, read-only filesystem, minimal base images, vulnerability scanning. Securing what's INSIDE the container.
💻 Code (Application)
Input validation, SQL injection prevention, TLS for communications, secrets management. Application-level security.

18.2 Authentication — Who Are You?

👤 Normal Users

Humans managing the cluster. Authenticated via client certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC (Google, GitHub, Azure AD). Managed OUTSIDE Kubernetes — K8s has no "User" object.

🤖 Service Accounts

Identities for Pods and services INSIDE the cluster. Every Pod gets a ServiceAccount. Used when anihpj Pod needs to call the K8s API. Managed by K8s — created with kubectl create serviceaccount.

18.3 RBAC — Role-Based Access Control

🔐 RBAC — Subject → Binding → Role → Permissions
👤
Subject

User, Group, or ServiceAccount — WHO wants access?

→
🔗
Binding

RoleBinding (namespace) or ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide) — CONNECTS subject to role

→
📋
Role / ClusterRole

WHAT can they do? get pods, list deployments, create services...

🔑 Role vs ClusterRole
  • Role: Namespace-scoped. Permissions only within ONE namespace.
  • ClusterRole: Cluster-wide. For resources that aren't namespaced (nodes, namespaces, PVs).
📋 Common RBAC Verbs — What You Can Allow
  • get, list, watch: Read access. get=single resource, list=all resources, watch=stream changes
  • create, update, patch: Write access. create=new, update=replace, patch=partial update
  • delete, deletecollection: Remove resources

KCNA Tip: Know that RBAC is additive (allow only). There's no "deny" rule. Use `kubectl auth can-i` to test if a subject can perform an action.

18.4 Security Context — Pod-Level Security

❌ Insecure Pod
  • Runs as root (UID 0)
  • All Linux capabilities enabled
  • Writable root filesystem
  • Can escalate privileges
✅ Secure Pod
  • Runs as non-root (UID 1000)
  • Drops ALL capabilities, only adds needed ones
  • Read-only root filesystem
  • Privilege escalation disabled

18.5 Pod Security Standards — Three Levels

LevelDescriptionUse Case
PrivilegedUnrestricted. Anything goes.System pods, CI/CD runners. NOT for application pods.
BaselineMinimal restrictions. Prevents known privilege escalations.Default for most workloads. Good starting point.
RestrictedHeavily restricted. Follows pod hardening best practices.Production workloads with strict security requirements.
🔑 The Full Auth Flow — Authentication → Authorization → Admission Control

Every API request goes through three stages at the API server:

  1. Authentication: "WHO are you?" — Verify identity via cert, token, or OIDC.
  2. Authorization: "WHAT can you do?" — RBAC checks permissions.
  3. Admission Control: "Is this SAFE?" — Mutating (modify request) and Validating (accept/reject). Enforces PSS, quotas, etc.

KCNA Tip: AuthN=identity, AuthZ=permissions (RBAC), Admission=safety checks (PSS, quotas). Each stage can independently reject a request.

📊 Chapter 18 — Security: Key Takeaways

🛡️ 4 Cs

Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code. Defense in depth. Each layer assumes lower layers are secure.

👤 Auth

Users (external OIDC/certs) vs ServiceAccounts (internal, for Pods). Every Pod gets a ServiceAccount.

🔐 RBAC

Subject → RoleBinding → Role → Permissions. Role=namespace, ClusterRole=cluster-wide. Least privilege.

🔒 SecurityContext

runAsNonRoot, drop capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem. Basic hygiene for every pod.

📏 PSS

Privileged → Baseline → Restricted. Increasing security. Use Restricted for production.

🔑 KCNA Focus

Know concepts, not implementation. Understand 4Cs, RBAC objects, PSS levels. No YAML writing for security.

💼 Chapter 18 — In Daily Work

You create a dedicated ServiceAccount for anihpj, bind it to a Role that only allows get/list on pods in the anihpj namespace. You configure securityContext to run as non-root with read-only root filesystem. You set the namespace to enforce Restricted PSS. These are not optional — they're baseline security hygiene.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 18
🛡️ 4 Cs

Cloud→Cluster→Container→Code. Layered defense. Each layer assumes the one below is secure. Defense in depth for cloud native.

👤 RBAC

Role (namespace) + RoleBinding. ClusterRole (cluster-wide) + ClusterRoleBinding. Permissions are ADDITIVE only. No deny rules.

🤖 ServiceAccount

Identity for PODS. Auto-mounted at /var/run/secrets. Every pod has one (default if not specified). Separate from User accounts.

📏 Pod Security

Privileged (unrestricted) → Baseline (minimal) → Restricted (heavily locked down). Enforced at namespace level.

📝 Chapter 18 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
What are the 4 Cs of cloud native security?
Show Answer
Answer

Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code. A layered defense model where each layer assumes the layers below are secure.

Q2
What is the difference between a User and a ServiceAccount?
Show Answer
Answer

Users: humans, managed outside K8s (OIDC, certs). ServiceAccounts: identities for Pods, managed inside K8s. Every Pod gets one.

Q3
What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
Show Answer
Answer

Role: namespace-scoped permissions. ClusterRole: cluster-wide permissions (nodes, PVs, namespaces).

Q4
What does a RoleBinding do?
Show Answer
Answer

Connects a Subject (User, Group, ServiceAccount) to a Role, granting the permissions defined in that Role.

Q5
What does runAsNonRoot: true do?
Show Answer
Answer

Prevents the container from running as root (UID 0). The container will fail to start if the image is configured to run as root.

Q6
What are the three Pod Security Standard levels?
Show Answer
Answer

Privileged (unrestricted), Baseline (minimal restrictions), Restricted (heavily restricted, production-ready).

Q7
What is the principle of least privilege?
Show Answer
Answer

Give a subject ONLY the permissions it needs to do its job — nothing more. This minimizes damage if credentials are compromised.

Q8
Which RBAC object would you use for permissions on Nodes?
Show Answer
Answer

ClusterRole — because Nodes are cluster-scoped resources (not in any namespace).

Q9
What security benefit does readOnlyRootFilesystem provide?
Show Answer
Answer

Prevents the container from writing to its filesystem. Attackers can't install malware or modify binaries even if they compromise the container.

Q10
How do Pods authenticate to the Kubernetes API server?
Show Answer
Answer

Using their ServiceAccount token — automatically mounted into the Pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token.

Chapter 19: Observability — Seeing Inside Your Cluster

You can't fix what you can't see. Observability is the ability to understand what's happening inside your system through logs, metrics, and traces. Kubernetes provides the foundation — stdout/stderr for logs, the Metrics API for resource data — but you add tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and Jaeger to build a complete observability stack.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📊 Observability 🔍 Monitoring

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The 3 pillars of observability: Logging, Metrics, Tracing
  • ✅ How logging works in K8s — kubectl logs, aggregation with Fluentd/Loki
  • ✅ Metrics pipeline: kubelet → Metrics Server → Prometheus → Grafana
  • ✅ Health probes (review) and their role in observability
  • ✅ Autoscaling: HPA (more pods), VPA (bigger pods), Cluster Autoscaler (more nodes)
🎓 KCNA Relevance Cloud Native Observability 8% Kubernetes Fundamentals 46%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 19
  • 3 Pillars — Logging (what happened), Metrics (how much/how fast), Tracing (the journey of a request). Know all three.
  • Tool Mapping — Prometheus=metrics, Grafana=dashboards, Jaeger=tracing, Fluentd/Elasticsearch=logs. Know which tool does what.
  • HPA vs VPA — HPA scales pods OUT/IN (horizontal). VPA scales pods UP/DOWN (vertical). Cluster Autoscaler adds/removes nodes.
  • Metrics Server — Lightweight cluster-wide aggregator. Required for HPA and kubectl top. Doesn't persist data — Prometheus does.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 19

Observability tool mapping is the #1 tested concept. 4 key questions:

  1. "Which tool does what?" — This is THE most common KCNA observability question. Prometheus = METRICS (time-series DB, pull model, PromQL). Grafana = DASHBOARDS (visualization of Prometheus/others). Jaeger = TRACING (distributed request tracking). Fluentd = LOGGING (log aggregation). OpenTelemetry = STANDARD (generates telemetry, exports to backends). NEVER confuse these!
  2. "Monitoring vs Observability — what's the difference?" — Monitoring: watching KNOWN metrics (CPU > 80% = alert). Observability: ability to ask NEW questions from telemetry (metrics + logs + traces). Observability helps you debug issues you DIDN'T anticipate. Monitoring catches what you EXPECTED.
  3. "HPA vs VPA vs Cluster Autoscaler?" — HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): more/fewer PODS based on CPU/memory/custom metrics. VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler): bigger/smaller PODS (more or less CPU/RAM per pod). Cluster Autoscaler: more/fewer NODES when pods can't be scheduled. All three work together!
  4. "What is the Metrics Server?" — Lightweight resource usage aggregator. Required for HPA and kubectl top. Collects CPU/memory from kubelet. Does NOT persist data — just provides real-time snapshots. Prometheus is for historical metrics; Metrics Server is for current usage.

19.1 What is Observability? — The 3 Pillars

📜 Logging

"What happened?" — Application events, errors, debug info. Containers write to stdout/stderr. Aggregated by Fluentd → Elasticsearch/Loki. Viewed in Kibana/Grafana.

📊 Metrics

"How much? How fast?" — CPU, memory, request rate, error rate, latency. Prometheus scrapes metrics from Pods. Grafana visualizes dashboards.

🔍 Tracing

"What was the journey?" — Follow a request across microservices. Jaeger collects spans. See where time is spent, where errors occur.

19.2 Logging — What Your Apps Are Saying

📜 Log Flow in Kubernetes

Container stdout/stderr → kubelet captures → container runtime log files → kubectl logs (direct) OR Fluentd (aggregation) → Elasticsearch/Loki → Kibana/Grafana

kubectl logs POD: simplest way to see logs. Add -f to follow, --tail=50 for last 50 lines, -c CONTAINER for multi-container pods.

19.3 Metrics — Measuring Your System

📊 Metrics Pipeline
📦
Pods

Expose /metrics endpoint

→
⚡
Prometheus

Scrapes metrics every 15-30s

→
📈
Grafana

Dashboards, alerts, visualization

📈 RED Metrics — The 3 Golden Signals
  • Rate: How many requests per second?
  • Errors: What percentage are failing?
  • Duration: How long do requests take? (P50, P95, P99 latency)

19.4 Health Checks and Probes

ProbeQuestionOn FailureObservability Role
Liveness"Is the app alive?"Restart containerDetects deadlocked apps that need restart
Readiness"Ready for traffic?"Stop routing trafficPrevents sending requests to unready pods
Startup"Has boot completed?"Restart containerProtects slow-starting apps from liveness kills

19.5 Resource Monitoring and Autoscaling

📈 HPA

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. Adds/removes PODS based on CPU/memory. "More waiters when the restaurant is busy."

📊 VPA

Vertical Pod Autoscaler. Increases/decreases POD resources. "Bigger plates for hungrier customers."

🖥️ Cluster Autoscaler

Adds/removes NODES when cluster is full/empty. "Open more tables when the restaurant is packed."

📊 Chapter 19 — Observability: Key Takeaways

📜 Logging

stdout/stderr → kubelet → kubectl logs (simple) or Fluentd → Elasticsearch/Loki (production).

📊 Metrics

Prometheus scrapes → Grafana visualizes. RED: Rate, Errors, Duration. Metrics Server for HPA.

🔍 Tracing

Jaeger for distributed tracing. Follow requests across microservices. Identify bottlenecks.

💚 Probes

Liveness (restart), Readiness (stop traffic), Startup (protect slow boot). All contribute to observability.

📈 HPA

Scales pods OUT/IN based on CPU/memory. Needs Metrics Server. "More waiters when busy."

🖥️ CA

Cluster Autoscaler adds/removes nodes. Pods can't be scheduled → add node. Nodes idle → remove node.

💼 Chapter 19 — In Daily Work

You deploy anihpj with Prometheus scraping metrics. Grafana dashboards show request rates, error rates, and latency. kubectl logs helps debug individual pods. HPA is configured to scale anihpj from 3 to 10 replicas when CPU exceeds 70%. Jaeger traces show you exactly where slow requests spend time. This is what production readiness looks like.

🔑 Key Terms Lightning Round — Chapter 19
📊 Prometheus

METRICS collection. Pull model (scrapes HTTP endpoints). TSDB storage. PromQL queries. Grafana visualizes. CNCF Graduated. De facto standard.

📜 Fluentd

LOGGING aggregation. Collects, transforms, routes logs. CNCF Graduated. NOT a metrics tool — Fluentd=logs, Prometheus=metrics.

🔍 Jaeger

Distributed TRACING. Follows request across microservices. Shows latency at each hop. CNCF Graduated. NOT logging or metrics.

📈 HPA/VPA

HPA: more/fewer pods (scale OUT). VPA: bigger/smaller pods (scale UP). Cluster Autoscaler: more/fewer NODES. All 3 work together!

Q10
Where do containers write logs in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

To stdout and stderr. The container runtime captures these, and kubelet makes them available via kubectl logs.

Chapter 20: CI/CD, GitOps, and Deployment Strategies

Building containers is only half the story. Delivering them to production — safely, quickly, and repeatedly — is where CI/CD, GitOps, and deployment strategies come in. This chapter covers the tools and practices that take your anihpj code from a git push to a running production deployment.

🎓 KCNA Relevance Cloud Native App Delivery 8% Cloud Native Architecture 16%
💡 KCNA Exam Tips for Chapter 20

  • GitOps — Git is source of truth. Tools: ArgoCD, Flux. Changes via PR → auto-sync to cluster.
  • Helm — Package manager for K8s. Charts = pre-configured resource bundles. Helm Hub = public chart repository.
🎯 KCNA Exam Hotspot — Chapter 20

Application delivery is a smaller domain (8%) but tests precise concepts. 4 key questions:

  1. "CI vs CD vs CD — what do all three mean?" — CI: Continuous Integration (build + test automatically). CD (Delivery): always deployable, push-button to prod. CD (Deployment): deploy to prod automatically, no human gate. KCNA uses "CD" for Delivery. Remember: CI = test, CD = ready to deploy, CD = auto-deploy.
  2. "4 deployment strategies — which has downtime?" — Recreate: DOWNTIME (stop all old, start all new). Rolling Update: DEFAULT, zero downtime, gradual replacement. Blue-Green: instant switch, instant rollback, 2× resources. Canary: gradual traffic shift (5%→25%→50%→100%), safest, test with real users.
  3. "GitOps push vs pull — what's the difference?" — Push: CI/CD pipeline pushes to cluster (traditional: kubectl apply from Jenkins). Pull (GitOps): agent inside cluster pulls from Git (ArgoCD/Flux). Pull is more secure — no external cluster access needed. Git is always the source of truth.
  4. "What is Helm and why was Tiller removed?" — Helm 3 = no server-side component. CLI talks directly to K8s API. Helm 2 had Tiller (cluster-admin by default — massive security risk). If "Tiller" appears in an answer, it's a distractor. Helm charts = pre-configured K8s resource bundles.

20.1 What is CI/CD?

CI/CD is the automation engine that takes code from a developer's machine to production — without manual steps. It's the heart of modern software delivery.

📖 CI vs CD — What's the Difference?
  • CI (Continuous Integration): Automatically build, test, and validate every code change. Catch bugs early. Developers merge to main often — multiple times per day.
  • CD (Continuous Delivery): Automatically deploy to staging. Every change is "ready to release" with the push of a button. The release decision is still human.
  • CD (Continuous Deployment): Automatically deploy to PRODUCTION. Every passing change goes live — NO human gate. Used by Netflix, Amazon, GitHub.

🎯 KCNA Tip: The exam uses "CD" for Continuous Delivery. You don't need to deploy to production automatically — just be ready to.

🔄 CI/CD Pipeline for anihpj (Fully Automated — ~5-10 Minutes)
💻
Code

git push to main

→
🔨
Build

Docker build anihpj image

→
🧪
Test

Django unit tests + linting

→
📦
Package

Push to Docker registry

→
🚀
Deploy

kubectl apply to K8s cluster

🛠️ Popular CI/CD Tools: GitHub Actions (built into GitHub, most popular), GitLab CI, Jenkins (granddaddy, self-hosted), Tekton (Kubernetes-native), Argo Workflows, CircleCI, Travis CI. KCNA focuses on the CONCEPT, not any specific tool.

20.2 GitOps — Git as the Single Source of Truth

GitOps is a paradigm where Git is the control center for your entire cluster. Instead of running kubectl apply manually, you commit your desired state to Git — and a tool automatically makes the cluster match.

🔄 The GitOps Loop

Developer pushes YAML to Git → ArgoCD/Flux detects change → syncs to K8s cluster → Cluster state matches Git

📤 Push Model

CI/CD pipeline pushes changes to cluster (traditional: Jenkins, GitHub Actions).

📥 Pull Model (GitOps)

Agent INSIDE cluster pulls changes from Git (ArgoCD, Flux). More secure — no external access to cluster API needed.

🎯 Benefits of GitOps
  • Audit trail: git log shows every change, who made it, and when
  • Easy rollback: git revert the bad commit, auto-syncs back
  • Collaboration: Use pull requests for infrastructure changes — just like code
  • Disaster recovery: Lost your cluster? Re-clone the repo and re-sync — everything's in Git
  • Drift detection: If someone manually changes a resource, GitOps auto-corrects it back

20.3 Deployment Strategies — 4 Ways to Ship to Production

Once your CI/CD pipeline builds a new container image, how do you get it running in production? You have 4 strategies — each with different trade-offs between speed, safety, and cost.

🎯 Strategy Decision Matrix — Which One When?
StrategyDowntimeRollback SpeedResource CostRisk LevelBest For
Recreate❌ YESSlowLowHighDev/test only

Blue-Green✅ None⚡ Instant2× NormalLowCritical apps, enterprise
Canary✅ None⚡ InstantSlightly higherLowestHigh-traffic, cautious teams
⚠️ How Kubernetes Actually Does Rolling Updates

When you update a Deployment, K8s creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales it up while scaling the old one down. The maxSurge (default 25%) controls how many extra pods can exist above the desired count during the update. The maxUnavailable (default 25%) controls how many pods can be unavailable. This is why K8s rolling updates are zero-downtime by default — there are always enough healthy pods serving traffic.

🎯 KCNA Tip: You don't need to memorize maxSurge/maxUnavailable values. Just know that Rolling Update = DEFAULT strategy = zero downtime and that K8s manages the pod replacement count automatically.

20.4 Helm — The Kubernetes Package Manager

Helm is like apt, yum, or pip for Kubernetes. Instead of writing 5 YAML files (Deployment + Service + ConfigMap + Secret + PVC), you run helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql — one command, complete database deployment with all dependencies configured.

📦 Helm Architecture (Helm 3 — Tiller REMOVED!)
📊
Chart

Package of K8s resource templates + default values + metadata

→
📤
helm install

CLI renders templates with values, sends to K8s API directly

→
📦
Release

Installed instance tracked as a Secret in the namespace

✅ No server-side component (Tiller removed in Helm 3) ✅ RBAC-safe 🔑 KCNA: Helm 3 is the standard

📦 Helm Core Concepts
  • Chart: Package of pre-configured K8s resources — templates + default values + Chart.yaml metadata
  • Release: An installed instance of a chart in a namespace. Multiple releases from the same chart are possible.
  • Repository: Collection of charts. Artifact Hub (formerly Helm Hub) is the public repository — Bitnami, Elastic, Grafana, etc.
  • Values: Customizable parameters — override defaults: helm install my-db bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret
⚠️ Helm 2 vs Helm 3 — KCNA Only Tests Helm 3!

Helm 2 had Tiller — a server-side component that ran inside the cluster with cluster-admin privileges. This was a massive security risk because Tiller had unrestricted access to the K8s API. Helm 3 removed Tiller entirely — the Helm CLI now talks directly to the K8s API using your kubeconfig credentials. This means Helm operations have the same permissions as the user running them — RBAC-safe by design.

🎯 KCNA Tip: If you see "Tiller" in an answer choice, it's a distractor — Tiller doesn't exist in Helm 3 which is the version tested on KCNA.

20.5 Infrastructure as Code (IaC) for Kubernetes

Manage K8s configuration the same way you manage application code — in version control, with reviews, with automated deployment.

Terraform HCL / Pulumi code / Crossplane YAML

→
📂

→
🔄
Apply

CI/CD runs terraform apply → K8s API

→
✅
Converge

Cluster matches IaC declaration

🏗️ Terraform

Most popular. HashiCorp. HCL language. Declarative. Manages K8s + cloud infra together.

💻 Pulumi

Use real programming languages (Python, TypeScript, Go). Infrastructure as real code.

🔗 Crossplane

K8s-native. CRDs for cloud resources. Declare cloud infra the K8s way.

🎯 KCNA Tip: IaC + GitOps = the dream team. IaC defines the infrastructure, GitOps ensures it matches the cluster. Together: version-controlled, audited, automated infrastructure.

  1. "What are the most important 12-Factor principles?" — III. Config (env vars, never in code). VI. Processes (stateless, share nothing). VII. Port Binding (app binds to port, self-contained). IX. Disposability (fast startup, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM). XI. Logs (write to stdout, let platform route). These 5 appear most on KCNA.
  2. "Service Mesh — what problem does it solve?" — Service-to-service (EAST-WEST) communication. Provides mTLS (automatic), traffic control (retries, timeouts, circuit breaking), observability (metrics, tracing). Sidecar proxy pattern (Envoy in Istio). Mesh ≠ Ingress (which handles NORTH-SOUTH, external→cluster).
  3. "Serverless / FaaS — what is it and what is it NOT?" — You write code; platform handles scaling/servers. Pay-per-invocation. Auto-scales to ZERO. NOT "no servers" — servers still exist, you just don't manage them. K8s-native: Knative. Cloud: Lambda/Azure Functions. Trade-offs: cold starts, time limits, vendor lock-in.
  4. "What's the KCNA certification path?" — KCNA (conceptual, entry) → CKAD (app developer, hands-on) / CKA (administrator, hands-on) → CKS (security, requires CKA). All CNCF certs valid 3 years. Earning a higher cert renews lower ones. PCA, ICA, CGOA are specialized certs for Prometheus, Istio, GitOps.

21.1 Cloud Native Design Principles & The 12-Factor App

Before deploying to Kubernetes, your application needs to be designed for the cloud. The 12-Factor App methodology (created by Heroku co-founder Adam Wiggins) is the gold standard for building portable, scalable, cloud native applications.

🏛️ The Complete 12-Factor App — All 12 Principles
I. Codebase

One codebase per app, tracked in Git. Many deploys (dev/staging/prod) from the same repo.

II. Dependencies

Explicitly declare and isolate. Use requirements.txt, go.mod, package.json. No system packages.

III. Config

Store config in environment variables. NOT in code. anihpj uses .env files.

IV. Backing Services

Treat DB, cache, queue as attached resources. Swap via config change. No code change.

V. Build, Release, Run

Strict separation: Build→Release→Run. No changes at runtime — immutable releases.

VI. Processes

Stateless. Share nothing. Store persistent data in backing services, never in memory/disk.

VII. Port Binding

App binds to a port. Self-contained. Django on :8000. Export HTTP as a service.

VIII. Concurrency

Scale via process model. Gunicorn workers = horizontal scaling. Don't daemonize.

IX. Disposability

Fast startup + graceful shutdown. Pods come and go — app must handle SIGTERM cleanly.

X. Dev/Prod Parity

Keep dev, staging, and production as similar as possible. Same backing services, same tools.

XI. Logs

Treat logs as event streams. Write to stdout/stderr. Let K8s route them — don't manage log files.

XII. Admin Processes

Run admin tasks as one-off processes. Django migrations = kubectl exec or init containers.

🏛️ Three Pillars of Cloud Native Design (KCNA Must-Know)
🔗 Loose Coupling

Services should be independent. Changing one service shouldn't break another. Use well-defined APIs. Each microservice can be deployed, scaled, and updated independently.

🩹 Graceful Degradation

If one component fails, the system continues working partially — not a total crash. Example: if Redis cache goes down, the app falls back to the database — slower, but still running.

💥 Design for Failure

Assume things WILL break. Network partitions, node crashes, container OOM kills. Design with retries, circuit breakers, timeouts, health checks. K8s helps — but your app must cooperate.

21.2 Service Mesh — Networking Decoupled from Code

A Service Mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication. Instead of coding retry logic, TLS, and tracing into every microservice, the mesh does it transparently via sidecar proxies.

🕸️ Service Mesh Architecture — Sidecar Proxy Pattern
🧠 Control Plane

Istiod (Istio) or Linkerd Controller — manages proxy configuration, issues certificates, collects telemetry

Pod A (Service)

🧩 App Container
🔷 Envoy Sidecar

🔒 mTLS →
Pod B (Service)

🔷 Envoy Sidecar
🧩 App Container

Every pod gets a sidecar proxy (Envoy). The control plane tells proxies what to do. All traffic goes through the proxy — mTLS, retries, metrics, tracing — all automatic.

🕸️ What a Service Mesh Provides
🔒 mTLS

Automatic mutual TLS between services. Certificates issued and rotated automatically. Zero code changes.

📊 Observability

Traffic metrics (request rate, latency, error %), distributed tracing across services, access logs — built in.

🛤️ Traffic Control

Load balancing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection (test resilience!), traffic splitting (canary).

CNCF Service Mesh Projects: Istio (Envoy-based, most popular, feature-rich), Linkerd (ultra-lightweight Rust, simplest to operate), Consul Connect (HashiCorp), Kuma (Envoy-based, Kong). 🎯 KCNA: Know that service meshes exist and what problems they solve — not how to configure them.

21.3 Serverless / FaaS — Functions, Not Servers

Serverless ≠ no servers. It means you don't manage the servers — the platform does. You write code, upload it, and the platform handles scaling, patching, and availability. You pay only when your code runs.

📊 The Serverless Spectrum — From Containers to Fully Managed
Containers

You manage everything: OS, runtime, scaling

→
Kubernetes

Orchestrated containers. K8s handles scheduling, scaling

→
K8s Serverless

Knative/OpenFaaS. Scale-to-zero. Event-driven on K8s

→
Fully Serverless

Lambda/Azure Functions. No servers visible. Pay-per-invocation

☁️ Cloud FaaS

AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Run. Upload code → platform runs it on events. Pay-per-invocation (e.g., $0.20 per million invocations). Auto-scales to zero — you pay $0 when idle.

📦 K8s-Native Serverless

Knative — CNCF project. Run serverless workloads on YOUR K8s cluster. Scale-to-zero. Event-driven via CloudEvents. OpenFaaS — functions as a service, simpler than Knative, uses Dockerfiles to build functions. Kubeless — native K8s FaaS (uses ConfigMap for functions). Fission — fast serverless framework with cold-start optimizations.

🎯 KCNA Tip: Know the difference: Containers = you manage runtime + scaling. K8s = orchestrates containers. Serverless = you only write code, platform handles everything. Knative = brings serverless to K8s. Key use cases: Event-driven data processing (image resizing, ETL), API backends with variable traffic, scheduled jobs, chatbots/webhooks.
⚠️ Serverless ≠ Always the Right Choice

Serverless is great for sporadic, event-driven workloads but has trade-offs: Cold starts (latency when scaling from zero), execution time limits (Lambda: 15 min max), vendor lock-in (cloud FaaS uses proprietary APIs). For long-running services with predictable traffic, containers on K8s are usually more cost-effective and portable.

Build container images, design pods, deploy apps with Deployments/StatefulSets, expose with Services/Ingress, use ConfigMaps/Secrets, debug apps. Hands-on terminal exam — you type real kubectl commands.

⚙️ CKA — Administrator

Cluster architecture, install/upgrade clusters, etcd backup/restore, RBAC, networking, storage, troubleshooting. Most respected K8s cert. Requires deep operational knowledge.

🔒 CKS — Security Specialist

Supply chain security, runtime security, system hardening, minimizing microservice vulnerabilities. Requires CKA first. The hardest CNCF exam.

📡 Other CNCF Certs

PCA (Prometheus Certified Associate), ICA (Istio Certified Associate), CGOA (GitOps Associate — ArgoCD/Flux). Specialize in specific CNCF projects.

💡 Recommended Path

KCNA → CKAD → CKA → CKS is the logical progression. CKAD is slightly easier than CKA because it focuses on application development (what you build) vs CKA's cluster administration (everything else). Both are 2-hour hands-on exams. CKS requires CKA as a prerequisite.

📝 Chapter 21 — KCNA Practice Questions (10 MCQs)

Q1
Where does the 12-Factor App methodology say config should be stored?
Show Answer
Answer

In environment variables. Not in code, not in config files committed to Git.

Q2
What pattern does a Service Mesh use to attach a proxy to each pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Sidecar proxy pattern. Each pod gets a proxy container (e.g., Envoy) that handles all network traffic.

Q3
What is Knative?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes-native serverless platform. Runs serverless workloads on K8s with scale-to-zero and event-driven invocation.

Q4
What is the first stage of the Cloud Native Maturity Model?
Show Answer
Answer

Monolithic — single application, manual deployment, no automation.

Q5
Which two KCNA domains together make up 66% of the exam?
Show Answer
Answer

Containers (20%) + Kubernetes Fundamentals (46%). Master these and you pass!

Q6
How does a Service Mesh provide mTLS?
Show Answer
Answer

Automatically, via the sidecar proxy. No code changes needed — the mesh handles certificate issuance and rotation.

Q7
What is the certification path after KCNA?
Show Answer
Answer

CKAD (application developer) or CKA (administrator), then CKS (security specialist).

Q8
What does "stateless processes" mean in 12-Factor App?
Show Answer
Answer

Processes share nothing. Any persistent data MUST be stored in a backing service (database, cache, object store).

Q9
What is FaaS?
Show Answer
Answer

Function as a Service. Upload code, it runs on event triggers. Pay-per-invocation. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions.

Q10
How many questions and what time limit does the KCNA exam have?
Show Answer
Answer

60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes. Plenty of time — average 1.5 minutes per question.

🔄 kubectl Command Workflow — From Your Terminal to the Cluster
🖥️
kubectl CLI

You type a command. Reads ~/.kube/config for cluster address + credentials.

→
🔗
HTTPS + Auth

kubectl sends REST request to API Server with TLS + token/certificate auth.

→
🏛️
API Server

Validates, authenticates, authorizes. Writes desired state to etcd.

→
⚙️
Controllers

Watch for changes, reconcile: Scheduler assigns pod→node, kubelet starts container.

→
✅
Result

Pod runs on a node. kubectl get pods shows the status.

Appendix B: Kubernetes Terminology Glossary

Every important K8s term you'll encounter on the KCNA exam — defined simply. Master these and you'll never be confused by Kubernetes jargon again.

📖 Glossary 🔤 A-Z 🎓 KCNA Essential

B.1 Core Concepts (A-Z)

API Server

Front door to Kubernetes. ALL communication (kubectl, controllers, kubelets) goes through it. Validates and processes REST requests.

Cluster

A set of nodes (machines) running containerized applications, all managed by the Kubernetes control plane.

ConfigMap

Stores non-sensitive configuration data — environment variables, config files, command-line arguments.

Container

An isolated, lightweight package containing an application and ALL its dependencies. Runs the same everywhere.

Control Plane

The "brain" of K8s. Includes API server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager. Manages the entire cluster state.

DaemonSet

Ensures exactly one pod runs on every node (or selected nodes). Used for monitoring, logging, storage agents.

Deployment

Manages ReplicaSets. Handles rolling updates, scaling, and rollback for stateless applications.

etcd

Distributed key-value store. The cluster's memory — stores ALL cluster state and configuration.

Ingress

HTTP/HTTPS routing rules. Routes external traffic to Services based on hostnames and URL paths. L7 load balancing.

Job

Creates pods that run to completion — good for one-time tasks like database migrations or batch processing.

kubelet

Agent running on every node. Communicates with the API server and ensures containers are running in pods.

kubectl

Command-line tool for interacting with the Kubernetes API. Your primary interface to the cluster.

Namespace

A virtual cluster within a physical cluster. Isolates resources. Default namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public.

Node

A worker machine (physical or VM) in the cluster. Runs pods via kubelet + container runtime.

Pod

Smallest deployable unit in K8s. A pod wraps one or more containers that share network and storage.

PersistentVolume (PV)

Cluster-wide storage resource provisioned by an admin. Exists independent of any pod.

PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)

A request for storage by a user. Binds to a PV. Like a pod requests CPU — a PVC requests storage.

ReplicaSet

Maintains a stable set of replica pods. Ensures the specified number of identical pods are always running.

Secret

Stores sensitive data — passwords, tokens, SSH keys. Base64-encoded. Encrypted at rest in etcd (if configured).

Service

A stable network endpoint that sits in front of pods. Provides a consistent IP and DNS name, even as pods come and go.

ServiceAccount

An identity for pods. Used when pods need to communicate with the K8s API. Automatically mounted as a token.

StatefulSet

For stateful applications (databases). Provides stable pod identities, ordered deployment/scaling, and persistent storage per pod.

StorageClass

Defines classes of storage — fast SSD, slow HDD, encrypted. Enables dynamic PV provisioning.

Volume

Storage that outlives individual containers within a pod. Types: emptyDir, hostPath, configMap, secret, PV, CSI.

B.3 Common Confusions — Clarified

Don't Confuse...With...The Difference
PodContainerPod CONTAINS containers (1+). Pod is the scheduling unit; container is the runtime unit.
ServiceIngressService = L4 (TCP/UDP) routing internal to cluster. Ingress = L7 (HTTP/S) routing with host/path rules.
DeploymentStatefulSetDeployment = stateless (any pod is identical). StatefulSet = stateful (each pod has identity + own storage).
ConfigMapSecretConfigMap = non-sensitive (settings, URLs). Secret = sensitive (passwords, tokens, keys). Secrets can be encrypted at rest.
NodePortLoadBalancerNodePort = access via NodeIP:30000-32767 (any node). LoadBalancer = cloud external IP (AWS ELB, Azure LB).
etcdSQL Databaseetcd = distributed consensus key-value store (Raft). Not SQL, not relational. Designed for configuration, not application data.
ReplicaSetDeploymentReplicaSet = ensures N pods exist. Deployment = manages ReplicaSets + rolling updates + rollbacks. You rarely create ReplicaSets directly.
CronJobJobJob = runs once to completion. CronJob = creates Jobs on a schedule (like Linux cron).

🐳 Docker Image Lifecycle — Build → Ship → Run
📝
Dockerfile

Write instructions: FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD

→
🔨
docker build

Build image layers. Each instruction = one layer. Cache accelerates rebuilds.

→
📤
docker push

Upload to registry (Docker Hub, Harbor, ECR). Image becomes shareable.

→
📥
docker pull

Download image on target machine. Only pulls layers not already cached.

→
▶️
docker run

Start container from image. Add a thin writable layer on top.

🏆 Docker Best Practices for KCNA
✅ DO
  • ✅ Use specific image tags (anihpj:v1.2.3 — not :latest)
  • ✅ Combine RUN commands with && to minimize layers
  • ✅ COPY requirements.txt BEFORE source code (layer caching!)
  • ✅ Use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files
  • ✅ Run as non-root user (USER directive)
  • ✅ Use multi-stage builds for smaller production images
  • ✅ Use slim/alpine base images for smaller attack surface
❌ DON'T
  • ❌ Don't use :latest tag in production
  • ❌ Don't store secrets in Docker images (use K8s Secrets)
  • ❌ Don't run containers as root (security risk!)
  • ❌ Don't put database data in containers (use volumes!)
  • ❌ Don't copy your entire project before installing deps
  • ❌ Don't ignore .dockerignore — it speeds up builds
  • ❌ Don't use EXPOSE as security — it's documentation only
🎯 Docker on the KCNA Exam — What You Actually Need to Know

The KCNA exam tests Docker concepts, not hands-on CLI skills. You won't type a single docker build command during the exam. Focus on understanding:

  • Dockerfile instructions: FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD, EXPOSE, ENV — what each does and the order they should appear
  • Layer caching: Why COPY requirements.txt before COPY . . makes builds 10x faster
  • Registry concepts: Docker Hub vs private registries (ECR, ACR, GCR), push vs pull
  • Container vs Image: Image = blueprint (class), Container = running instance (object)
  • Docker vs K8s: Docker builds images; K8s orchestrates containers. K8s no longer uses Docker as its runtime (uses containerd via CRI)

Appendix D: Complete anihpj Docker Setup

A complete, production-ready Docker configuration for the anihpj Django project — including Dockerfile, .dockerignore, docker-compose.yml, and local setup instructions. This is the exact setup we've referenced throughout this guide.

🐍 Django 🐳 Docker 📦 anihpj + jobpost

D.1 Dockerfile — Fully Annotated

🐳 anihpj Dockerfile — Production-Ready
# ─── BASE IMAGE ───────────────────────────────────
FROM python:3.11-slim

# ─── METADATA ─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL maintainer="anihpj-team"
LABEL description="anihpj Django application with jobpost app"

# ─── WORKING DIRECTORY ────────────────────────────
WORKDIR /app

# ─── SYSTEM DEPENDENCIES ──────────────────────────
# Install only what Django + PostgreSQL need
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# ─── PYTHON DEPENDENCIES (Layer Caching!) ──────────
# Copy requirements FIRST — Docker caches this layer
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# ─── APPLICATION CODE ─────────────────────────────
COPY . .

# ─── NON-ROOT USER (Security Best Practice) ───────
RUN useradd -m anihpj && chown -R anihpj:anihpj /app
USER anihpj

# ─── ENVIRONMENT ──────────────────────────────────
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# ─── STATIC FILES ─────────────────────────────────
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ─── EXPOSE & RUN ─────────────────────────────────
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4"]
🔑 Key Design Decisions: (1) Slim base image — smaller attack surface. (2) requirements.txt copied FIRST — leverages Docker layer caching; requirements rarely change. (3) Non-root user — container runs as 'anihpj', not root. (4) Gunicorn with 4 workers — production-grade WSGI server, not Django's dev server.
📖 Dockerfile — Line-by-Line Explanation
FROM python:3.11-slim
Base image: ~150MB Debian + Python. "slim" = minimal (no compilers, docs, dev headers). Always pin a specific version, not :latest.
LABEL maintainer / description
Metadata only — doesn't affect the image. Helps identify who owns this image and what it does.
WORKDIR /app
Creates /app if it doesn't exist. All subsequent COPY, RUN, CMD run from this directory. Cleaner than cd /app.
RUN apt-get update && install... && rm -rf
Installs system deps (gcc for psycopg2, libpq-dev for PostgreSQL). Chained with && to keep as ONE layer. Cleanup in same layer so temp files are truly gone.
COPY requirements.txt .
Copied FIRST before source code. If requirements.txt doesn't change, this layer + the next RUN layer are CACHED — builds go from 5 min to 5 sec!
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir
Installs Django 4.2, djangorestframework, psycopg2, gunicorn. --no-cache-dir keeps the image smaller by not caching downloaded packages.
COPY . .
Copies all source: manage.py, anihpj/, jobpost/, templates/, static/. This layer changes on EVERY code change — that's why deps were copied first.
RUN useradd + USER anihpj
Security: creates non-root user and switches to it. Containers running as root can break out. This is a critical security best practice.
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
Prevents Python from writing .pyc files. Keeps the image smaller and cleaner.
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
Pre-compiles static files (CSS, JS) into one directory. --noinput skips the interactive prompt. Must come BEFORE non-root user if writing to protected dirs.
EXPOSE 8000
Documentation: tells readers the app listens on port 8000. Does NOT publish the port — use -p 8000:8000 at runtime. Purely informational.
CMD ["gunicorn", ...]
The process that runs when the container starts. Gunicorn = production WSGI server. 4 workers handle 4 concurrent requests. Only one CMD per Dockerfile.

D.2 .dockerignore — What NOT to Send to Docker

📋 anihpj .dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.pyo
*.egg-info/

# Virtual Environment
env/
venv/
.venv/

# Git
.git/
.gitignore

# Django
db.sqlite3
staticfiles/
media/
*.log

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# Docker
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
.dockerignore

# Documentation
*.md
docs/

# Environment
.env
.env.*
🔑 Why .dockerignore matters: Every file sent to Docker's build context slows down docker build. Excluding env/ saves hundreds of MB. Excluding .git/ prevents accidentally shipping Git history. Excluding db.sqlite3 keeps your local dev database out of the image.
📋 .dockerignore — What Each Entry Protects
PatternWhat It ExcludesWhy It Matters
__pycache__/ *.py[cod]Python bytecode cacheGenerated at runtime — not needed in image. Would invalidate layer cache.
env/ venv/ .venv/Virtual environment (100MB+)You install deps INSIDE the image via pip. Don't copy your local venv!
.git/ .gitignoreGit historySecurity: don't ship your entire commit history inside the image.
db.sqlite3Local SQLite databaseDev database should never be in production images. Use PostgreSQL.
.env .env.*Environment secretsCRITICAL: .env often contains SECRET_KEY, API keys. Never in images!
.vscode/ .idea/IDE settingsYour editor config doesn't belong in a production container.
Dockerfile docker-compose.ymlDocker configs themselvesNot needed at runtime — just build instructions.

D.3 docker-compose.yml — 3-Service Stack

🐳 anihpj docker-compose.yml — Web + PostgreSQL + Redis
version: '3.8'

services:
  # ─── DJANGO WEB APPLICATION ────────────────────
  web:
    build: .
    container_name: anihpj-web
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj:password@db:5432/anihpj
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
      - DEBUG=False
      - SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY:-changeme}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/staticfiles
      - media_volume:/app/media
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ─── POSTGRESQL DATABASE ───────────────────────
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-db
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=anihpj
      - POSTGRES_USER=anihpj
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${DB_PASSWORD:-password}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ─── REDIS CACHE ───────────────────────────────
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-redis
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:
  static_volume:
  media_volume:
🔑 Key Patterns: (1) depends_on with condition: service_healthy — web waits for PostgreSQL to be truly ready, not just started. (2) Named volumes — data persists across container restarts. (3) restart: unless-stopped — auto-restart on crash. (4) Alpine images — smallest possible images for PostgreSQL and Redis.
🔧 Production Compose vs Simple Compose — What We Added
FeatureSimple (kcna.txt)Production (This Guide)Why
DB Imagepostgres:15postgres:15-alpineAlpine = ~70MB smaller, fewer CVEs
Healthcheck❌ None✅ pg_isready every 10sdepends_on with condition: service_healthy needs this
depends_ondb, redis (start order only)db: service_healthy, redis: service_startedWaits for DB to accept connections, not just start
restart❌ None✅ unless-stoppedAuto-restart on crash. Survives docker daemon restart.
SECRET_KEY❌ Hardcoded✅ ${SECRET_KEY:-changeme}Uses env var with fallback. Never hardcode secrets.
container_name❌ Auto-generated✅ Explicit namesPredictable names for docker compose exec and logs.

D.4 How to Build and Run Locally

🏗️ anihpj 3-Service Architecture — How They Connect
🌐 User Browser

http://localhost:8000/jobs/

⬇️ Port 8000 ⬇️
🐍 Django Web (anihpj-web)

Gunicorn + Django + jobpost app | Port 8000

⬇️ postgres://anihpj:password@db:5432/anihpj ⬇️
⬇️ redis://redis:6379/0 ⬇️
🐘 PostgreSQL (anihpj-db)

Port 5432 | Persistent volume

⚡ Redis (anihpj-redis)

Port 6379 | Session + Cache

🚀 Quick Start — 6 Steps
  1. Navigate: cd anihpj/
  2. Build: docker compose build
  3. Start: docker compose up -d
  4. Migrate: docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate
  5. Visit: http://localhost:8000/jobs/
  6. Stop: docker compose down (when done)

🔧 Useful extras: Create superuser: docker compose exec web python manage.py createsuperuser | View logs: docker compose logs -f | Shell into web: docker compose exec web bash

Appendix E: KCNA Exam Preparation Guide

Everything you need to know about registering for, preparing for, and passing the KCNA exam — from logistics to study plans to exam-day checklists.

E.1 Exam Registration & Logistics

📋 Registration Details
  • Register at: training.linuxfoundation.org/certification
  • Cost: $250 USD (frequently on sale for $125-175 during events like KubeCon, Black Friday)
  • Includes: 1 exam attempt + 1 free retake (if you don't pass on the first try)
  • Format: Online-proctored — take from home or office
  • System requirements: Webcam, microphone, Chrome/Chromium browser, stable internet (2+ Mbps)
  • ID check: Government-issued photo ID required (passport, driver's license)
  • Validity: 3 years from date of passing
🎯 KCNA Exam Scoring & Time Strategy
⏱️ Time Budget

90 minutes ÷ 60 questions = 1.5 min/question. First pass: answer easy (30 sec), flag hard. Last 20 min: review flagged. Never spend >2 min on one question.

🏆 Scoring

~75% to pass (~45/60). No penalty for wrong answers — GUESS if unsure. Unanswered = wrong. Flag and return if stuck.

🧠 Strategy

Eliminate obviously wrong first. Watch for "NOT", "EXCEPT". If 2 answers are opposites, one is usually right. "All of the above" is often correct.

⚠️ Important: Exam Rules

Closed book. No notes, no second screen, no phone, no papers on your desk. Your webcam must show your face at all times. You cannot leave the room. A clear glass of water is allowed. The proctor will ask you to scan your room with the webcam before starting.

E.4 Frequently Asked Questions

❓ Do I need K8s experience?

No! KCNA is designed for beginners. This guide assumes zero prior knowledge.

❓ Is there hands-on lab work?

No — it's 100% multiple-choice. Conceptual understanding is key.

❓ Can I use notes during the exam?

No — it's closed book. Everything must be in your head.

❓ How long until I get results?

Immediately after completing the exam. Certificate PDF within 24 hours.

❓ What if my internet drops?

The exam pauses. You can reconnect and resume — your timer is preserved.

❓ How long is the cert valid?

3 years from date of passing. Renew by retaking the KCNA exam or earning a higher CNCF certification (CKA, CKAD, CKS — any of these resets your KCNA clock too).

❓ How do I renew my KCNA?

You have two options: (1) Retake the KCNA exam before it expires, or (2) Earn a higher CNCF cert (CKA, CKAD, or CKS) — this automatically renews KCNA. You'll get a reminder email 90 days before expiry.

❓ Can I reschedule my exam?

Yes — you can reschedule up to 24 hours before your exam time at no cost. Use the Linux Foundation portal. Within 24 hours, you may forfeit the attempt.

📅 Week 1: Foundations (8 hrs)

  • Day 3-4: Ch3 (Docker Deep Dive) + Ch4 (Docker Compose)

  • Day 7: Review + Practice MCQs (Ch7-12)
📅 Week 3: Advanced (8 hrs)

  • Day 3-4: Ch15 (Services) + Ch16 (Storage)
  • Day 5-6: Ch17 (ConfigMaps/Secrets) + Ch18 (Security)
  • Day 7: Review + Practice MCQs (Ch13-18)
📅 Week 4: Delivery + Review (8 hrs)
